items.title: Discos’ Band A of sorrow
items.description: By SUNNY IKHIOYA The time for another round of elections is drawing close. The people seem to be unaware of where to hold the government responsible. Politicians are only concerned about personal insults and vain things. But in recent times, they have upped the tempo to begin to talk about petroleum subsidy and palliatives for the common man. One thing that the people have not been sensitive about is the fraudulent manner in which the electricity distribution companies are taking advantage of the government’s inability to monitor their activities properly. The NERC, the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission, is there, invisible to consumers. We have also been informed that some states have established their own regulatory commissions, like Lagos, Enugu and others. They, too, do not seem to be making their presence felt. Just like petrol, electricity is also at the centre of a people’s development. A country that cannot independently generate its own electricity is as good as staying dead at the bottom. Manufacturers cannot produce, skilled and small businesses will not grow, and the people will remain unhappy. Presently, the high-handedness of the electricity distribution companies is a principal cause of the downward drop in our poverty ratings. The middle class has been completely wiped out, businesses are dying, and no one seems to care. You know why our situation is so despicable: the state of Iran has been at war with the US and Israel for close to a year now, with critical infrastructure badly destroyed. In the midst of all these disruptions, it is still able to supply vital electricity to its people and businesses. The same thing is happening to Ukraine against Russia. Without light, the people are finished. It is a basic principle and also has some spiritual undertone. When you have light, you prevail over challenges and adversaries. That is why our situation is so pathetic. And so they came up with the structuring of the billing system, arguing that with a cost-reflective—no subsidy—tariff system in place, the power companies could be motivated to produce satisfactory power supply to the people and businesses. They embarked on classifying consumers into Classes A–D categories. Although this did not go well with the people, because it clearly was discriminatory and assumed to favour only the wealthy class, it has all turned out to be a scam on the consumers in that category. The Discos have used the monopoly they possess to fleece innocent consumers and businesses of their hard-earned income, with many of them finding it difficult to cope. Yet, on a monthly basis, the bills will arrive. In announcing the cost-reflective tariffs, the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission emphasised that Band A customers will enjoy a minimum of 20 hours of uninterrupted power supply in a day. They went further to say that, if the Discos are unable to meet up with the terms and conditions of the Band A category, the tariffs must be adjusted downward. What this means is that you enjoy a minimum of 20 uninterrupted hours of power supply, you pay the rate; and if you do not get that service, you do not pay. For serious businesses, they were willing to take the hard route, assuming that their use of alternative power supply, like diesel, will be reduced to the barest minimum. It was assumed also that the power supply will be predictable, therefore allowing for proper operational planning. But what are we seeing? Intermittent power outages without any prior notification. They even go without supply for days, without any notification or apologies from the operators, and they still bring up the outrageous Band A bills. Businesses are dying, investors are suffering, and so many people are becoming jobless because of the inefficient operational methods of these distribution companies. They say you should report to NERC. Where is NERC? Try to get to them, either by phone or email, and see what their reaction will be. They are overseeing nothing. Recently, staff of BEDC regulators, who cover Ekiti, Edo and Delta states, went on strike over poor welfare conditions and shut down the control rooms for a whole week. When they returned, it was business as usual. A week after resumption, they brought their bills. You will not believe that the one-week work stoppage did not reflect on the tariff. They have again passed the burden to the consumers. Under normal circumstances, they are expected to apologise for the lengthy supply disruptions and follow that up with a discount, in the form of not using the Band A calculation during this period. The Nigerian operator has failed to realise this; they are wont to shift blame from grid collapse to transmission failures. Even if we accept all of these failures, why should consumers be made to pay the price of their failure? The people are suffering. Band A is killing businesses, and the authorities must do something about it. This is why the people must be sensitive as we approach another election cycle. The people of a local government in Isoko, Delta State, recently came out to protest the electricity situation in their villages. The chant was, “No light, no voting in Isoko land.” I do not know how far the government has gone in pacifying them, but the governor recently undertook a successful campaign tour in that region. Sometimes, you have to cry and protest loudly for your situation to be addressed. Former Lagos State Governor Raji Fashola, while trying to defend this government’s performance, touched on the challenges of policy formulation and implementation. It is a big gap in bringing intentions to reality. We have had so many good policies recorded in our files and archives, and the Band A policy was supposed to work hitch-free, allow manufacturers and big businesses to enjoy a free flow of electricity supply and bring about growth and development, but it has become a nightmare for everyone. If you cannot improve on a situation, do not attempt to change it. We have failed with many good policies because we have left room for excuses. Even the government is not left out in this blame game; the money they are owing the electricity companies is enough to cause a significant shift in the electricity supply performance, but again, there is always a reason for their failure. The people must push for a reversal of the Band A policy. It has failed woefully. On a final note, given the manner in which the national grid is crumbling at regular intervals, it is now time for the federal government to totally decentralise grid management. Even suspected terrorists are now exploiting its fragility to sabotage government efforts. Diversity does not mean that all should be one and develop at the same pace. Once a little healthy competition is brought into it, the various regions will sit up and confront their own challenges head-on. We must give serious thought to this option. •Ikhioya writes from Lagos. The post Discos’ Band A of sorrow appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027: Shunning ethnicity and religion
items.description: As Nigerians prepare for next year’s general elections, they must move beyond the unhealthy politics of ethnicity and religion in the campaigns and choice of leaders. While diversity and equitable representation deserve recognition, they must not take precedence over competence, accountability and proven track records of service delivery. Nigeria cannot build a united democracy on religious intolerance, ethnic suspicion and political exclusion. The country’s numerous ethnic nationalities, languages, cultures and religious traditions should be sources of strength. Sadly, politicians and influential interest groups increasingly manipulate these identities to deepen divisions, promote intolerance and weaken national unity. The emerging political atmosphere is reminiscent of the 2023 general elections, when ethnic and religious considerations dominated campaigns and public discourse. The European Union Election Observation Mission (EU-EOM), in its final report, expressed concern over divisive language and the mobilisation of ethnic and religious sentiments during the elections. It is particularly disturbing that candidates are increasingly judged not by their competence, records and policy proposals but by their faith, language or geographical origin. Political differences or disagreements are sinisterly framed as grievances against entire ethnic or religious communities. Such tendencies undermine democratic competition and threaten peaceful coexistence. The Constitution (1999, as amended) provides clear safeguards against this divisive politics. Section 10 prohibits the adoption of any religion as a state religion, while Section 15 promotes national integration and prohibits discrimination based on place of origin, religion, ethnic or linguistic association. Section 42 further guarantees protection against discrimination on these grounds. These provisions must translate into political practice. No Nigerian should be denied the opportunity to aspire to public office because of religious belief or ethnic origin. Equally, political appointments and access to public opportunities must be guided by fairness, merit and competence rather than narrow identity considerations. Religious leaders must also recognise their responsibility to promote peace, tolerance and mutual respect. Pulpits and religious platforms should never become instruments for spreading political hatred or hostility against people of other faiths. Traditional rulers, community leaders and ethnic associations must similarly resist manipulation by partisan interests. Cultural pride should never become an excuse for intolerance. Politicians who exploit religious and ethnic sentiments for electoral advantage must understand that the divisions they create often outlive their political ambitions. The consequences can undermine national cohesion long after elections have ended. As the general elections approach, political parties and candidates must be challenged to focus on issues that affect all Nigerians, such as insecurity, unemployment, poverty, education, healthcare and economic recovery. These are the issues that should define electoral choices, not religious or ethnic affiliations. Nigeria’s diversity should enrich its democracy, not undermine it. The Nigerian state belongs to all citizens, and its leadership must remain open to every qualified Nigerian. The time has come to put competence above identity, citizenship above religious affiliation and national interest above ethnic loyalty. That is the path to a united, inclusive and sustainable democracy. The post 2027: Shunning ethnicity and religion appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Broadcasting, an industry in search of peace and little details, by Okoh Aihe
items.description: I am sure that Section 6 of the National Broadcasting Commission Act was created for Ministers like Mohammed Idris who will not take advantage of the overwhelming power at their disposal but, at all times, manage such power to meet stakeholder and public expectations from the broadcast industry. Section 6 states that “Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Minister may give the Commission directives of a general character relating generally to particular matters with regard to the exercise by the Commission of its functions under this Act and it shall be the duty of the Commission to comply with such directives.” Looking at it closely, the Section gives the Minister the yam and the knife, leaving at his discretion whoever may get a piece of the yam. More like the sword of Damocles, it can come down anytime, dear friend. I have been against that Section of the Act and have actively canvassed for it to be amended. Reason being that it has been abused serially and is responsible for most of the failures in the broadcast ecosystem, including a number of cases in the court whose outcomes may continue to invalidate the authority of the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC), who is the regulator of the broadcast industry. But life is full of contradictions. It doesn’t mean however that such contradiction, which could be arbitrary, should be accepted as reality irrespective of brilliant intention and outcome. Idris has managed all the arbitrariness of Section 6 quite different from the reality visited upon us not too long ago, and he continues to bear the elements of a good man who has control over his environment. Receiving a delegation of the Broadcasting Organisation of Nigeria (BON), which visited him in his office in Abuja recently, Idris directed that all talks about increasing broadcast license fees be suspended following fears raised by broadcast operators that the escalating cost of operations is almost running them out of business. It means there were simmering discontents and disagreements in the broadcast ecosystem threatening to burst into the open which the public never noticed but the minister has moved swiftly to nip those issues in the bud, as they say. “Any increase in license fees is hereby put on hold. All reviews relating to licenses are suspended until further notice. I am directing the NBC to ensure strict compliance while we review the situation,” Idris was quoted to have said. He called the suspension part of the effort of the Nigerian government to create a more conducive environment for broadcasters. Only if for selfish reasons, Idris needs the broadcast operators to be at the top of their game especially as we approach the 2027 elections. Unfortunately for Nigerian broadcasters, they are hardly prepared for such challenging undertaking, not because of capacity and competence in the profession, but more because of the business environment that has been shrinking. This point was registered vehemently by BON Chairman, Tony Akiotu, when he painted a dreary picture of the industry, saying that “today, it is difficult if not impossible to count stations that operate up to 12 hours daily. This portends danger as information is the lifeblood of a functioning democracy acting as the foundation for civic participation, transparency and accountability.” Akiotu made an appeal for the government to grant access to affordable financing to save broadcasting, beside another major concern, for the minister to encourage political parties to present their candidates for Political Debate which is traditionally put together by the gathering of broadcasters before the Presidential Election. It is possible to see the razzle dazzle of a few flagship programmes on television and get to the erroneous conclusion that the broadcast industry is having a good ride. No. The sector is more like the metaphor of the monkey which sweats profusely but for the hair on its back. There were two other directives also given by the minister. One. The NBC to expedite the review of the Nigeria Broadcasting Code to ensure that its provisions reflect current developments and emerging realities in the industry; and Two: the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON) to ensure full enforcement of the 45-day payment period for advertising services. However, there is a third issue which remains troubling, but the minister has promised to handle it by himself – to convene a stakeholders’ meeting to address outstanding concerns on the Digital Switch-Over (DSO). Although Nigeria opted for the satellite option to launch a concluding variant version of the DSO on June 17, there remains a number of sensitive issues awaiting urgent attention of stakeholders, including NBC and BON members, among others. This writer gathered that the minister was very unhappy with the regulator after receiving complaints from BON that 147 days after his personal intervention pre-DSO launch, it was yet to be involved in any process or meeting to ensure seamless implementation of the resolutions. The simple conclusion is that the DSO has slipped into hibernation and that doesn’t deodorize this government that needs a lot of sprucing up. On this matter, BON reiterated its belief in the principle of dialogue, consultation and mediation to avert breakdown of Industrial harmony, particularly between licensees and the regulator. Even sources within NBC confessed they have not carried out any appreciable consultation with stakeholders. The minister doesn’t want that either and has urged that something be done urgently by the NBC. The DSO is a significant development globally and there is no need flogging a dead horse anymore that Nigeria has been sluggish in implementation with the June action shrouded in more uncertain hue and a halo of suspicion. This writer is of the opinion that a resolution of the entire process is much closer and quite easily affordable now only if the regulator can build a coalition of relationships with concerned stakeholders. In all this however, the minister deserves some commendation for choosing not to flaunt the overwhelming power of Section 6 of the Broadcasting Act but has instead chosen the path of peace in working with the various stakeholders to achieve results that bring common good to the industry in particular and the country in general. I corrected only clear grammatical and punctuation errors, including spacing after punctuation, capitalization of “Industrial harmony,” and a few minor phrasing adjustments. I preserved the author’s style, sentence structure, and intended meaning. The post Broadcasting, an industry in search of peace and little details, by Okoh Aihe appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: A campaign of violence, by Rotimi Fasan
items.description: With more cases of political violence across the country, our politicians are not about to tread the path of peace. They say one thing in the morning and do another in the night. What they say before the cameras is not what you hear from their mouths when the cameras are turned off. The cameras are becoming more of an energiser than a discourager of violence. Not a few of them have been caught inciting violence before the cameras. What happened in Ughelli North yesterday is sad. In this game, nobody is left out, from the most educated technocrat and intellectual to the career scoundrels and thugs that kill and maim for a living. Some Nigerians have been losing their humanity as a demonstration of faith in the power mongers they support in the name of politics. It is no longer sufficient to call for peace. What is needed is to impose heavy sanctions on perpetrators of violence and their promoters. The ruling APC-led government must understand that the greater responsibility lies with it to ensure that the next election and the period thereafter are violence-free. The opposition has less to lose under this climate of fear. It is good that President Bola Tinubu is suing for peace, both in his party and in the country as a whole. But that is not sufficient. He has to go beyond the rhetoric of politicking to actual action, making an example of people, including members of his own party, who are seen as or known to be promoting violence. It is bad enough that his own comment that all is fair in politics has been turned into a cudgel that is not only being used to beat him. It is the justification some have for promoting violence. Even if what he said is not a direct endorsement of violence, he left room for the narrow interpretation that has been given to it. He should have made a full-throated condemnation of some members of his own party who have been found to be violence-prone. Just as he would not give his opponents a quarter, he cannot expect them to give him one. Last week, he encouraged his supporters to drown his opponents with votes. How does he expect them to respond? They would drown him in and with whatever is at their disposal. He must now draw a firm line between rhetoric and action; between making remarks he might well mean to be light-hearted and saying something open-ended that his opponents can seize upon for their own sinister purposes. He should not be seen to be encouraging Machiavellian schemes in the pursuit of power. Contrary to the claims of his opponents, who made a meal of his initial campaign itinerary that limited his visits to twelve states, Nigerians can see that he has been doing the work. Not just him but also members of his immediate family have been on the road. All of this while his opponents are the ones whose campaigns have been limited to the few states and places they could manage. Rather than see the President’s decision to restrict his campaign to less than half of the states in the country as their own opportunity to expand the latitude of their message to Nigerians, they draped themselves in sackcloth and ashes, crying themselves blind that the President was too weak to campaign. A few weeks on, the President has changed his itinerary and increased the number of states he will cover before January 16, 2027. He is clearly making good progress. This would all count for nothing if the ruling APC or the government of President Bola Tinubu allows things to slide out of its control and the country plunges into violence. Nobody would be exonerated. There is hardly any political party, major or minor, that can be given a clean bill as far as its involvement in the violence of this season is concerned. Certainly not any of the leading parties. Which brings me to the ADC and the NDC and other parties that some people tend to see as innocent victims of the intolerant politics of the APC. Nothing could be further from the truth. They are as much perpetrators of violence against others, including the APC and weaker elements within their own parties, as they are victims of violence from the APC and other parties. Their hands, too, are covered in blood. The presidential candidate of the ADC, Atiku Abubakar, has been doing all within his power, for instance, to fish in troubled waters. For very good reasons, he sees Bola Tinubu as the only obstacle to his lifelong dream of becoming a tenant in Aso Villa. While Peter Obi and his supporters can deceive themselves as they like, Atiku Abubakar knows where his problem lies, and it is right now in Abuja and specifically in Aso Villa. Not Onitsha, Agulu or anywhere else Obi calls home. It is why he has been throwing all the barbs in his arsenal at Tinubu, from name-calling to tantrums, insults to rage-baiting and the commissioning of lobbyists and investigators to dig up all the dirt they can on him. In all of this, Peter Obi only comes into the conversation when Atiku is looking to persuade him to drop his ambition for 2027. His attacks on Tinubu have not had the desired effect. They are not hurting the man who has been teaching the Waziri advanced lessons in politics and strategy. Atiku’s last refuge is now the bare-faced promotion of ethnicity, regional and religious separatism. It is clear that Atiku is a wounded politician whose desperation to be president knows no limit. His situation has grown more desperate and testier since Justice Peter Lifu booted out his side of the faction involved in the ADC’s leadership crisis. Since then, he has only come short of calling for civil disorder. Which is what appears to be the strategy of Peter Obi and his followers. Their behaviour, as that of Atiku and his followers, suggests an acceptance of defeat and the idea that the only way to stop a Tinubu victory next year is to plunge the country into civil disorder. It is why Peter Obi would be encouraging his supporters to sing the old national anthem at the official campaign of a supposed national party that promotes someone who hopes to lead Nigeria. The post A campaign of violence, by Rotimi Fasan appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Taxation or imposition: The state, economy and citizenship in Nigeria (2), by Usman Sarki
items.description: “We cannot demand twenty-first-century compliance with twentieth-century communication .” — Mohammed Idris Bultu The first part of this article examined taxation as a relationship between the state and the citizen and ended with a fundamental question: what does the state owe the citizen after collecting his money? Two thoughtful responses to that article have since helped to sharpen the inquiry considerably. Barrister Muhammad Betara, an Abuja-based lawyer, approached the subject mainly from the standpoint of law and public administration, while Mohammed Idris Bultu, a Tax Controller with the Nigeria Revenue Service in Kano, responded from the practical experience of a tax administrator who encounters taxpayers, assessments, compliance and collection in the field. Taken together, their observations provide an important bridge between theory, law and administrative practice. Barrister Betara’s central point is that Nigeria is not without a legal framework for taxation. On the contrary, the Constitution and the recent tax reforms impose clear duties upon citizens and create elaborate machinery for assessment, collection and administration. According to him, Section 24(f) of the 1999 Constitution places upon every citizen the duty to declare his income honestly and pay his tax promptly. That obligation is direct and enforceable. At the same time, the Constitution declares that the security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government and places upon the state broad responsibilities relating to economic welfare, justice and social order. Betara’s important observation is that an imbalance exists between these two sides of the constitutional bargain. The citizen’s obligation to pay tax is concrete and enforceable, while many of the wider welfare obligations of government cannot be enforced by the citizen in quite the same manner. This immediately raises the problem of reciprocity. If the state possesses machinery to compel compliance from the citizen, what equivalent machinery exists which enables the citizen to compel transparency, accountability and adequate service delivery from the state? This lies very close to the heart of the distinction between taxation and imposition. The recent tax reforms have sought to strengthen and modernise the administrative capacity of government. They aim to harmonise tax administration, rationalise procedures, improve taxpayer identification, expand the tax base and provide mechanisms for objection and appeal. Barrister Betara therefore makes the important point that the Nigerian problem is not simply the absence of laws. The problem is that the machinery of collection often appears stronger, more visible and more immediate than the machinery of public accountability. Tax Officer Mohammed Bultu’s practical observations reinforce this point from another direction. His first proposition is simple but profound: legitimacy makes collection possible. A tax may be perfectly lawful, but if taxpayers do not understand why they are paying, under what authority, or what purpose the revenue is intended to serve, resistance increases and enforcement becomes more difficult. This is particularly striking because it comes from a practising tax administrator. What might appear to an academic as a question of legitimacy is, to the tax officer, an operational reality that could become an impediment. Taxation with understanding is therefore not merely a philosophical ideal but an administrative necessity. This takes us back to the historical reflections in the first part of this series. From Buchan and Morel to the present day, governments have repeatedly confronted the same question: how can taxation be made legitimate in the eyes of those who are compelled by law to pay? Legality is indispensable, but legitimacy requires something more. Bultu’s second observation concerns the effect of the oil era on the Nigerian fiscal relationship. For decades, governments relied heavily upon petroleum revenues rather than upon the direct contributions of citizens. This relaxed the psychological link between taxation and citizenship. The citizen did not always feel that government depended financially upon him, and government did not always feel compelled to explain itself to the citizen in the manner that a truly tax-dependent state might have required. That era is now changing. As taxation becomes increasingly central to financing government, the psychology of government and citizenship must change with it. Citizens will naturally demand greater explanation of what government costs, what it collects and what it delivers. Bultu’s third point is equally important: law alone does not create trust. A modern tax regime may expand the tax base and improve collection, but if implementation is perceived as aggressive, rushed or overly focused on targets and penalties, citizens may experience reform not as a social contract but as an imposition. This is why taxpayer education becomes crucial. His memorable observation that Nigeria cannot demand twenty-first-century compliance with twentieth-century communication deserves to be deeply understood and taken seriously. A taxpayer who understands his obligations, his rights and the procedures available to him is more valuable to the state than one who complies merely out of fear and with resentment. Taxation should therefore not be organised simply around collection targets. It must also be organised around explanation, simplicity, fairness and confidence. Barrister Betara similarly draws attention to rights already available to taxpayers, such as rights to proper assessment, objection, appeal and protection from unlawful or multiple taxation. But rights are of little practical value where citizens do not know that these exist or cannot exercise them without excessive cost and difficulty. Both responses therefore converge on one principle: the state must not only collect efficiently; it must also communicate efficiently, account efficiently and protect the taxpayer efficiently. A second area of convergence concerns taxable capacity. The law may identify income and calculate liability according to established rules, but this does not necessarily reveal the citizen’s real economic condition. A Nigerian may earn what appears on paper to be a taxable income, while much of that income may already be committed to privately providing electricity, water, transportation, healthcare, education and security. This affects not only personal welfare but the capacity to save, accumulate assets, invest and achieve long-term financial security. The Nigerian who appears reasonably comfortable on paper may, in reality, possess very little disposable income after meeting expenses that, in other societies, are substantially supported by public services. The same problem confronts businesses even more starkly. An enterprise may pay taxes and levies while still providing its own electricity, water, security, communications and sometimes access roads, in addition to absorbing transportation costs created by deficient infrastructure and meeting minimum wage requirements for its employees. This creates what might be described as a double fiscal burden, under which the citizen finances the state and then privately finances the substitutes for services the state has failed adequately to provide. This raises a question that deserves greater attention in Nigerian fiscal policy: should taxable capacity be considered simply in terms of nominal income, or should government become more sensitive to the total economic burden already borne by citizens and businesses? Both Betara and Bultu also emphasise accountability. If the taxpayer must keep records, disclose income, file returns and prove compliance, then government should be equally capable of showing what it collected, where the money went, who authorised the expenditure and what public value resulted. This symmetry is indispensable. The taxpayer should not be transparent to the state while the state remains opaque to the taxpayer. There should therefore be a traceable public chain of collection, receipt, appropriation, expenditure, delivery, audit and reporting. Citizens should be able to understand, in reasonably simple language, how public revenue moves from their pockets into the treasury and from the treasury into roads, schools, hospitals, water systems, security and other public services. This need not require every Nigerian to become an accountant or forensic auditor. Governments themselves should make fiscal information intelligible and accessible in this digitally connected world. Imagine if every tier of government periodically told citizens, in plain language: this is what we collected; this is what we received; this is what we spent; these are the projects completed; this is what remains; and this is what the auditors found. Such a practice would not weaken government but would strengthen it considerably and grant it legitimacy. For taxation does more than raise revenue. Properly organised, it strengthens democratic governance and creates a citizen who asks questions, scrutinises expenditure and recognises public money as partly his own contribution to the commonwealth. Nigeria therefore needs more than a tax-paying culture. It needs a tax-accountability culture. The true reform is not simply a new tax rate or collection mechanism but a new fiscal bargain. The citizen should be able to say: “I will declare honestly, comply with the law willingly and pay what is lawfully due diligently.” The state must also be able to answer: “We will make the system fair, simple, transparent and accountable, and we will show you what your contribution has achieved.” Until both sides of that bargain are visible and credible, the Nigerian taxpayer will continue to ask the question around which this series revolves: Is this taxation, or is it merely collection? And when does collection become imposition? That question leads naturally to the third and final part, which concludes with the profound issues that Betara and Bultu raised. The post Taxation or imposition: The state, economy and citizenship in Nigeria (2), by Usman Sarki appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Saving Enyimba FC from relegation, by Ochereome Nnanna
items.description: This article is not about football per se. It is about Enyimba International Football Club of Aba, Abia State. Before the coming of our phenomenal and algorithmic Governor, Dr Alex C. Otti, to the saddle, Enyimba FC was about the only thing that made us Abians proud of our state. We were like the eagle chained by bad governance for so long that we forgot to fly. Enyimba is the most prestigious and dominant force in Nigerian football. Three football clubs have historically personified the irrepressible, resilient, successful and enterprising spirit for which the Igbo nation is famous all over the world. The Enugu Rangers International served notice that though we lost the Biafra War, we were not a defeated people. However, though the Rangers dominated Nigerian football and the Green Eagles in the 1970s, their Ibadan rivals, IICC Shooting Stars, beat them to the first achievement of winning the African Winners Cup in 1976. The following year, Rangers achieved the same feat, but IICC fans retain the bragging rights of being there first. Later on, the Spartans FC of Owerri, which was formed around the same time as Enyimba in 1976, became Iwuanyanwu Nationale and dominated the so-called “professional” era. The Owerri club was renamed Heartland FC, a name it wore until it was relegated for the fourth time to the Nigeria National League (NNL) on 25th May 2025 under the hand of Governor Hope Uzodimma. Its first relegation took place in 2016. Imo has seemingly ceased to be a notable footballing state despite an abundance of talents. Enyimba FC of Aba is the real “agba baller” of Nigerian football. It is to Nigeria what Real Madrid is to Spain. It also compares only to Liverpool FC in England in terms of comprehensive domestic dominance and continental conquests. Enyimba remains the only Nigerian club to win the CAF Champions League – back-to-back in 2003 and 2004 – with two African Super Cups. This is apart from dominating in the local league and sharing top prizes in the FA Cup series. If there is any one lasting legacy for which Senator Orji Uzor Kalu will be forever remembered, it is the Enyimba CAF Champions League achievements, which happened under his watch as Governor of Abia State. If you check how our mighty Enyimba FC is doing in the 14th week of the current NPFL season, you will be shocked to see it slumbering in the 18th position – topping the relegation zone! That was how Heartland started before it became a regular customer in the second-class NNL. God forbid that Enyimba will suffer this fate. It will be so abominable, a taboo! Experience has shown that once a mighty club tastes relegation, it always goes back for more. Enyimba must NEVER be relegated! It must return to its pride of place – at the top currently occupied by its elder brother, Rangers. In truth, Enyimba has been suffering since 2015 when Dr Okezie Ikpeazu took over as governor. When Otti assumed office, one of the steps he took to revive the fortunes of the club was the appointment of Nigeria’s international star and most decorated hero, Nwankwo Kanu, as Chairman in July 2023. The reasoning behind this was impeccable. Kanu, with his wealth of professional experience, influence and network, should bring back the days of glory. In football circles, there is always this argument that former top players are the natural choices to inherit football coaching and management because they know where the shoe pinches. The stupendous successes recorded by superstar Zinedine Zidane at his former club, Real Madrid, made this case for ex-players. During his 2016–2018 and 2019–2021 tenures as Madrid manager, Zidane won eleven major trophies, including the historic three consecutive Champions League victories. By contrast, Enyimba FC did not win anything under Kanu’s reign. It only managed to place 3rd in 2023/2024, sixth in 2024/2025 and 18th in the current season before the board was dissolved recently. Another former Eagles star, Finidi George, managed to win an NPFL trophy as Enyimba coach but could not subsequently maintain a strong standing in the league, hence the change. So, being a former intercontinental star and national hero alone isn’t automatic credentials to be a successful coach or manager. Orji Kalu is widely acclaimed to have personally provided the leadership for Enyimba’s success, though he was never a footballer. He loved the game, followed it and learned all the tricks around it. Kalu attended Enyimba training sessions and engaged in football politics. He understood the off-the-pitch intrigues that often resonate in on-pitch victories. He also had in Victor Agwu Anyansi a club Chairman in the same mould, though Anyansi, like me, never played football except as a hobby. OUK would have been more useful to Nigeria as a football administrator, not a lawmaker. The lesson here is that a person does not have to be an ex-player to be a good club chairman whose job is political and managerial. It requires a person who understands the game, player psychology, referee intrigues and the gamut of politics around football. It also requires a person with a rugged character and a “killer instinct”, who will not back down from anything required for victory. Nwankwo Kanu is a jolly good fellow, a gentleman who would probably refuse to break a head. Governor Otti did well to intervene. Thank God, the season is still young. Enyimba still stands an excellent chance to bounce back up if the right hands are found to steer the Board and Bench. I hope Governor Otti brings his usual savvy in team selection for effective governance to bear in the search for Kanu’s successor. The person must “know” football, its political intrigues, inner games and the ability to motivate action. Enyimba FC is more than a football club. It is the spirit of our people. The post Saving Enyimba FC from relegation, by Ochereome Nnanna appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: NPP chairman arrested over alleged theft of Nkoko Nkitinkiti birds – Agric Minister claims
items.description: The Minister of Food and Agriculture, Eric Opoku, has disclosed that the New Patriotic Party (NPP) Constituency Chairman for Nadowli-Kaleo was arrested over the alleged theft of birds distributed under the government’s Nkoko Nkitinkiti programme. He said the police had confirmed the incident and recovered some of the birds following reports of the alleged theft. Mr Opoku made the disclosure in Parliament on Tuesday, November 24, as he responded to criticism from the Minority over the implementation of the government’s poultry intervention. He challenged the opposition’s criticism of the programme, arguing that while its leaders were questioning the initiative in Parliament, a party official in the Upper West Region had allegedly been involved in taking birds meant for beneficiaries. “While their leaders are in Parliament condemning the programme, their people back there are stealing the birds,” he told the House. Mr Opoku said the matter first came to his attention through a report by Tolon TV, owned by 1st Deputy Minority Whip Habib Iddrisu. He explained that his ministry subsequently contacted the Nadowli-Kaleo District Police Command to establish the facts, and was informed that the report was accurate and that some of the birds had been retrieved. “I engaged Honourable Habib, and I told Honourable Habib, ‘Your station reported this,'” he said, referring to the Tolon MP, Habib Iddrisu, who is associated with the television station. The minister said Mr Iddrisu had responded that the incident did not occur in his constituency but in Nadowli-Kaleo. About the programme The Nkoko Nkitinkiti initiative is part of the government’s poultry development agenda under the broader Feed Ghana Programme. It is intended to increase domestic poultry production, improve household food security and create income opportunities, particularly for rural households. The government announced plans to distribute three million birds across the country, with an estimated 60,000 households expected to benefit. The programme has, however, faced questions about its implementation, the selection of beneficiaries and the distribution of birds in some constituencies. Mr Opoku’s disclosure added a new political dimension to those concerns, as the government and the opposition continue to debate the programme’s effectiveness and accountability in the use of public resources.

Destinée à un public adulte, cette séance met à l’honneur une œuvre poignante inspirée d’une histoire vraie qui traverse l’histoire et la création artistiquen racontant une amitié née derrière les barbelés. items.title: Bellingham stunner helps Real Madrid see off PSV
items.description: Jude Bellingham came off the bench to score a stunning goal as Real Madrid came from behind to beat PSV Eindhoven and maintain their 100% record in the Champions League. With Jose Mourinho’s side trailing to Ivan Perisic’s penalty, Bellingham was sent on as part of a triple change at the break and made an immediate impact. Arda Guler’s backheel set up Federico Valverde to finish off a lovely Madrid move for the equaliser before Bellingham put the hosts in front with a glorious goal. A bouncing ball fell to the England midfielder 25 yards out, he controlled it with his left foot, chipped it up for himself with his right and then sent a sumptuous volley arcing in off the post with the outside of his boot. PSV were reeling and when Kodai Sano gave the ball away cheaply inside his own half, the hosts pounced with Guler finding Kylian Mbappe to rifle in a third goal in 14 minutes. Mbappe was on target again late on, racing onto Guler’s perfectly weighted through-ball to round the goalkeeper and slot him his 19th goal in 18 games this season before Vinicius Jr, played in by Bellingham, ran clear to add a fifth. A fifth-straight win in the competition takes the 15-time European champions to the top of the standings, while PSV remain outside of the play-offs spot with just four points from five games. The visitors will know it could all have been very different as they bossed the first half with Reuben van Bommel missing a big early chance, and Sven Mijnans and Kodai Sano spurning glaring opportunities late in the half. Between times, PSV did find the net as Perisic converted from the penalty spot after Mijnans’ foot was trodden on by Aurelien Tchouameni – a foul given after the referee was sent to the screen by the video assistant referee. Madrid had been well off the pace and were fortunate not to be further behind but emerged from half-time a different team. Bellingham’s introduction brought an energy and intensity to the hosts that had been sorely lacking, and one that it soon became clear PSV could not handle. The quality Madrid possess turned a potentially difficult night into a thumping victory at the Bernabeu.

items.title: Jensen Huang Isn’t Worried. But You Should Be.
items.description: L ast week , Anthropic went public. The IPO was heavily oversubscribed , spurring the company to sell more shares at a higher price than it had originally intended. The five-year-old start-up took in a record-breaking $81 billion from investors around the world, giving it a gobsmacking $1.5 trillion valuation and minting an estimated 600 centimillionaires . Nevertheless, the IPO arrived at a dour moment on Wall Street, and did not exactly brighten the mood. Investors had been selling off equities for weeks, spooked by rising interest rates, the midterm landslide, concerns about AI’s capacity to boost corporate profits, and Nvidia’s ouster of its allegedly honey-trapped CEO. When Nvidia’s board announced that it had unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang yesterday, its share price surged. Then it slouched back down, joining Anthropic stock, the S&P 500, foreign-equity markets, gold, crypto, and Nasdaq in the red. The AI boom seems to be turning into an AI bust. Maybe we’ll end up thinking of it as an AI bubble. Maybe it will spur an AI recession. The worst possible outcome would be an AI financial crisis—and it is not a far-fetched outcome at all, given the astronomical sums, convoluted deals, and cavernous regulatory lacunae involved. The question is whether the AI whatever-it-is will play out more like the dot-com bubble of the 1990s or the housing bubble of the aughts. In the former, Nasdaq lost 78 percent of its value and the country entered a brief recession. Still, the banking system remained solvent and the credit markets liquid. In the latter, the housing market faltered, the stock market collapsed, and the entire global financial system seized, precipitating the worst recession since the Great Depression. [ Read: A shameless valley ] The difference wasn’t the amount of money at stake. The collapse of the dot-com bubble wiped out more wealth than the collapse of the housing bubble , as former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke observed in a 2012 speech. The difference was that the dot-com losses were transparent, widely distributed, and easily understood. People got excited about the World Wide Web; they bought stocks at absurd valuations; some of the companies they invested in proved to be duds; they lost money. The losses from the housing bubble, in contrast, were opaque, concentrated, and impenetrable. Where to even start? The erosion of lending standards, the explosive growth in derivatives contracts, the mispricing of mortgage-backed securities, the misguided faith in market self-regulation , the insufficient capital buffers, the regulatory gaps, the Sun Belt speculation, the low interest rates? I suppose it came down to one thing: Investors seemed like they were making a lot of different bets. But they were making one bet, on housing prices. And when that bet went sour, they panicked. However the AI story ends, it is starting the same way that the dot-com and housing stories began—with trillions of dollars. Normally, software is relatively inexpensive to develop and cheap to scale. (Mark Zuckerberg wrote most of the code for Thefacebook.com by himself in his dorm, shelling out $85 a month for a server.) But ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude Code require a tremendous amount of “compute”—basically, computing power. So AI start-ups and Silicon Valley giants are spending $600 billion this year alone on silicon chips and data-center construction. They aren’t footing the bill themselves. They are issuing shares, as Anthropic did last week. They’re selling bonds: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle issued $223 billion in debt in the first eight months of the year. They are also making arrangements with private creditors. Here’s where things start to feel very 1996. The markets are making a massive wager on AI revolutionizing the business world, just as they made a massive wager on the World Wide Web revolutionizing the business world. The value of AI-related stocks has climbed $27 trillion since the launch of ChatGPT, according to Goldman Sachs. Even given the recent correction, the country is in the midst of a hell of a bull market. Yet the markets are making that bet on the basis of some awfully rosy assumptions. By 2031, AI-linked companies will need to generate $6 trillion a year in revenue to justify the cost of the build-out , according to calculations by the consultancy Bain & Company. That is six times as much as American businesses and households spend on gasoline and other petroleum products each year, to give a sense of scale. It is eight times as much as U.S. firms shell out for software. It’s more than the country spends on health care . AI revenue seems highly likely to fall short of expectations, while AI overhead costs seem highly likely to exceed them. Anthropic is committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on compute in the coming years. And many AI firms have hefty borrowing costs to deal with, as well as hefty infrastructure costs. CoreWeave, an AI cloud-computing firm, is spending a quarter of its revenue servicing its loans. [ Read: The economy is a hostage situation ] The disconnect between the two sides of the balance sheet is making the markets feel bearish. Some AI companies are having a harder time raising the cash they need to refine and run their algorithms. In time, that could force them to cancel construction projects and miss payments to their creditors, deepening the market rout. So would we end up in 2000, facing a sharp correction and perhaps a soft recession? Or in 2007, staring into the abyss? T he first big issue , well-known at this point, has to do with concentration and circularity. Much like during the housing bubble, today’s investors are all-in on one big bet: that AI will pay off. Moreover, they are staking that bet on a small family of companies with downright Hapsburgian relationships with one another. Amazon has invested $33 billion in Anthropic, which has committed to buying $110 billion in Amazon web services. Microsoft has spent $13 billion on a stake in OpenAI, which is signed up to purchase $250 billion in cloud-computing services from Microsoft. One firm’s investment is another firm’s revenue is another firm’s operating budget is another firm’s interest payment is another firm’s profit. “The chip maker, the data-center developer, the person who’s leasing the data center, and, also remember, the end customers too—if any of those things start drying up, for any reason, everybody is affected,” Evan LeFlore, the director of AI, innovation, and economic opportunity at Better Markets, a nonpartisan research and advocacy group, told me. “You will then see, potentially, a chain reaction.” Which firms would get hit the hardest? That is the second issue. Nobody knows with any precision. AI companies are “outsourcing a lot of the data-center development and increasingly the investment in IT as well—subcontracting it to private companies, third-party private landlords,” Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, an economist at Columbia, told me. They are inventing financing mechanisms, using things like graphics processing units as collateral. (Cool, cool, cool.) And they are keeping these deals off their balance sheets. The Wall Street Journal recently estimated that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta have $604 billion worth of conventionally tallied liabilities and $2.4 trillion tucked away in the footnotes . “It’s a mix of a shell game and a Ponzi scheme,” Phillip Basil, the director of economic growth and financial stability at Better Markets, told me. That gets to the third issue. The financiers staking the AI boom are “reasonably sophisticated,” says Douglas Holtz-Eakin, the president of the American Action Forum and a member of the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission. They know that “these are high-risk, high-yield opportunities,” he told me, and “are correctly trying to hedge their own books.” Still, markets do not always discipline themselves, as the world found out in 2008. They’re especially terrible at disciplining themselves when dealing with imperfect information, borrowed money, and heady doses of irrational enthusiasm. If traditional banks were the predominant financiers of the AI build-out, the country’s regulators would have ample insight into counterparty exposure, asset quality, and other fiddly-but-important metrics. They’d have the authority to conduct stress tests. They’d have tools to reduce leverage and prevent contagion. But traditional banks aren’t the predominant financiers of the AI build-out. (Nvidia, the chip maker, is known as the “central bank of AI,” making Jensen Huang today’s Bernanke, I guess.) Much of today’s dealmaking is happening in the loosely regulated shadow-banking system. When an AI “neocloud” takes out a loan from a private-credit company, for instance, “even the Fed doesn’t really monitor that,” Van Nieuwerburgh said. “They’re not responsible for the supervision of non-bank financial institutions.” A number of AI firms do fall under the purview of the Securities and Exchange Commission. But Donald Trump has hobbled the agency : Its case volume is half of what it was three years ago, and its penalty assessments are a quarter of what they were. The Office of Financial Research, created after the housing crisis and tasked with assessing novel risks, has monitoring responsibilities and subpoena power. Trump has not so much hobbled it as gutted it . The Financial Stability Oversight Council, chaired by the Treasury secretary, is meant to coordinate among regulators and promote market discipline. It is busy convening AI stakeholders for “ cross-sector dialogue on high-value AI use cases, practical approaches to scaling innovation, and regulatory impediments” to the technology’s adoption. As for Trump himself, he’s pulling strings at Nvidia, a company he was directly invested in as of the end of September. “God knows what is happening in the regulatory structure and the supervisory structure right now,” Phil Angelides, the chair of the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, told me. AI’s creditors and debtors seem to be pretty much free to make deals as they see fit, and to keep the details to themselves, too. [ Josh Tyrangiel: Three theories of Jensen Huang’s resurrection ] If AI revenue fails to take off in the way investors expect that it will, the tech industry might be able to act as its own backstop, Van Nieuwerburgh said, preventing a surge of defaults and write-downs. Alphabet, for instance, generates close to $1 billion a day from advertisements, and has a 21 percent profit margin. It has essentially unlimited capacity to raise money by issuing bonds and shares. The company could easily cover enormous AI-related losses, as could firms such as Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon. We could end up in a dot-com scenario, with most of the pain coming from falling equity prices. Or a chip manufacturer or a hyperscaler could go bankrupt. A software firm might allow its debt-laden data-center subsidiaries to go under, defaulting on their liabilities. Financiers could write down the value of their investments, meaning a flurry of margin calls and asset sales. Chaos could spread throughout the financial system, amplified by leverage and amplified again by a lack of clarity about who owes what to whom. American banks, which have $1 trillion and counting in exposure to the build-out , could falter . Households would watch their retirement savings evaporate and pull back on spending. The engine of GDP growth would sputter. It might look like the housing bubble, if perhaps less severe. At least the head of the “central bank of AI”—a man who reportedly romanced a few of his subordinates while being romanced by a Chinese spy , a man who Trump describes as “a Great Patriot and National Treasure”—is not worried. “The money we’ve invested is going to generate tremendous returns,” Huang promised on CNBC a few months ago. “I think the risk is low.”

items.title: Semaine du numérique : Le Burkina Faso place la souveraineté technologique au cœur de la 21e édition
items.description: Le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a présidé, ce mardi 24 novembre 2026, au Salon international de l'artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO), la cérémonie d'ouverture de la 21e édition de la Semaine du numérique. Pendant quatre jours (du 24 au 27 novembre), les acteurs du secteur échangeront sur les moyens d'accélérer la transformation digitale et de renforcer la souveraineté technologique du Burkina Faso et de l'espace confédéral. Cette 21e édition de la Semaine du numérique se veut un cadre d'échanges, de partage d'expériences et d'exposition pour les entreprises et les acteurs du secteur. Ces derniers auront l'occasion de présenter leurs solutions et innovations numériques, ainsi que les opportunités qu'elles offrent pour accompagner la transformation digitale. Au-delà des expositions, les échanges porteront notamment sur les infrastructures numériques, la cybersécurité, les innovations locales et la gouvernance numérique dans l'espace confédéral. Autant de questions qui s'inscrivent dans les réflexions sur l'autonomie technologique et le développement du numérique dans les pays concernés. Le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo a invité les étudiants, élèves et autres à participer à l'évènement Dans son discours d'ouverture, le Premier ministre a rappelé que la souveraineté numérique constitue une priorité pour le gouvernement. À cet effet, il a dit attendre des propositions « réalisables » à l'issue de cette rencontre, afin que les réflexions engagées puissent déboucher sur des actions concrètes. « Sous l'impulsion du camarade président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, notre gouvernement met de la souveraineté numérique en priorité. Elle suppose de maîtriser nos infrastructures et nos données, de disposer des compétences pour les exploiter et de garder la liberté de choisir nos solutions », a-t-il soutenu. Au deuxième trimestre 2026, confie-t-il, notre pays comptait 328 764 abonnements en internet fixe et 20 439 942 en internet mobile. Cette progression, poursuit-il, rend plus urgent l'obligation d'assurer un accès fiable et utile à chacun. Pour y parvenir, ajoute-t-il, l'action du gouvernement s'organise pour les trois priorités. Il s'agit de la maîtrise de nos infrastructures et de nos données, la simplification des services publics et l'accélération de la transformation digitale sécurisée et inclusive. La ministre en charge de la transition digitale, Dr Aminata Sabané a salué la mobilisation Cette 21e édition se déroule sous le thème « Souveraineté technologique : accélérer la transformation digitale, sécurisée et inclusive ». La ministre en charge de la transition digitale, Dr Aminata Sabané, a expliqué la particularité de la thématique. Pour elle, la thématique engage les acteurs du numérique à examiner le processus de transformation digitale en cours et de s'assurer que dans la mise en œuvre de chaque chantier, la dynamique souverainiste puisse être tenue en compte. « Nous ne pouvons pas parler de développement numérique, ou encore de levier de la refondation de notre État si nous sommes dépendants », a-t-elle laissé entendre. Les officielles de la cérémonie d'ouverture Pour elle, la dynamique souverainiste selon la vision du président du Faso et de son gouvernement, se résume à deux aspects. Il s'agit de la sécurité et de l'inclusion. La sécurité pour garantir la maîtrise des données, des plateformes et des infrastructures. L'inclusion pour tenir compte de tout le monde, de toutes les localités du pays. « L'inclusion, parce qu'il ne faut pas que le numérique creuse les inégalités », a-t-elle indiqué. Le Mali et le Niger sont les pays invités spéciaux de cette 21e édition. Les ministères en charge de la famille et de l'administration territoriale parrainent l'évènement. Le message des parrain a été lu par la ministre en charge de la famille qui a salué la tenue de cet évènement. Serge Ika Ki Photos : Bonaventure Paré Lefaso.net

items.title: Cherki rescues point for Man City against Napoli
items.description: Rayan Cherki rescued a late point but Manchester City’s poor run of form continued as they were held to a draw at home in the Champions League by Napoli. Enzo Maresca’s side started the season in perfect fashion but have dropped off dramatically since, now having won just one of their past six games in all competitions. City had chances in the early stages. Elliot Anderson marauded forward and saw a low strike in the opening minute batted away by Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, before Nico O’Reilly headed over from close range. But the opportunities dried up and it was Napoli who almost broke the deadlock on the stroke of half-time when Sam Beukema rose highest to meet Kevin de Bruyne’s corner, but the header was kept out by Gianluigi Donnarumma’s sharp save. Against the run of play, the visitors opened the scoring in the second half as former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund turned Marc Guehi inside out before drilling home an unerring finish. City boss Maresca sent on Jeremy Doku and the Belgium international was the catalyst for the equaliser, picking out Ayyoub Bouaddi in the box for the Moroccan teenager to stroke home his first goal for the club. But the Serie A side restored their lead on 76 minutes courtesy of Noa Lang smacking home a sensational volley from Leonardo Spinazzola’s cross towards the far post. The home supporters were becoming frustrated and Josko Gvardiol rattled the post as they searched for an equaliser, but Cherki showed quick footwork and drilled low into the bottom corner to salvage a draw. Man City ratings Gianluigi Donnarumma: Made an important save at the end of the first half to deny Sam Beukema but could do little about either goal. 6 Matheus Nunes: Returned to the side after injury and provides City with more width. 6 Marc Guehi: Poor defending for the first goal, Didn’t know which way to turn and was punished by Hojlund. 5 Josko Gvardiol: Played in his preferred centre-back role, the Croatian looked more comfortable in that position, contributing two tackles and two interceptions. 6 Nico O’Reilly: Left a gaping hole for Napoli’s second goal after trying to nick the ball up the pitch. 5 Ayyoub Bouaddi: Starting to gain confidence. Steady in the middle of the park and always unruffled, before scoring the equaliser. 8 Elliot Anderson: The England international played further forward and proved to be a goal threat, forcing Milinkovic-Savic into a couple of decent saves. 7 Enzo Fernandez: Disappointing. Restored to the starting line-up after being dropped at the weekend but the Argentine needs to start performing and living up to his hefty price tag. 5 Allan: Quiet. Given a rare start but saw little of the ball and was substituted early in the second half. 5 Rayan Cherki: Attempted to pull of his box of tricks and was rewarded for his perseverance with the equaliser. 7 Erling Haaland: Captain for the night, he was visibly frustrated by the lack of chances early on and it didn’t get any better as the match wore on. 6 Subs: Jeremy Doku (on 54, Allan) Lifted the place after coming on and was a constant threat. Provided the assist for Bouaddi’s goal and one of his better outings. 7 Iliman Ndiaye (on 63, Fernandez) Lovely ball slipped through for Cherki’s late leveller. 7 Subs not used: Rulli, Dias, Kovacic, Ait-Nouri, Reis, Khusanov, Foden, McAidoo, Samba, Lewis.

items.title: Chiens errants | Le Lions Club poursuit sa campagne à La Manouba
items.description: ​L'engagement sur le terrain se poursuit pour le Lions Club Tunis Médina, qui a dévoilé les résultats de la quatrième semaine de sa campagne permanente dédiée à la stérilisation et à la vaccination des chiens errants à La Manouba. Dans son rapport le Lions Club affirme que trois chiennes ont été stérilisées au cours de cette période grâce au soutien des cliniques vétérinaires partenaires, à savoir la Clinique Poils et Plumes à Ennasr et la Clinique du Dr Seiffeddine, ajoutant que des opérations de vaccination sur le terrain ont également été menées auprès des chiens déjà pris en charge et traités la semaine précédente, garantissant ainsi la continuité des soins et l'efficacité de l'initiative. ​Au-delà des nouvelles prises en charge, le club insiste sur l'importance de ce suivi régulier pour inscrire l'action dans la durée, saluant au passage l'implication de ses vétérinaires partenaires, de la Municipalité de La Manouba ainsi que de l'ensemble des contributeurs mobilisés. ​Fidèle à sa devise « Engaged to serve », le Lions Club Tunis Médina rappelle que la protection animale repose sur une présence continue, semaine après semaine, plutôt que sur des actions isolées. items.title: Corruption : Benalilou plaide pour plus grande implication de la société civile dans le contrôle des institutions
items.description: La lutte contre la corruption ne peut se limiter à l’action des institutions. Elle suppose aussi de rendre l’information accessible, d’associer les citoyens aux décisions publiques et de soumettre les organismes chargés de la probité à une véritable obligation de reddition des comptes. C’est le message défendu par Mohamed Benaliou, président de l’Instance nationale de la probité, de la prévention et de la lutte contre la corruption (INPPLC), lors d’une rencontre continentale organisée à Marrakech autour des « Instances de lutte contre la corruption ouvertes ». Pour le responsable marocain, la réhabilitation de la confiance entre les citoyens et les institutions passe nécessairement par une rupture avec les modes de gestion institutionnelle cloisonnés. La transparence, la participation de la société et la reddition des comptes doivent désormais constituer les piliers d’une nouvelle approche, permettant aux citoyens et aux organisations de la société civile de prendre part à l’identification des risques de corruption, à la hiérarchisation des priorités et à l’évaluation des résultats de l’action publique. « Il ne peut y avoir ni prévention ni lutte contre la corruption dans un environnement où l’information est dissimulée ou la société exclue. De même, il ne peut y avoir de reddition des comptes sans des institutions qui communiquent et expliquent leurs actions, ni sans une société en mesure d’assurer le suivi et d’apporter sa contribution », a souligné Mohamed Benaliou. Organisée en partenariat avec le Partenariat pour un gouvernement ouvert (PGO), la rencontre de Marrakech ambitionne de poser les bases d'un modèle africain inédit, baptisé « Instances de lutte contre la corruption ouvertes ». L'initiative entend étendre les principes du gouvernement ouvert aux instances indépendantes chargées de la probité, sans remettre en cause leurs spécificités constitutionnelles, juridiques et organisationnelles ni leur indépendance. Il s'agit, selon le président de l'INPPLC, de dépasser le stade des orientations stratégiques pour parvenir à des engagements communs, susceptibles d'être progressivement développés et mis en œuvre. Cette évolution implique de ne plus considérer l'ouverture comme une simple prérogative des gouvernements ou comme un dispositif essentiellement technique. Elle doit concerner l'ensemble de l'architecture institutionnelle de l'État et se traduire concrètement dans la conception et l'exécution des programmes publics, l'association des parties prenantes, la publication des résultats et la révision des interventions à la lumière des enseignements tirés de l'expérience. Benaliou inscrit cette démarche dans le prolongement des Hautes Orientations royales, qui ont consacré la lutte contre la corruption comme une « affaire de l'État et de la société ». Une conception qui suppose, selon lui, une répartition plus large des responsabilités et une mobilisation collective en faveur de la préservation de la probité et de l'intérêt général. Elle appelle également à renforcer la coopération et la complémentarité entre les différents acteurs concernés. Dans le dispositif envisagé, les trois principes de transparence, de participation citoyenne et de reddition des comptes sont étroitement liés. Le premier doit garantir à la société l'accès aux informations nécessaires à la compréhension des politiques publiques et des interventions institutionnelles. Le deuxième doit permettre aux citoyens et aux acteurs de la société civile de contribuer, en connaissance de cause, à la définition des priorités et à l'élaboration des politiques. Le troisième doit assurer le suivi des engagements et permettre d'évaluer la manière dont les institutions prennent en considération les observations, les recommandations et les conclusions des évaluations. L'enjeu est également de renforcer l'efficacité des instances de lutte contre la corruption en les incitant à rendre publiques les données relatives aux risques de corruption, à associer les acteurs concernés à leur identification et à rendre compte des résultats de leurs interventions. Une telle démarche pourrait consolider leurs capacités en matière de prévention, de détection et de reddition des comptes, tout en renforçant la confiance du public dans leur action. Le président de l'INPPLC a, dans ce contexte, plaidé pour une place plus importante de la société civile engagée au sein des mécanismes de gouvernance ouverte. Il s'agit notamment de dépasser une participation cantonnée à la consultation pour permettre aux organisations concernées d'influer effectivement sur la décision publique. Cette évolution devrait s'appuyer sur une complémentarité fonctionnelle et une coordination institutionnelle entre les différentes parties prenantes. Le modèle africain proposé s'appuie sur les référentiels internationaux et continentaux relatifs à la lutte contre la corruption. Il prévoit notamment la publication proactive des informations, la production et la mise à disposition de données et d'indicateurs fiables, ainsi que la mise en place de mécanismes structurés de participation. Au-delà de la communication institutionnelle à sens unique, les citoyens, la société civile, le secteur privé et les médias seraient ainsi associés à l'identification des risques, à la définition des priorités et au suivi de la mise en œuvre des engagements. Le dispositif entend également instaurer des mécanismes de reddition des comptes adaptés aux missions et aux capacités de chaque institution. Chaque instance devrait pouvoir choisir et développer les instruments correspondant à ses compétences, à ses priorités et à ses moyens, en tenant compte de la nature des risques de corruption auxquels elle est confrontée et des besoins liés à leur prévention et à leur traitement. Cette souplesse ne devrait toutefois porter atteinte ni à son indépendance ni à ses particularités juridiques et institutionnelles. À l'échelle continentale, Mohamed Benaliou considère que la diversité des cadres juridiques et institutionnels encadrant les instances africaines chargées de la probité ne doit pas constituer un frein à leur rapprochement. Elle représente au contraire une ressource pour développer les échanges d'expertise, tirer profit de la pluralité des expériences et transformer les connaissances accumulées sur le continent en outils opérationnels face aux nouvelles formes de corruption. L'initiative traduit également une évolution du rôle de ces institutions, appelées à ne plus intervenir uniquement dans leurs cadres nationaux, mais à prendre part à une dynamique internationale multilatérale. Un repositionnement qui devrait accroître leurs capacités de coordination, d'influence et de partage d'expériences, tout en faisant émerger des espaces de convergence entre des organismes dont les systèmes et les compétences demeurent différents. Reste à dépasser le principal obstacle identifié par le président de l'INPPLC : le passage des principes à leur application. Pour Benaliou, le défi africain ne réside pas tant dans l'adoption des notions de gouvernance et d'ouverture que dans leur traduction en transformations effectives des pratiques institutionnelles. Le continent dispose, selon lui, d'atouts importants pour construire ses propres modèles, grâce à la diversité de ses expériences, à ses ressources humaines jeunes et au dynamisme de ses sociétés. « La réforme se mesure à la profondeur de son impact », a-t-il affirmé, estimant qu'une transformation réelle exige un système intégré dans lequel les institutions se répartissent les responsabilités et où la société s'engage de manière consciente et responsable. L'objectif est de faire sortir les principes de transparence, de participation et de reddition des comptes du registre des intentions pour les inscrire dans le fonctionnement quotidien des institutions. Au fond, a-t-il résumé, la lutte pour la probité est avant tout un « combat pour la confiance ». Les principes du gouvernement ouvert doivent contribuer à redéfinir les relations entre les citoyens et les institutions, en garantissant l'accès aux informations, leur compréhension et leur utilisation, mais aussi en permettant aux organismes publics d'entendre les personnes directement confrontées aux risques de corruption dans leurs démarches quotidiennes. L'ouverture institutionnelle ne saurait toutefois être évaluée à la seule multiplication des dispositifs de consultation ou des publications. Son efficacité se mesure à sa capacité à produire des changements : lorsque les contributions et les expériences des citoyens conduisent les institutions à revoir leurs priorités ou à modifier leurs méthodes d'intervention. Elle suppose également que chacun puisse connaître les engagements pris par les instances, vérifier ceux qui ont été réalisés et identifier ceux dont l'exécution reste en attente. L'évaluation de l'action institutionnelle doit ainsi s'apprécier à l'aune de ses résultats et de ses répercussions concrètes sur la vie des citoyens. Benaliou estime enfin que les institutions africaines chargées de la probité disposent des capacités nécessaires pour élaborer un modèle d'ouverture qui leur soit propre. La coopération continentale pourrait, dans cette perspective, devenir un levier de développement de l'intelligence collective et de mutualisation des connaissances et des expertises. Encore faut-il, a-t-il insisté, que cette dynamique débouche sur des initiatives concrètes, en phase avec les réalités, les capacités et les spécificités du continent. items.title: Énergie : la facture grimpe à 111 MMDH en neuf mois, Charafat Afailal mise sur un stock stratégique souverain
items.description: La facture énergétique du Maroc a atteint près de 111 milliards de dirhams (MMDH) au cours des neuf premiers mois de l'année 2026, enregistrant un bond de 37% par rapport à la période précédente. Ce constat chiffré a été dressé ce mardi 24 novembre devant la Chambre des conseillers par la ministre de l’Énergie, des Mines et du Développement durable, Charafat Afailal, qui a souligné combien ce renchérissement pèse lourdement sur les finances publiques dans un contexte international marqué par les tensions géopolitiques et la hausse des coûts de production. Vers un stock stratégique souverain sous le contrôle de l'État Face à la volatilité des marchés internationaux et aux aléas d'approvisionnement, la responsable gouvernementale a insisté sur l'impératif pour le Royaume de disposer d'un stock stratégique souverain de produits pétroliers. Conformément aux hautes hrientations royales, cette réserve doit être placée sous la responsabilité directe de l'État, seul habilité à en autoriser la mobilisation en cas de besoin, et répartie de manière équilibrée sur le territoire national afin d'en faciliter l'accès. Parallèlement à la mise en place de ce dispositif souverain, le ministère travaille en étroite coordination avec les opérateurs importateurs d'hydrocarbures pour porter les capacités nationales de stockage à 1,7 million de mètres cubes. L'objectif affiché est de consolider l'autonomie énergétique du Royaume et de prémunir le marché intérieur contre d'éventuelles ruptures d'approvisionnement liées à des crises politiques ou climatiques. Renouvelables : le Maroc en passe de franchir le cap des 60% d'ici 2030 Revenant sur le bilan de la stratégie énergétique lancée en 2009 pour réduire la dépendance extérieure du pays, Charafat Afailal s'est félicitée de la dynamique soutenue des investissements dans les énergies propres. Alors que la part des énergies renouvelables atteint aujourd'hui 47 % de la puissance électrique installée, la ministre a affirmé que le Maroc dépassera largement l'objectif initial de 52 % fixé à l'horizon 2030, pour franchir le seuil des 60 %. Qualifiant le Royaume de véritable « destination privilégiée » pour les investisseurs nationaux et étrangers dans l'éolien et le solaire, elle a également mis en avant les perspectives prometteuses de la filière de l'hydrogène vert pour intégrer durablement les énergies propres au tissu économique national. Efficacité énergétique, foncier et réseaux : les défis qui persistent La ministre a toutefois dressé un bilan lucide des chantiers qui accusent du retard. Elle a ainsi reconnu que les performances enregistrées en matière d'efficacité énergétique demeurent « très modestes » au regard de l'ambition nationale visant à réduire la consommation de 20 % d'ici 2030. Pour assurer une intégration fluide des énergies intermittentes dans le mix national, elle a plaidé pour une accélération des investissements dans les infrastructures gazières, considérées comme un pilier essentiel de la souveraineté énergétique. Enfin, Charafat Afailal a pointé deux contraintes majeures freinant le déploiement des projets renouvelables : la capacité d'absorption limitée des lignes de transport d'électricité reliant les zones de production aux bassins de consommation, ainsi que les difficultés persistantes liées à la mobilisation du foncier nécessaire aux investissements.
