items.title: Nigerian monarch, 92, suspended after sexual assault claims
items.description: One of Nigeria’s best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist. The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience. The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation – calls the Katsina state government has now heeded. Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension. He is one of several emirs – a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times – who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power. Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority. Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support. On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir’s palace on 14 November. She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap. After some moments she was heard saying: “Stop, stop” as the hands reached for her chest. According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations. The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee’s findings to determine the appropriate course of action. It said the committee’s findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served. However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report. The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

items.title: Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home
items.description: Click to expand Image Relatives of “drug war” victims hold a vigil a day before the International Criminal Court holds a pretrial hearing for former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte, on February 22, 2026 in Manila. © 2026 Ezra Acayan/Getty Images (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch said today. The ICC trial in The Hague against Duterte for crimes against humanity is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts. Families of victims seeking to file new cases face significant barriers. Meanwhile, government records and human rights group reports show that drug-war abuses continue, with police harassing, arbitrarily arresting, and at times killing suspected drug dealers and users. “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.” Between September and November 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed 13 people, including 7 drug-war victims and their families both under Duterte and Marcos, 4 human rights defenders, and 2 government officials; reviewed recent data and reporting on drug-related killings; and analyzed a database of local government Peace and Order and Public Safety Plans. Human Rights Watch also requested and received information from the Philippine Justice Department and Commission on Human Rights on drug-war cases before the courts. Relatives of drug-war victims described a justice system in which the burden of uncovering evidence of an unlawful killing fell mostly on them instead of government prosecutors. “It’s so hard to prove that you’re telling the truth,” said a woman whose husband was killed in 2016 in a police “buy-bust” drug sting operation. “It’s tiring pursuing a case here—it’s as if we can never pass the tests.” Some facing obstacles to justice have pinned their hopes on the ICC. “In the Philippines, what was our chance, given how the government works,” said another woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants in 2016. “In the ICC they are impartial, that’s where our hope is.” During the Duterte presidency from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine National Police reported 6,200 deaths during anti-drug operations, although United Nations agencies, the Philippine Commission on Human Rights, the Supreme Court, and domestic human rights groups put the number of killings by police and unidentified assailants at between 20,000 and 30,000. Only five cases of Duterte-era “drug war” killings, involving nine police officers, have resulted in convictions. Government prosecutors initiated the first three cases, following the successive murders of three teenage boys in Caloocan in August 2017, which sparked public outrage. The fourth and fifth cases—for killings in 2016—were filed through the efforts of nongovernmental legal groups and led to convictions in 2024 and 2025. In November 2024, the Justice Department created a task force to investigate and prosecute extrajudicial killings during Duterte’s “war on drugs” but only four cases it identified have advanced to trial, with three others under preliminary investigation, based on Justice Department data. EJK TASK FORCE (DOJ) - CASE ACCOMPLISHMENT & STATUS REPORTReferred To Task Force For InvestigationNumber of CasesPreliminary Legal / Operational FocusStatusFiled for Preliminary Investigation (PI)3Drafting & Preparation of Criminal ComplaintsDrafting complaints for crimes under RA 9851 & MurderFiled In Court4Criminal Prosecution / Direct Formal FilingsCase active in court / ongoing prosecutionKey Respondents & Personalities Identified Directly Named High-Profile Respondents in Criminal ComplaintsFormal Murder charges filed; Continuation of presentation of prosecution's witnessSource: Data provided by the Department of Justice of the Philippines to Human Rights Watch. The Marcos administration, after arresting and surrendering Duterte to the ICC in March 2025, announced renewed efforts to advance domestic accountability for the “drug war.” But families and human rights groups who met with Justice Department officials said that they were concerned the government’s witness protection program would not keep their families safe if they pursued charges against police officers. Meetings between victims’ groups and the Justice Department tapered off. Duterte will stand trial at the ICC for three counts of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder allegedly committed when he was mayor of Davao City, and then president between November 2011 and March 2019. The prosecution’s case focuses on a non-exhaustive list of 56 specific incidents and 87 victims, while noting that “[its] evidence demonstrates that the attack [against a civilian population] was broader than this representative sample of incidents.” The ICC is a court of last resort, only stepping in when domestic authorities are unwilling or unable to investigate and prosecute crimes under its jurisdiction. In November 2021, the Duterte government asked the ICC prosecutor to defer his investigation, opened in September 2021, claiming that national authorities had begun their own drug-war investigations of extrajudicial killings. In January 2023, ICC judges ruled that the Philippine government had failed to demonstrate that it took sufficient action to investigate and prosecute Duterte-era killings and authorized the resumption of the ICC prosecutor’s investigation. The decision was upheld on appeal. The ICC trial against Duterte begins as the court is under growing pressure from the US government, which has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick.” On October 9, the Trump administration sanctioned the ICC, escalating its attack on the court and adding to existing sanctions on ICC judges and prosecutors, three Palestinian groups, and a UN human rights expert. The Trump administration sanctions reaffirm the ICC’s critical role as a court of last resort, Human Rights Watch said. Marcos has never repudiated the “war on drugs” as a government policy and has yet to rescind the orders and other policy statements Duterte issued that underpinned the anti-drug campaign. In its review of a database of 2023-2025 local government budgets, Human Rights Watch found that 77 municipalities had allocated funds for anti-drug campaign awards and rewards, or for financial support to informants, police officials, and other local officials. Two of those municipalities, and another eight municipalities specifically referred to “neutralization” or “negation” of suspects; terms used as euphemisms for “killing” in 2016 police circular that set out the “war on drugs.” While such incentives are not necessarily unlawful, those linked to enforcement goals or operational results can create pressure to meet targets and encourage abusive practices, including extrajudicial killings. Despite a significant decline in drug-related extrajudicial killings during the Marcos administration, such killings and other abuses continue, particularly in low-income urban areas where they remain routine. As of November 7, there have been at least 1,342 public reports of drug-related killings under Marcos. These reports identified uniformed officers as responsible for 486 of those deaths. The Philippine government’s failure to hold those responsible to account perpetuates a climate of impunity. Families of drug-war victims under the Marcos administration encounter many of the same past obstacles when seeking justice, but the Justice Department has no task force or special mechanism to investigate post-Duterte cases, Human Rights Watch said. “Even if killings are down from the ghastly Duterte years, President Marcos’ pledged ‘bloodless campaign’ against drugs has been anything but bloodless,” Buan said. “To end these abuses, Marcos needs to stop the brutal ‘drug war’ and put in place a robust and impartial law enforcement and judicial system.” Elusive Justice for Killings during Duterte and Marcos Administrations Under the Duterte administration in 2020, the Justice Department opened an inter-agency panel to “reinvestigate” drug-war killings by the police. The panel identified 52 cases in which the Philippine National Police carried out internalinvestigations. However, by 2024, when Marcos was in office, the panel had only filed six cases in court. In November 2024, the Justice Department created a new task force on Duterte-era drug war killings. It began investigations anew and worked mainly with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI)—the Justice Department’s investigative arm—instead of with the police to avoid conflicts of interest when developing cases implicating police officers. Despite renewed Justice Department efforts, victims’ families still struggled to file charges. Many victims’ families who wanted to pursue charges could not do so because their relative’s death certificate declared an illness as the cause of death, even though they were found with gunshot wounds to their heads and bodies. During the height of Duterte’s “drug war,” police pressured families to sign waivers stating that they did not want to conduct autopsies or pursue charges, in exchange for faster retrievals of the bodies from funeral homes. Many families could not afford the autopsy fees, and without accurate government death records, they could not pursue charges. The woman whose husband was killed in a police operation in 2016 decided in 2022 to retrieve documents about his killing from the police because she believed the climate of fear had lifted under Marcos. “They were not really helping us,” she said. “They just left us there to search their logbooks.” Police officials had named the woman’s husband as a drug suspect killed in an “armed encounter” in a news report that featured her children wailing for their dead father. Yet she never found a police report of the operation, only a record of bystanders injured. She was unable to prove he was shot dead, because his death certificate lists the cause of death as pneumonia and his body was cremated. Government investigators have not pursued a case. The woman recalled the one conversation with the Justice Department: “They said, ‘If you have no document like police report or autopsy, it’s hard to file a case.’ So, what about me? I had no documents.” The woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants did not know for years the circumstances under which her husband was killed. She found his body with gunshot wounds at a funeral home in 2016 and signed a waiver not to conduct an autopsy. His death certificate listed pneumonia as cause of death. After Marcos became president, the woman sought help from a nonprofit law group. In 2023, she had her husband’s body exhumed and examined by a forensic pathologist, Raquel Fortun. The autopsy showed that he died from gunshot wounds to the head. That year, she finally found the police report from the night her husband died. It stated that police responding to reports of gunshots found him dead with three sachets of crystal meth, and a piece of cardboard that read “I’m a drug pusher, don’t be like me.” She had an interview with the NBI, who told her they had also summoned local officials and the funeral home. But nothing further happened in the investigation. “No one has followed up with me, I still wonder what happened to that NBI case,” she said. Fortun became a commissioner of the Philippine Truth Commission, a civil society initiative working closely with the Catholic Church to investigate Duterte-era drug war crimes. She has recorded 13 cases in which people were shot and killed but whose death certificates cite illnesses such as heart attack, pneumonia, and high blood pressure as causes of death. Fortun said during a Truth Commission briefing that government prosecutors have pushed back when presented with evidence of falsified death certificates in court. In one case, the government prosecutor acted on behalf of the defendant, instead of the victim: “I was grilled in cross-examination, and I was surprised that it was the prosecutor. I don’t understand it. So if you’re a poor family with a similar case, would you still have it corrected. It’s so hard.” The Commission on Human Rights told Human Rights Watch that its investigations of Duterte-era drug-war killings have resulted in cases moving through the justice system. Between 2016 and 2023, 25 cases were filed in court, 37 cases at the Office of the Ombudsman, and 42 with the Justice Department. No further progress was reported by the commission on the cases filed. The commission has no prosecutorial power and can only file cases in a manner similar to private complainants. Despite the Commission on Human Right’s limited powers, families seek confirmation from the commission that they have been victims of rights violations, which entitles them to limited financial assistance under the commission’s internal rules of procedure. Yet the commission denied assistance for lack of evidence to two women whose husbands were fatally shot in 2016. Only the woman who exhumed her husband’s body was able to challenge the decision; after she submitted the postmortem examination report in August 2026, the commission told her to file a petition for reinvestigation. “I just want to prove that what I’m saying is the truth,” she said. The commission told Human Rights Watch that it created its own task force, which is currently reinvestigating 493 cases of Duterte-era drug-war killings, with the goal of resolving 140 before the end of 2026. Duterte-Era Drug-War Policy Persists The mother of a man killed by police in Central Luzon in 2022—after Marcos became president—said that she tried to pursue murder charges. She cited a witness who told her that her son was lured to the location the night of the killing, and an autopsy report that indicated he had been shot execution-style and not during an armed encounter as police had claimed. The witness has since gone missing. Prosecutors dismissed her case twice, most recently in 2025, because a medical expert’s testimony was required. The mother said that she was working on finding a medical expert to testify, but even just the cost of reproducing copies of documents was weighing on her. No special task force has been created to investigate alleged drug-war crimes under the Marcos government. The government has claimed that its anti-drug campaign is “bloodless” and that “rather than resorting to violence, it focuses on strengthening prevention and rehabilitation efforts.” But Human Rights Watch found that disturbing Duterte-era language, such as “neutralization,” remains in plans for current anti-drugs campaigns. There is no legal definition of “neutralization,” but on July 1, 2016, Duterte’s police chief, Ronald Dela Rosa, issued Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, the operational document for the anti-drug campaign, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals. In 2017, two human rights groups, the Center for International Law (CenterLaw) and the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), filed petitions before the Supreme Court seeking to declare the anti-drug campaign unconstitutional, citing the use of the word “neutralization” in the circular. The Supreme Court has yet to rule on the case. ICC prosecutors have accused Duterte of developing “a State policy to ‘neutralize’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines who were perceived or alleged to be involved in drug-related and other crimes,” noting the language in the circular. In November 2025, the ICC issued a sealed arrest warrant for Dela Rosa. He is alleged to be responsible for the crime against humanity of murder as part of a common plan together with other co-perpetrators—including Duterte—with the aim of killing drug suspects between 2011 and 2019. This included issuing the Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals. The ICC unsealed the warrant in May 2026; Dela Rosa has since gone into hiding. The Marcos government has not rescinded that circular, but in 2024 the Philippine National Police told lawmakers that they were actually following a new circular without the word “neutralize.” The Marcos government also committed todrug policy reform as part of a US$4 million joint human rights program with the United Nations. A 2026 study by two organizations, No Box Philippines and Harm Reduction International, found that the Philippine government was still allocating millions of US dollars for local anti-drug campaigns whose policy documents retained similar language to the original circular, such as “neutralization” and “negation.” Their findings were based on an analysis of 2023-2025 local government “Peace and Order and Public Safety” budgets. Local governments are supervised by the Department of Interior and Local Government, the executive department that also supervises the police. Human Rights Watch analyzed local government plans obtained by the two groups, and found that 85 towns, municipalities, and cities allocated funds for rewards, awards, and incentives for successful anti-drug operations, including 10 municipalities where the funds were specifically for “conducting negation operations” or “neutralizing drug personalities.” During the Duterte presidency, for an area to declare itself “drug-free,” local councils had to monitor, surveil, and compile a drug “watch list.” Human rights groups frequently alleged the lists determined who would be killed, whether the assailants were police officers or masked police agents. Under public safety plans in effect under Marcos, local governments still offer financial rewards for making their areas “drug-free,” by giving “incentives to assets,” or “awards/rewards for significant illegal drugs accomplishment” or “neutralization of drug personalities.” ICC prosecutors alleged in their case against Duterte that “law enforcement personnel knew that extrajudicial killings would result in them being financially rewarded.” There have been fewer drug-related killings under Marcos, but human rights defenders who live in drug-war hotspots in Metro Manila and neighboring provinces said abuses continued. “Their raids are not as brazen, but they still plant evidence,” one rights defender said. The quota system—the number of arrests and kills under Duterte to qualify for rewards—“was still alive.” Arbitrary Arrest, Extortion Under Marcos, human rights defenders monitoring drug-war abuses in their communities have observed that the police are more likely to extort victims than to kill them, targeting many of the same people who were on drug “watch lists.” They said police still arbitrarily arrest people, threaten them with drug charges, and then detain them on criminal anti-street-gambling charges with lighter penalties. The Philippine organization PhilRights has documented that “police officers offer to cover the victims’ release costs in exchange for repayment with interest, effectively profiting from the arrest.” In 2025, a man came home one night to find police officers in the vicinity, his sister said. “They patted him down and found nothing,” she said. “But a police informant handed sachets of crystal meth and forced him to admit it was his.” The police arrested the man and took his bicycle. She said she made several visits to the police station where her brother had been detained. The police officials told her he had been charged with gambling. “I told them, ‘You said you found drugs, now the charge is gambling. How long are you detaining him?’” she said. “They told us we can ‘just pay P10,000 [$160].’ But we had no money at all at the time.” The sister took a month processing documents in several police stations before her brother was released. He was detained for a month without being brought before a judge in violation of his rights. “We can still see them surveilling our area from time to time,” the sister said.

items.title: Tambuwal commends Gov Ododo for granting ADC access to Buhari Square
items.description: Former Sokoto State Governor and African Democratic Congress chieftain, Aminu Tambuwal, has commended Kogi State Governor, Usman Ododo, for allowing the ADC to hold its rally at Muhammadu Buhari Square in the state. Tambuwal described the gesture as an act of statesmanship, saying political differences should not prevent leaders from respecting democratic rights and promoting peaceful coexistence. In a post on X on Tuesday, he thanked Ododo for granting the opposition party access to the venue, noting that such actions strengthened democracy and encouraged political tolerance. “I wish to express my sincere appreciation to the Governor of Kogi State, His Excellency, for his commendable show of statesmanship in granting the African Democratic Congress (ADC) the use of Muhammadu Buhari Square for its rally in Kogi State,” he said. Tambuwal said the governor’s action demonstrated that disagreements over political affiliations should not undermine the right of citizens and parties to participate in the democratic process. He said democracy was strengthened when political leaders respected the constitutional rights of others to assemble, associate and express their views regardless of party differences. The former governor also praised Kogi residents for their conduct during the rally, commending them for maintaining peace and order throughout the event. Tambuwal urged political leaders to promote tolerance and avoid treating political opponents as adversaries, stressing that disagreements should be settled through the exchange of ideas. “Democracy is not a contest of enemies but a contest of ideas, and that our political differences must never overshadow our shared commitment to the peace, unity and progress of our country,” he said. The post Tambuwal commends Gov Ododo for granting ADC access to Buhari Square appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
items.description: US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a “good corporate citizen” while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation. Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang’s security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump’s involvement in Huang’s comeback. Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: “I don’t know what you’re talking about.” Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia. The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China. In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 “for potential export control violations” . But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has “hundreds, if not more” export investigations occurring at any one time. “So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” he said. Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen. “Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn’t be the message that the president is saying to the American people. “It shouldn’t be what my message would be either.” While Nvidia’s stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang’s reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading. The company’s share price closed down nearly 6% – still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang’s return. The company’s board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia’s board, said Huang’s return was in the “best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”. The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk. On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company’s directors and convinced them to bring back Huang . Huang’s reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger. Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have “ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang”. Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang’s behaviour “doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips”. Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump’s “direct involvement” with Nvidia’s decision “raises serious national security and corruption questions”. Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to “investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement”.

items.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
items.description: Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US, AP reports. In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage. Huawei’s defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm’s success was due to its own innovation. In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal “confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years”. Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019. During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms ensure it had a competitive edge. However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said Huawei had grown into business with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff through hard work.

items.title: 21e Semaine du numérique: les fortes annonces de Moov Africa sur les tarifs de ses offres
items.description: Le Directeur général de Moov Africa-ONATEL au Burkina Faso, Mohamed Karim, a annoncé, «une baisse significative allant jusqu'à 65% des tarifs» des offres de sa société, ce mardi 24 novembre 2026, à l’ouverture de la 21e édition de la Semaine du numérique (SN) qui se tient du 24 au 27 novembre à Ouagadougou. Le thème de cette édition est: «Souveraineté technologique: accélérer la transformation digitale sécurisée et inclusive». C’est le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo qui a donné le top départ de l’activité. Le chef du gouvernement, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a ouvert ce mardi 24 novembre 2026, la 21e édition de la Semaine du numérique qui se déroulera dans la capitale burkinabè sur quatre jours autour du thème: «Souveraineté technologique: accélérer la transformation digitale sécurisée et inclusive». Les acteurs du domaine que sont des cadres de l’administration, des responsables de startups et des experts, entre autres, échangeront sur la thématique lors des ateliers et des compétitions. Une vue du présidium à l'ouverture de la 21e Semaine du numérique Cette semaine numérique traitera des infrastructures, de la cybersécurité, de l'innovation locale et de la gouvernance numérique dans l'espace confédéral. Plusieurs activités permettront aux entreprises et aux jeunes de présenter leurs solutions et leurs compétences et de rencontrer des partenaires susceptibles de les accompagner. Moov Africa-ONATEL annonce la vente d’«un smartphone 4G accessible au prix exceptionnel de 20 000 francs» Pour cette édition, Moov Africa-ONATEL est sponsor officiel. Dès l’entrée du Salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO) et à l’intérieur de la salle de la cérémonie, les couleurs et autres visuels de l’opérateur de téléphonie visaient à faire comprendre l’implication active de la société à la manifestation. Pour le premier responsable de la téléphonie, Mohamed Karim, Moov Africa-ONATEL sera toujours présent aux côtés de l’Etat pour un Burkina Faso plus connecté, plus inclusif, plus performant en matière de numérique. Le directeur général de Moov Africa-ONATEL prononçant son discours En tant qu'opérateur global, partenaire historique de développement numérique, Moov Africa-ONATEL, s’inscrit dans l’ambition nationale de la souveraineté numérique. «Nous sommes convaincus que la transformation digitale doit être accessible à chaque citoyen, à chaque entreprise et à chaque administration. C'est dans cet esprit que nous poursuivons depuis plusieurs années un vaste programme d'investissement visant à moderniser nos infrastructures de télécommunications, renforcer la qualité de services et démocratiser l'accès aux très hauts débits», a souligné Mohamed Karim, directeur général de Moov Africa-ONATEL dont l’engagement s'inscrit dans la vision nationale de souveraineté numérique. A cet effet, Moov Africa-ONATEL en appel à engager la construction d'infrastructures d'hébergement et de stockage de données à travers un datacenter moderne qui sera mis à la disposition des différents acteurs économiques nationaux. «Cette infrastructure contribue à renforcer l'hébergement des données sur le territoire national, à sécuriser les traitements numériques et à favoriser l'émergence d'un écosystème numérique national plus résilient et plus souverain conformément au chantier zéro donné à l'extérieur», a-t-il fait comprendre. Une vue des membres du gouvernement L’engagement de Moov Africa-ONATEL s'exprime également à travers sa participation active au Programme national d'inclusion numérique de couverture du territoire à travers l'initiative «Zéro zone blanche». «Nous sommes fiers de participer aux côtés de l'État aux projets structurants de réduction de la fracture numérique», s’est réjoui Mohamed Karim, pour qui, cet événement est également l'occasion pour l’opérateur de réaffirmer sa volonté de nourrir et d’offrir toujours plus de valeur à ses clients. «Nous sommes heureux d'annoncer plusieurs avancées majeures qui sont officiellement présentées dans cet événement. Nous procéderons ainsi à une baisse significative allant jusqu'à 65% des tarifs de nos offres FTTH, tout en augmentant les débits à l'ensemble de nos clients résidentiels et professionnels. Nous lançons également une nouvelle offre fibre optique permettant d'atteindre un débit de 500 mégabits par second (Mbps), positionnant le Burkina Faso parmi les pays les plus avancés de la région en matière d'accès au très haut débit fixe», a-t-il révélé. Selon le Directeur général, à cette évolution, le débit minimum proposé sur leurs propres FTTH sera «désormais 100 Mbps, accompagné d'une offre promotionnelle attractive à 10 000 francs seulement». Parce que l'inclusion numérique commence par l'accès aux équipements, Moov Africa-ONATEL lancera également «un smartphone 4G accessible au prix exceptionnel de 20 000 francs, afin de permettre à un plus grand nombre de Burkinabè d’accéder aux usages numériques et les opportunités qu'il offre. Ces initiatives traduisent une conviction profonde. La transformation digitale ne doit laisser personne au bord du chemin», foi du DG Mohamed Karim qui a invité l'ensemble des visiteurs à découvrir les innovations de sa société et à échanger avec leurs experts pour découvrir davantage leurs produits et leurs services. Enfin, le premier responsable de Moov-Africa-ONATEL lance un appel aux acteurs du numérique à unir davantage leurs forces, développer des solutions conçues au Burkina Faso pour répondre aux besoins des populations burkinabè. «Ensemble, faisons du numérique un levier de création de richesse, d'inclusion sociale et de souveraineté économique», a-t-il conclu. «Au deuxième trimestre 2026, notre pays comptait 328 764 abonnements à l'Internet fixe et 20 439 942 à l'Internet mobile» «Les réseaux et les plateformes soutiennent désormais nos services publics et notre économie. Une panne, une attaque ou la perte de donnée peut perturber le pays. Nous devons être capables de prévenir les risques, de rétablir nos services et de décider par nous-mêmes», a déclaré le Premier ministre Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo. Cette exigence, selon le chef de l’Exécutif, concerne les systèmes de l'administration tout comme les outils dont dépendent les entreprises nationales et les citoyens. «Au deuxième trimestre 2026, notre pays comptait 328 764 abonnements à l'Internet fixe et 20 439 942 à l'Internet mobile», a-t-il soutenu. Le Premier ministre Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo a présidé la cérémonie d'ouverture de la SN 2026 Cette progression rend plus présente l'obligation d'assurer un accès fiable et utile aux Burkinabè. Pour y parvenir, l'action du gouvernement s'organise autour de trois priorités. «La première est la maîtrise de nos infrastructures et de nos données. Deux centres de données modulaires de l'administration ont été achevés en 2025. Leur sécurité, leur maintenance et leur fonctionnement continu doivent être garantis. Chaque investissement doit répondre à un besoin réel et prévoir les ressources humaines et financières nécessaires à sa durée. Nos administrations doivent savoir où sont conservées leurs données, qui y accèdent et comment les récupérer», a affirmé Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo. La deuxième priorité, a poursuivi le patron de la cérémonie, est la simplification des services publics et l'essor de l’économie numérique nationale. «Numériser une procédure ne suffit pas. Nous devons supprimer les étapes inutiles et réduire les déplacements et les délais pour les usagers. Nous devons revoir les procédures avant de les mettre en ligne en tenant compte des besoins concrets des populations», a-t-il soutenu. Photo de famille Pour la troisième priorité, il concerne la sécurité des services et leur accessibilité. «La cybersécurité et la protection des données personnelles doivent être intégrées vers la conception des services. Chaque projet doit prévoir la prévention des incidents, la continuité des services essentiels et l'information des usagers. J'invite les services compétents à poursuivre l'extension de la connectivité et à agir avec les opérateurs sur la qualité et le coût», a laissé entendre le Premier ministre qui veut qu’avec le Mali et le Niger, l’Alliance des Etats du Sahel (AES) donne un contenu concret à la coopération numérique de la Confédération. «Former des spécialistes, partager certaines infrastructures et coordonner nos réponses aux menaces. Chaque projet commun devra préciser les moyens engagés et renforcer notre capacité de décision. Nos entreprises doivent pouvoir proposer les solutions adaptées aux besoins et en assurer la maintenance. Nos universités et centres de formation doivent préparer les compétences dont nos projets ont besoin», a-t-il souligné. Les patrons de téléphonie appelés à l'union pour réduire la fracture numérique Il faut noter que la 21ᵉ édition de la Semaine du numérique 2026 est couplée au Salon international des technologies de l'information, de la communication et de la bureautique (SITICO). items.title: Retraite de Forécariah : le gouvernement lance la « doctrine Mamadi Doumbouya »
items.description: Au terme de trois jours de travaux intensifs à Forécariah, le Premier ministre, Amadou Oury Bah, a refermé, ce mardi 24 novembre, la retraite gouvernementale en donnant le coup d’envoi de ce qu’il a présenté comme la « doctrine Mamadi Doumbouya : la neutralité stratégique pour une stabilité durable ». Dans son allocution de clôture, le chef du gouvernement a voulu inscrire l’action de l’exécutif dans une double dynamique : renforcer la discipline interne et l’efficacité budgétaire à court terme, tout en adossant l’État à une boussole stratégique de long terme. Dès l’entame de son discours, Amadou Oury Bah a exprimé sa gratitude au président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, saluant une vision qui fixe le cap de la nation et une confiance que l’équipe gouvernementale entend honorer par des résultats concrets. Il a également remercié les conseillers de la présidence mobilisés à l’ouverture, les équipes de la primature, du Secrétariat général du gouvernement, les personnels techniques et logistiques ainsi que les autorités locales de Forécariah pour leur accueil. Félicitant les ministres pour avoir accepté l’épreuve exigeante de la confrontation collégiale de leurs dossiers avec franchise et loyauté, le Premier ministre a souligné que ces échanges ont transformé les habitudes de travail en faisant ressortir l’interdépendance des départements et l’intérêt de préparer les projets en lien étroit avec les organes chargés du suivi de leur exécution. Au-delà de la cohésion affichée, le chef de la primature a insisté sur la nécessité d’un État qui prépare avant de s’engager, rompant avec le traitement isolé des dossiers. Il a annoncé un calendrier précis pour ancrer cette rigueur : une revue systématique des blocages des projets, ministère par ministère, avant la fin de l’année en cours, suivie en 2027 de la mise en œuvre du budget-programme liant chaque crédit à un responsable et à un résultat mesurable, ainsi que de la remise en début d’année de lettres de mission traduisant les priorités communes en engagements assignés à chaque département. Le suivi sera assuré par le Secrétariat général du gouvernement en liaison avec le cabinet du Premier ministre, ce dernier promettant un arbitrage personnel sur tout blocage porté à sa connaissance. Cette exigence de méthode s’est accompagnée de l’annonce de l’approbation, la veille 23 novembre par le conseil d’administration du Fonds monétaire international, du programme économique et financier de la Guinée pour la période 2026-2029. Pour Amadou Oury Bah, cette décision consacre les réformes engagées et le travail des administrations, mais constitue surtout un premier jalon qui impose d’en produire d’autres perceptibles dans le quotidien des citoyens. Élargissant son propos aux fondements historiques et géopolitiques du pays, le Premier ministre a rappelé que la Guinée s’est forgée à la croisée des héritages de la Haute-Guinée, du Fouta, de la Basse-Guinée et de la Guinée forestière, unis bien avant l’indépendance par les échanges de cola, de sel et d’or et convergents vers le choix de 1958. De cette mémoire collective découle, selon lui, une doctrine d’État fondée sur la souveraineté de la République, la primauté de l’intérêt national et la neutralité face aux rivalités entre grandes puissances afin de coopérer avec tous sans dépendre d’aucun. En orientant les ressources nationales vers la transformation économique dans le sillage du programme Simandou 2040, cette doctrine se veut à la fois une feuille de route pour les ministres, une règle de conduite pour les agents publics et un horizon de prospérité durable.

items.title: Les « daara » partenaires dénoncent le retard des financements
items.description: Les «daara » partenaires du Projet d’amélioration des performances du système éducatif (Papse) ont organisé une conférence de presse, hier, à Keur Massar pour attirer l’attention des autorités compétentes et l’opinion publique sur leurs difficultés. Celles-ci, selon eux, sont la conséquence du non-respect des engagements pris. Dans le cadre du Projet d’amélioration des performances du système éducatif (Papse), 1098 «daara » (écoles coraniques) étaient sélectionnées en s’engageant à produire les résultats attendus au titre d’un contrat de performance. Deux ans plus tard, les maîtres coraniques disent avoir constaté que les engagements qui ont été pris envers eux n’ont pas été respectés. Craignant que cette situation ne déteint sur les performances attendues d’eux, ils sont montés au créneau pour lancer un cri du cœur. Coordonnateur de l’association nationale des écoles coraniques partenaires du Papse, Oumar Ba a révélé hier lors d’une conférence de presse à Keur Massar que 150.000 FCfa étaient prévus par élève coranique, mais aucun versement n’a été fait pendant l’année 2025, date du démarrage du projet. Pour l’année 2026, un seul versement a été effectué, alors que l’année arrive à son terme et que les engagements financiers restent largement insatisfaits. « Cette situation place les «daara » dans de grandes difficultés qui compliquent leur fonctionnement, faisant qu’elles poursuivent difficilement leurs missions éducatives et sociales », a-t-il indiqué. Dans le même ordre, il a ajouté que les «daara » partenaires souhaitent obtenir des précisions sur le montant total prévu pour l’accompagnement financier des «daara » partenaires du Papse. « Quels sont les montants réels qui ont effectivement été décaissés par les partenaires financiers et transférés ? », s’interroge-t-il en se demandant quelle est la situation exacte des financements destinés aux «daara » ayant signé les contrats de performances. Le porte-parole des maîtres coraniques s’interroge sur le fait que les «daara » n’ont-ils reçu aucun versement en 2025,et un seul en 2026. De la même manière, Oumar Ba et ses camarades souhaitent disposer du calendrier précis du paiement des tranches restantes et de celui de mise à disposition des équipements et matériels annoncés aux «daara ». En effet, face à un tel désarroi, les maîtres coraniques sollicitent des autorités la publication d’informations claires sur les fonds prévus, décaissés et effectivement transférés aux «daara ». Ils demandent également la clarification des raisons du retard des paiements de même que la communication d’un calendrier précis et officiel pour le règlement des montants prévus dans des contrats de performance. La clarification de la situation des «daara » qui ont signé leurs contrats et qui n’ont pas encore bénéficié de l’accompagnement attendu fait aussi partie des exigences des maitres coraniques. Il en est de même de la distribution des équipements et matériels prévus dans le cadre du projet. Après avoir reconnu l’importance du Papse et les efforts consentis pour améliorer les conditions d’apprentissage dans les «daara », ils ont appelé les autorités compétentes, les responsables du projet et les partenaires concernés à ouvrir un dialogue sérieux afin de trouver rapidement des solutions. Abdou DIOP

items.title: DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
items.description: The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east. The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following “poor weather conditions”. The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added. On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a plane of the same type that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province. Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive. On Tuesday, the FRN said the plane they had shot down was a Cessna 208, which had been “converted into a light attack aircraft” enabling it “to carry and launch precision-guided bombs and missiles”. Its wreckage now lies 10km (6 miles) from Minembwe, a rebel statement said, adding that a Ugandan and South African “mercenaries” had been captured. The BBC has not independently verified the rebel claim, or whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one the rebels say they shot down. South Africa’s government has not commented, while Uganda’s military has denied any involvement. A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: “UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company.” The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed. Gen Kainerugaba later posted that “no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]”. Uganda’s denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane’s wreckage. In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man’s identity. He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors. South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a “mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy”. “Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC,” deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet. In 2022, DR Congo’s army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it. The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels. In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas. The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year. Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services. Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities. The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

items.title: Man jailed for 48 months for stabbing firefighter
items.description: The Achimota Circuit Court has sentenced a 21-year-old unemployed man to 48 months’ imprisonment for stabbing a firefighter during a firefighting operation at Adjiringanor in Accra. Sampson Azumah was convicted of causing unlawful harm after attacking a Ghana National Fire Service (GNFS) officer with a screwdriver on November 14, 2025. Chief Inspector Emmanuel Addo, the prosecutor, told the court that the complainant, Leslie Adjei Tetteh, is a firefighter stationed at the GNFS Headquarters and resides in Teshie, while Azumah lives in Adjiringanor in the East Legon area. He said the incident occurred at about 2330 hours, when firefighters responded to a fire at an eight-room, single-storey residential building owned by Ms Yvonne Okoro. The fire attracted several residents, including Azumah, who was among the bystanders. The prosecutor said some bystanders pelted the firefighters with stones while they worked to extinguish the blaze. He said after the fire had been brought under control, the complainant was folding a fire hose when Azumah emerged from the crowd and accused him of deliberately sprinkling water on him. Azumah pulled a screwdriver from his waist bag and stabbed the firefighter in the left arm before fleeing the scene. The injured officer was rushed to hospital for treatment and later reported the matter to the East Legon Police. Chief Inspector Addo said the police issued the complainant with a medical form for treatment. He said police arrested Azumah at his hideout on November 17, 2025. During the investigation, Azumah admitted the offence, and police recovered the screwdriver used in the attack. Azumah, who pleaded not guilty to the charge, was found guilty after trial and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment.

items.title: I have an incurable form of cancer - Farooq Oreagba opens up
items.description: The Managing Director of NG Clearing Limited, Farooq Oreagba, has disclosed that he is living with an incurable form of cancer, saying his treatment is progressing well and he hopes to return to remission next year. The 60-year-old investment banker said he was diagnosed on February 4 following a medical screening but had continued working and maintaining his lifestyle despite the condition. In an interview with TheCable Lifestyle on Monday, Oreagba said he had learnt to manage the illness and remained optimistic about his recovery. “I have an incurable form of cancer. It comes, I treat, and it goes. I was diagnosed in February, after which I rode at Ojude Oba, celebrated my 60th and continued as if nothing was wrong,” he said. Oreagba said he was responding well to treatment and expected to return to remission around March or April 2027. “I am very fine, working as usual and doing what I always do. My treatment is going well, and I expect to be back in remission by March/April next year,” he added. Popularly known as the ‘King of Steeze’, Oreagba became an internet sensation in 2024 after his stylish appearance and horseback display at the Ojude Oba Festival in Ijebu-Ode, Ogun State, attracted widespread attention. However, his battle with cancer dates back to 2014, when he was diagnosed with bone marrow and skin cancer. He underwent a transplant in August of that year and has since continued managing the condition, receiving treatment in Johannesburg, South Africa. Oreagba urged Nigerians to prioritise routine medical examinations, saying his condition was detected early during a screening exercise. He said he undergoes medical checks every three months, adding that people should not wait until they experience symptoms before seeking medical attention. “Early detection saves lives, and I recommend regular checks. I do mine every three months, but even every six months would suffice,” he said. He added, “It is important to know that a cancer diagnosis is not a death sentence. I am making great progress.” The post I have an incurable form of cancer - Farooq Oreagba opens up appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nnamdi Kanu’s appeal: Earlier hearing date still being pursued — Lawyer
items.description: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — The legal team of detained Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) leader, Mazi Nnamdi Kanu, says efforts are still being considered to secure an earlier hearing date for his appeal against conviction, insisting that the January 25, 2027 date is not sacrosanct. Kanu’s Special Counsel, Aloy Ejimakor, disclosed this in a press release on Tuesday, clarifying that the legal team had contemplated moving the appeal forward almost two months ago when the January 25 date was initially communicated to Kanu and his lawyers. Ejimakor said the decision to seek an earlier hearing had remained unchanged, dismissing any impression that the scheduled date was a settled matter. He explained that the Rules of Court allow an appellant to formally apply for an abridgment of time, a procedural mechanism through which a court can be asked to fast-track an appeal and hear it earlier than originally scheduled. According to him, the option remains under active consideration in view of the critical issues involved in the appeal and the urgency attached to it. “Nothing is yet set in stone,” Ejimakor declared, assuring that legal avenues for expediting the hearing remained available and were being carefully weighed to prevent justice from being delayed. The clarification comes amid expectations surrounding Kanu’s appeal, with his legal team signalling its intention to explore available judicial procedures to bring forward the hearing date. Ejimakor, who signed the statement on behalf of Kanu, said the pursuit of an earlier date had been on the table since the original January 25, 2027, date was made known to the defendant and his lawyers. The legal team, however, did not disclose whether an application for abridgment of time had already been formally filed or when such an application might be made. Kanu was sentenced to life imprisonment since November, 2025, and his efforts to appeal the judgment have suffered unnecessary setbacks for one year. The post Nnamdi Kanu’s appeal: Earlier hearing date still being pursued — Lawyer appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Two arrested on suspicion of burglary at Prince and Princess of Wales’s Norfolk home
items.description: Two men have been arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespass at the Prince and Princess of Wales’s country home on the Sandringham estate, police say. Norfolk Police said it received a call just before 18:00 GMT on Monday following a report of suspicious activity at Anmer Hall. Police deployed dogs, drones and a helicopter to search the area and arrested two men on the estate, who remain in custody. The property was unoccupied at the time, police added. Kensington Palace said it did not comment on security matters. William and Catherine do not live at Anmer Hall full-time, but use the estate as a country retreat during the holidays. Val Blackmur, an 83-year-old resident who lives on the road leading up to the house, told the BBC it was “amazing” if anybody had been “stupid” enough to try breaking in. The country retreat, which has 10 bedrooms, was a gift to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II following their wedding in 2011. The red brick Georgian mansion is on the private Sandringham estate in Norfolk and is about two miles (3km) east from Sandringham House, one of the King’s private residences. The Prince and Princess’s main home is on the Windsor Castle estate in Berkshire. The Sandringham estate spans approximately 31 sq miles (80 sq km). Members of the public can visit it, although the house and its gardens are currently closed. The Royal Parkland, which is the woodland to the west of the main house, is open to the public all year round. Many other members of the Royal Family also live on the estate, including Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, who moved on to Marsh Farm in February. Despite tight security around members of the Royal Family, there have been several intrusions on their property in recent decades. One of the more recent incidents was in 2024, when Thames Valley Police said burglars had broken into a farm on the Windsor Castle estate and stolen two vehicles. Val Blackmur said in all the 50 years she had lived near Anmer Hall, she had not heard of a break-in happening in the area Blackmur said: “We never seem to have any trouble so when something out of the ordinary happens that sort of makes you prick your ears up and think, what was all that about?” The 83-year-old said it was not unusual to hear police cars or helicopters in the area. “We’ve lived here 50 years now… we’ve never heard nothing like that,” she said. “Up at Anmer Hall it’s so secluded and out of the way, not in full view – I should think people would be shocked.”

items.title: Hunter remanded for allegedly shooting charcoal producer
items.description: The Nkawie Circuit Court has remanded a hunter into police custody for allegedly shooting a charcoal producer in a forest in the Atwima Nwabiagya South Municipality of the Ashanti Region. The court did not take Abanga Aminga’s plea because police investigations were ongoing. He is expected to reappear before the court on December 11, 2026, to answer charges of causing harm and possession of firearms without authority. Police Sergeant Ernest Derry, prosecuting, told the court, presided over by Mr Robert Addo, that the complainant, Charles Afriyie, was the Unit Committee Chairman of Bayerebon Number Seven, near Nyinahin in the Atwima Mponua District. He said the suspect was both a hunter and a charcoal producer in the Bayerebon community, where the victim, Mahama Yussif, also engaged in charcoal production. The prosecution said that on November 19, 2026, at about 1000 hours, the victim went to burn charcoal in the Asenano Forest, where he was allegedly shot. He reportedly saw the suspect holding a gun about 20 metres away and pursued him while bleeding profusely and screaming, but the suspect escaped through the bush. The victim made his way home, where he met a farmer popularly known as Checki, who called another farmer, Umar. Together, they assisted him home. They rushed him to the Bayerebon Number Seven Clinic for first aid and later transferred him to the Nyinahin Government Hospital for further treatment. He later reported the incident to the Nyinahin Police, and on November 20, 2026, some youth in the town arrested the suspect and handed him over to the police. During investigations, the suspect led the police to the forest, where a locally manufactured single-barrel gun and two cartridges of ammunition were retrieved. The suspect admitted possessing the firearm and the two cartridges but denied shooting the victim with the gun. Following preliminary investigations, he was charged and brought before the court.

items.title: A Good Gift Is More Ordinary Than You Think
items.description: This is an edition of Ordinary Extraordinary, Ian Bogost’s guide to making everyday life vivid. Sign up for the newsletter here. The holidays are the worst time to give a gift. Expectations are just too high. Chocolate or socks received on a random Wednesday in August would be incredible; the same socks on Father’s Day or chocolate on Valentine’s Day veer toward cliché. A gift is a paradox: As it becomes more socially expected, it also becomes harder to give well. I learned to give gifts from my late mother, who was terrible at gift giving no matter the time of year. She would agree to buy a specific thing for my kids but renege at the last minute, for mysterious reasons. Or she’d ask for the kids’ clothing sizes, then send garments in different ones. Once, she bought me a new set of flatware—nice!—but not in sufficient quantity to actually supply the kitchen, so I had to buy more to make the gift useful. Over the years, my wife received innumerable scarves and folk-art objects that matched Mom’s tastes but not her own. Mom didn’t mean to be terrible at gift giving, and I now understand her effort as a struggle rather than a slight. She seemed to recognize that she couldn’t conceptualize the desires of other people. Often, she tried to make up for that deficiency with sheer volume. A birthday parcel would contain lots of little junk—the kind of stuff you’d collect as trade-show swag. Each delivered the earnest desire to make a gift connect, along with the tragedy of connection’s failure. In the end, by getting the practice so wrong, Mom gave me the gift of understanding gifts better. The best gifts give something greater than any one thing: the message that you know the recipient in a nuanced and personal way. To give well is first to see, and to receive well is to allow yourself to be seen. This is very hard to do. Over time, people have developed ways to reduce gift giving’s burden: Wish lists, for example, were once limited to kids but now cross generations. Telling someone else exactly what you want is good, in that it disambiguates desire. But it also frees a person from the difficult work that can make a gift truly meaningful. Think about the people closest to you—your spouse or children or parents, for example. You know so much about them, but when it comes to thinking of a gift, you might find yourself stumped. My wife likes knitting. I could try to learn about yarn or yarn-wrangling tools, and doing so might connect me to her through a deeper understanding of her interests. But it could also lead me astray. When I think about my own hobbies and avocations—home espresso and gelato, for example—I closely guard my tools and materials and don’t want someone else getting involved. Similarly, my adult son is really into photography, and because of that passion I know that he already owns a version of almost anything I might think of. Setting aside the most obvious interests of your gift recipient can help avoid this mess. But doing so makes giving a gift even harder, because now you must find an even less apparent feature of the other person to develop into an opportunity for communion. Unfortunately, this is where many people settle on options from the gift-guide mainstay, “the person who has everything.” That usually means things nobody wants or needs—superfluous curiosities such as a neck massager or an electric gravy warmer. An indulgent or expensive gift might also not fit the bill. You might feel formidable or magnanimous when you give a lavish gift, but receiving one can be disquieting. Or, if a wish list is on offer, it might entice you to choose a variation on the category of item listed. Do not do this; this is very bad. (Everyone remembers getting the wrong version of the popular toy as a kid.) Understandably, you will want to make your mark on their wishes. But the best gift is not about you at all—not even your generosity in the giving. A gift entails the attempt to set yourself aside as much as possible, and to wrap a bow around the most nuanced and tender understanding of someone else that you can muster. To do this, you will have to dig deep. Think back over the past year or so, and try to recall when your gift recipient may have revealed a desire, problem, aspiration, or fact that felt distinctive. I’m not talking about a specific yearning for a consumer good, although that is one option. I mean a moment that, when revisited, reveals something fundamental about their current self. Focus on the most ordinary events and encounters, the ones even the person on your mind may not remember. Those moments can offer the richest information about what makes someone who they are. Perhaps a friend delighted at a specific jam served at a brunch out. Maybe, while unloading the dishwasher, a family member noted that their favorite old teaspoon had lost all its counterparts over time. Maybe you witnessed a parent’s struggle to haul out a large appliance, which a smaller version could ease. Many times, these gifts are the most meaningful, yet also decidedly affordable and easy to find besides. These gifts need not be substantial or even useful. You might give a friend who couldn’t come on a group vacation an especially smooth stone found at the destination. You could bake your own rendition of a cookie your spouse had recalled buying from a long-closed shop as a child. Identifying the pattern for a singleton china teacup purchased from an antique store might be more appreciated and enduring than splurging on the rest of the set. Likewise, finding an exact replacement for a wind chime that fell in a storm, or secretly arranging the repair of a zipper on a favorite sweater, will make them feel seen rather than simply checked off a list. (Imagine how delighted you would be to unwrap that old sweater you’d tossed aside to discover that it had been revived.) Giving a gift truly well is so hard to do, it happens very infrequently. You may not give or receive a good one this year, or any year. I wish we had a better name for when it really works (or that gift had not become so hollowed out as a noun). In addition to the thought and the act, giving requires an alignment of circumstance and timing. It rarely succeeds. That’s okay. Think of gifts not merely as good intentions or as things offered but as a way to practice the act of giving—and to appreciate the sanctity of those moments when we get it right. PS A long time ago, I made a ridiculous game called Cow Clicker, which was about clicking cows (or pictures of them anyway). I’ve written about it before for The Atlantic , and I’ll send you to that story instead of trying to explain it. I drew a lot of cute and unusual cows for the game, and they became a sort of trademark. That year, my wife had a custom cookie cutter made in the shape of my cows, and then she used it to make dozens of detailed cookies that looked like them. We still have the cookie cutter and bring it out for most holidays, a reminder of my bovine period. It’s one of the most memorable gifts I’ve received. Courtesy of Ian Bogost I would love to hear about your favorite gifts. That could mean the best gift you’ve received, or one you recall giving with fondness or intensity, or even one whose unwrapping you witnessed and found particularly delightful. Tell us in the comments. We may share your answer, including your first name and last initial, age, and/or location, with fellow readers in a future edition of this newsletter or on our website or social-media platforms.
