items.title: Avengers: Doomsday to The Debut: 12 of the best films to watch this December
items.description: From Marvel’s latest superhero jamboree to an Oscar-tipped role for Julianne Moore, here are the films to watch at the cinema and stream at home this month. 1. Dune: Part Three Never mind Barbenheimer: Friday 18 December is Dunesday, which means that there are two blockbusters squeezing into US and UK cinemas on the same day. One is Marvel’s Avengers: Doomsday (see below). The other is Dune: Part Three, the conclusion of Denis Villeneuve’s sweeping science-fiction trilogy. Adapted from Frank Herbert’s 1969 novel, Dune Messiah, the film takes us back to the sandworm-infested desert planet of Arrakis, 17 years on from the seismic events of the last instalment. Robert Pattinson joins a starry cast that already includes Zendaya, Rebecca Ferguson, Jason Momoa, Florence Pugh, Josh Brolin and Javier Bardem. And Timothée Chalamet returns as Paul Atreides – once a rebel warrior but now the all-powerful Padishah Emperor of the Known Universe. “We are back with the same characters,” Villeneuve said in Empire , “but this time their psyches, their perspective on reality has totally changed, and Paul is living with the burden of what he created, trying to find a way out of this spiral of violence.” Released on 16, 17 and 18 December internationally 2. Avengers: Doomsday Avengers: Endgame is the highest grossing film ever made. Can Marvel match it with their latest megabudget superhero jamboree, Avengers: Doomsday? The studio is certainly throwing everything they possibly can at the film. Most of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s favourite characters are back in action, including Chris Evans’s Captain America and Chris Hemsworth’s Thor. There is also a crowd of Marvel characters from different cinematic universes, such as the Fantastic Four and the X-Men. The former Iron Man, Robert Downey Jr, returns to the MCU as the evil Doctor Doom. And the directors of Avengers: Endgame, Joe and Anthony Russo, have also been lured back to Marvel. The question is: With so many different characters from different worlds squashed into one film, will there be any room left for a coherent plot? Released on 16, 17 and 18 December internationally 3. The Debut Jesse Eisenberg’s second film as a writer-director, A Real Pain, was a critical and commercial hit, and its star, Kieran Culkin, won an Oscar. Eisenberg’s third film, The Debut, could have a similar fate. Julianne Moore plays a timid New Jersey housewife who is taken for granted by her husband and children. She auditions for a musical put on by a local theatre group (Eisenberg wrote all of the songs), just to give herself a hobby. But when the musical’s director (Paul Giamatti) teaches her to express her emotions, the explosive results are hilarious and bizarre – and they could well secure an Oscar for Moore. Barry Levitt in Time Out says that that Eisenberg’s “wildly entertaining” comedy is “whip-smart and exceptionally funny”, while Moore is “utterly dazzling”. Released on 11 December in the US, 18 December in Canada, 8 January in Ireland and 15 January in the UK 4. Ray Gunn Brad Bird, the legendary director of The Incredibles and Ratatouille, has been planning this sci-fi cartoon since the 1990s, which could help to explain how dizzyingly detailed Ray Gunn is. It’s a mystery thriller set in the retrofuturistic city of Metropia, where flying cars and rocket packs are no big deal, but where the design and dialogue hark back to the hard-boiled detective yarns of the 1930s and 1940s. Sam Rockwell provides the voice of Raymond Gunn, the city’s last human private eye, Tom Waits is his one-eyed alien sidekick, and Scarlett Johansson is a glamorous, scandal-prone pop star entangled in a criminal conspiracy. “This is a fantastic film, in all senses of the word,” says David Jenkins in Little White Lies. “Bird and Matthew Robbins’ screenplay is a thing of pristine beauty, retooling the pop and crackle of classic-era noir patter but with a sassy modern edge… [and the action] heaves with breathless set pieces, dazzling character choreography, and awe-striking edifices.” Released on 4 December in the US and UK, and on 18 December on Netflix globally 5. 14th The 14th Amendment to the US Constitution is the one that deals with citizenship and civil rights. Politicians have been arguing about it since 1868, when it was formulated to address the status of freed slaves following the American Civil War. And, according to Ava DuVernay ‘s documentary, 14th, these arguments are raging more fiercely than ever today. Her wide-ranging history lesson is a companion piece to 13th, which was nominated for a best documentary Oscar in 2017. The new film is “just as lucid and galvanising as its predecessor, with an updated, more pressing urgency befitting a democracy in distress,” says Adrian Horton in The Guardian. “It’s a bracing, riveting torrent dense with facts and figures [which] burns with righteous anger and alarm… Quibbles aside, 14th is a rare feat, at once informative, infuriating and undeniable.” Released on 4 December on Netflix globally 6. Artificial Luca Guadagnino’s provocative comedy drama about OpenAI was financed by Amazon MGM studios. But after Amazon invested in OpenAI, the company announced that it wouldn’t be releasing the film. “The timing raised eyebrows,” noted Caryn James in her BBC review . But even without the behind-the-scenes shenanigans, Artificial is a must-see. Andrew Garfield stars as Sam Altman, the co-founder of OpenAI. Yura Borisov – who was Oscar-nominated for his role in Anora – plays Ilya Suskever, a scientist who believes that artificial general intelligence can save the world. Mark Rylance is Geoffrey Hinton, the mild-mannered “godfather of AI”. And Ike Barinholtz plays a not-so-mild-mannered Elon Musk. James commented that while the film has “witty, relatable comic moments”, Artificial “is about nothing less than a battle for the soul of humanity, asking: Who gets to control AI and thus our entire future? It is a story of idealism v commerce, AI safety v recklessness, and angels v devils.” Released on 25 December in the US and Canada, and on 22 January in the UK 7. Werwulf What could be more festive than a grisly monster movie set in Europe’s brutal past, and directed by Robert Eggers? Two Christmases ago, Eggers brought us Nosferatu , his remake of the vampire classic. And this year his Christmas present is Werwulf, featuring Aaron Taylor-Johnson as a 14th-Century farmer who sprouts fur and fangs when the full Moon rises. Lily-Rose Depp is unrecognisable as his wife, and Eggers regular Willem Dafoe plays the obsessive hunter on his trail. Judging by the trailer, they’re all having a grim time in the bleak, muddy, misty countryside. “After Nosferatu, I kind of said, ‘Let me try to write the scariest thing I can write,'” Eggers announced at the film’s press launch. “I don’t know that I did that, but I definitely wrote the darkest thing.” Merry Christmas! Released on 25 December in the US and Canada, and on 1 January in the UK and Ireland 8. Tender Loving Care Mike Leigh has been making comedy dramas for 55 years, the most acclaimed of which have been politically charged, quietly funny, heart-wrenchingly sad portraits of working-class and middle-class English life, such as Life is Sweet, Secrets & Lies and 2024’s Hard Truths. The 83-year-old has suggested that Tender Loving Care will be his final film – but his powers show no signs of fading. Alice Bailey Johnson and Kate O’Flynn (Widow’s Bay) star as Rosie and Amy, two thirty-something best friends who share a flat in west London. Both are social workers who remain defiantly cheerful even when dealing with society’s most unfortunate and hostile people. But can they cope with a case of dementia in the family? Brian Tallerico on RogerEbert.com calls Tender Loving Care a “a devastating and truly beautiful swan song, a movie that works as both a character study and a commentary on his entire career. This is one of [Leigh’s] best.” Released on 4 December in the US, and on 12 February in the UK and Ireland 9. Behemoth! This tragicomic character study from Tony Gilroy – the writer-director of Michael Clayton and the creator of the Andor TV series – stars Pedro Pascal as Alex, a gifted cellist: Pascal had to learn to play the cello from scratch for the role. Having been in prestigious orchestras around the world, Alex has returned to his hometown of Los Angeles to play on film soundtracks, but his own life has more conflict, mystery and farce than any of the films he accompanies. He has run-ins with his resentful brother (Will Arnett), his dying mother (JoBeth Williams), an ex (Olivia Wilde) who is stalking him, and another ex (Eva Victor) he can’t stop thinking about. Aside from Alex, though, the film’s main character is the music itself. “Working with nine different composers – credited as the Behemoth! Collective – Gilroy has crafted a film where image and sound are inextricably linked,” says Zachary Lee in The Wrap. “This is not quite a project that you just ‘watch’ and ‘hear’, but experience in unblemished totality.” Released on 4 December in the UK, the US, Canada and Ireland 10. Rose Sandra Hüller has been excellent in four films this year, but her job in three of them was, in part, to support a male character: she was the mission controller in Project Hail Mary , a tycoon’s sister in Digger , and an author’s daughter in Fatherland. Rose is the film that focuses squarely on her character. And, suitably, Markus Schleinzer’s starkly black-and-white historical drama tells the story of a woman fighting for status in a male-dominated world. In fact, her character disguises herself as a man. Having fought in the Thirty Years War, she lays claim to a farm in Germany that belonged to a fallen comrade-in-arms. But how long can her deception continue before the suspicious villagers discover her secret? “Rose is nothing short of shattering,” says Ryan Lattanzio in IndieWire. “Schleinzer is a master craftsman in total, unclenching control of his material from start to crushing finish… [and] Hüller annihilates your heart.” Released on 11 December in the US and on 5 February in the UK 11. Clarissa Virginia Woolf’s peerless 1925 novel Mrs Dalloway examines the class system in England between the two world wars. But Arie and Chuko Esiri’s film transposes the story to Lagos in contemporary Nigeria, where it retains its melancholy magic. Sophie Okonedo plays Clarissa, a society wife who seems happy and fulfilled and as she prepares to host a party in her elegant home, but she is actually daydreaming of the summer, many years earlier, when she was in love with a young poet. David Oyelowo plays that poet as a middle-aged man, who drops by and reminds Clarissa how much their lives have changed. Tomris Laffly in Elle says that this “gorgeous reimagining is both as classical as movies come and quietly revolutionary in its mining of new ideas in an old text. From queries into identity to class divides and deeply rooted devastations of colonialism, no stone gets unturned in Clarissa, one of the most radical films that will reach our theatres this year.” Released on 11 December in the US and Canada 12. La Gradiva Marine Atlan’s directorial debut isn’t just one of the films of the year – it’s being hailed as one of the greatest coming-of-age films ever – a piercingly sharp and sensitive picture of the moment when youth is engulfed by adulthood. Antonia Buresi plays a Latin teacher who is taking her Parisian students on a school trip to Pompeii and Naples. Her teenage charges are played by first-time actors who were spotted on the streets and in the schools of Paris – and they are all heartbreakingly convincing. Gradiva is “a sprawling chronicle of teenage angst that starts off as a laidback class trip to Italy and gradually turns into a devastating tale of loss,” says Jordan Mintzer in The Hollywood Reporter. “Featuring an impressive cast of unknowns and a fluid style that captures them with both lyricism and verisimilitude, this deserved winner of the Cannes Critics’ Week Grand Prize announces the arrival of a formidable new talent.” Released on 18 December in the US and on 1 January in the UK

items.title: Ark Foundation urges Ghana to ratify ILO convention to tackle workplace harassment
items.description: The Ark Foundation, Ghana, has called on the government and Parliament to urgently ratify and domesticate the International Labour Organisation’s (ILO) Convention 190 to strengthen protection against sexual harassment, exploitation and abuse in workplaces. The Foundation said the move was necessary to close gaps in Ghana’s legal framework that leave workers, job seekers, interns, apprentices, volunteers and National Service personnel vulnerable to workplace violence and harassment. In a statement issued on November 24 ahead of the 2026 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, the organisation also called for stronger safeguarding and child-protection systems in second-cycle educational institutions to address abuse against students. The campaign, which runs from November 25 to December 10, is being held under the global theme, “ UNiTE to End Violence Against Women and Girls: Ensure Justice, Protect Survivors, End Impunity. ” The Ark Foundation said Ghana had yet to ratify ILO Convention 190, adopted in 2019 to address violence and harassment in the world of work, five years after it entered into force internationally. It urged the Executive and Parliament to prioritise the reintroduction and passage of the convention’s ratification bill and formally deposit Ghana’s instrument of ratification with the ILO. The Foundation cited a baseline survey of more than 20,000 workers conducted by the Ministry of Employment and Labour Relations and the ILO, which found that 71.7 per cent of respondents had experienced violence or harassment at work, while 41.9 per cent reported experiencing sexual violence in their lifetime. It further cited estimates that 95 per cent of workplace violence and harassment cases in Ghana go unreported because of fear of retaliation, victim-blaming and the absence of safe reporting channels. The organisation warned that job seekers, interns, apprentices, volunteers and National Service personnel were particularly vulnerable to exploitation, including demands for sexual favours in exchange for employment opportunities. It also cited research in Ghana’s mining sector indicating that 37 per cent of women experienced workplace harassment, while 17 per cent reported sexual demands linked directly to recruitment. The Foundation said persistent reports of sexual exploitation and demands for sex in exchange for academic grades in second-cycle institutions also highlighted the need for stronger protection systems in schools. It argued that existing laws, including the Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651), the Domestic Violence Act, 2007 (Act 732), the Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038) and the Affirmative Action (Gender Equity) Act, 2024 (Act 1121), still contained gaps that left some categories of people inadequately protected. According to the organisation, the Labour Act’s focus on formal employer-employee relationships leaves job applicants, interns, apprentices, volunteers and National Service personnel exposed to exploitation without adequate legal safeguards. It described practices such as “sex-for-jobs” as not only human rights violations but also governance and economic concerns that undermine meritocracy, public trust and productivity. The Foundation welcomed recent policy initiatives, including the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection’s rollout of the revised Domestic Violence Policy and the African Union Convention on Ending Violence Against Women and Girls. However, it said these efforts needed to be matched with stronger legislation, enforcement and institutional accountability. As part of its proposed roadmap, the Foundation called for tripartite consultations involving organised labour, employers, civil society organisations and survivors to build consensus on implementing Convention 190 across formal and informal sectors. It also urged the government to amend the Labour Act to explicitly cover job applicants, interns, National Service personnel and informal workers, while strengthening safeguarding standards and reporting systems in second-cycle schools. Other recommendations include establishing independent and confidential reporting channels, providing medical, legal and psychosocial support for survivors, protecting whistleblowers and introducing workplace and school-based prevention programmes. The organisation further called for independent oversight and annual public reporting on complaints and cases of workplace harassment, with labour inspectors, education authorities and safeguarding institutions empowered to enforce compliance. The Foundation said it was working alongside a coalition of organised labour, civil society organisations, legal advocacy groups and industry networks to push for stronger action against sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment. The coalition includes the Trades Union Congress and its affiliate unions, FIDA-Ghana, the Domestic Violence Coalition, NETRIGHT, ActionAid Ghana and Women in Mining Ghana. “The 16 Days of Activism is more than a calendar observance—it is a demand for structural accountability,” the Foundation said. It urged Ghana to build on its history of supporting international human rights instruments by ratifying Convention 190 and strengthening protection systems in workplaces, schools and communities. The organisation said such measures were necessary to ensure that justice, safety and dignity became a reality for all Ghanaians.

items.title: GAPHTO warns of heightened yellow fever, meningitis risks as Ghana enters dry season
items.description: The Ghana Association of Public Health Technical Officers (GAPHTO) is urging Ghanaians to heighten their vigilance against yellow fever and cerebrospinal meningitis as the country enters the dry season. The Association says changing weather patterns, rising temperatures and dry-season conditions could increase exposure to disease-carrying mosquitoes and heighten the risk of meningitis, particularly in vulnerable communities. The warning follows the Ministry of Health’s October 9, 2026 declaration of a yellow fever outbreak in the Upper West Region, which triggered surveillance, case investigations and a reactive vaccination campaign in affected districts. In a press statement issued on Tuesday, November 24, GAPHTO expressed concern about the seasonal disease threats and called on residents, health professionals and government institutions to intensify preventive measures to avert further infections and deaths. The Association extended its condolences to families who have lost loved ones to yellow fever, while commending residents of Sissala East, Sissala West, Wa West and other affected districts for cooperating with the October 14 to 18 reactive vaccination campaign. It also praised Disease Control Officers and other frontline health workers for their efforts in containing the outbreak but cautioned that sustained surveillance remains critical as authorities await laboratory confirmations. GAPHTO says the transition into the dry season presents additional public health concerns, particularly as rising temperatures may compel people to sleep outdoors without adequate protection against mosquito bites. It cautioned that yellow fever mosquitoes primarily bite during the day, stressing that reliance on insecticide-treated mosquito nets alone may not provide sufficient protection. The Association is therefore encouraging the public to wear long-sleeved clothing, apply mosquito repellents and eliminate potential mosquito breeding sites by emptying, covering or clearing water containers, old tyres and other stagnant-water sources. It has also urged Ghanaians to familiarise themselves with the symptoms of yellow fever to ensure early detection and treatment. According to GAPHTO, the early signs include sudden fever, headache, muscle and back pain, nausea, vomiting and general weakness. It warned that the disease could progress to severe symptoms, including yellowing of the eyes and skin, dark urine and bleeding from the nose, mouth or gums. The Association cautioned that yellow fever could easily be mistaken for malaria, urging anyone experiencing the symptoms to report promptly to a health facility rather than resorting to self-medication. On vaccination, GAPHTO has reiterated that the yellow fever vaccine is safe and effective, providing lifelong protection with a single dose. It is encouraging everyone aged nine months and above in affected districts to take the vaccine when offered, while reminding parents and caregivers to ensure children receive their routine yellow fever vaccination at nine months. Beyond yellow fever, the Association is warning of the risk of cerebrospinal meningitis as Ghana moves deeper into the dry season. It has urged residents and travellers, particularly those in communities within the meningitis belt, to avoid overcrowded spaces, practise good respiratory hygiene and seek immediate medical attention when experiencing fever, severe headache or neck stiffness. Call for stronger surveillance and protection of health workers GAPHTO has also called on public health professionals to intensify surveillance and community-level interventions to prevent further spread of the diseases. It has specifically urged Disease Control Officers to strengthen active case searches in health facilities and communities, ensure the timely collection and transportation of samples, and submit complete weekly surveillance reports, including zero reports. Health Information Officers have been asked to ensure accurate and timely entry of surveillance and vaccination data, while Health Promotion Officers are expected to intensify public education in local languages through traditional leaders, religious institutions and community radio. The Association is also asking Nutrition Officers to audit child welfare clinic records to establish whether eligible children have received their required vaccinations, including the yellow fever vaccine at nine months. Field and community health workers, meanwhile, have been tasked to support vaccination and mop-up exercises, trace people who may have missed vaccination and lead household-level efforts to eliminate mosquito breeding sites. GAPHTO has further drawn attention to the safety of frontline officers, particularly those deployed to hard-to-reach communities. It is urging health workers who travel on motorbikes to wear helmets, observe road safety regulations and avoid night travel whenever possible. Government urged to strengthen laboratory capacity and resource frontline officers The Association is appealing to government and development partners to strengthen Ghana’s capacity to respond to emerging disease outbreaks. It wants the country to upgrade laboratory testing capacity and logistics, and adequately equip national public health reference laboratories to conduct confirmatory testing within the country. GAPHTO says this will strengthen the country’s ability to detect and respond to disease outbreaks promptly. It is also calling for the provision of fuel, motorbikes, sample transportation kits, personal protective equipment and allowances for district surveillance teams and community-based surveillance volunteers. The Association has, however, raised concerns about the welfare of health workers who sustain injuries while carrying out national public health assignments. It is demanding institutional arrangements to guarantee timely medical care, insurance coverage and compensation for officers injured in the line of duty. GAPHTO cited the case of a colleague, Mr Solomon Gyabaah, who sustained life-altering injuries during the 2014 polio vaccination campaign and, according to the Association, continues to lack government support. The Association says protecting frontline health workers must be an integral part of Ghana’s public health response, particularly as they continue to undertake high-risk assignments in difficult and remote communities. GAPHTO says it remains committed to working with the Ministry of Health, Ghana Health Service, the World Health Organisation, District Assemblies and other stakeholders to contain the yellow fever outbreak and strengthen public health preparedness. It insists that sustained vaccination, active surveillance, early detection, prompt clinical care, mosquito control and public cooperation will be essential to safeguarding communities as Ghana enters the dry season. The Association is urging every citizen, community leader and health professional to play an active role in preventing further disease outbreaks.

items.title: Togbe Afede XIV backs Mahama government’s efforts to fight illegal mining
items.description: The President of the Asogli State Council and Former National House of Chiefs President, Togbe Afede XIV, has endorsed the Mahama administration’s efforts to tackle illegal mining, describing the menace as a product of corruption that must be addressed at its roots. He has also urged traditional authorities across the country to support the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, in the campaign against galamsey. Togbe Afede made the call on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, when the minister and his delegation paid a courtesy call on him. He praised the steps taken by the ministry to address the destruction of forests and pollution of water bodies, despite what he described as opposition from forces working against the campaign. “Fighting galamsey is like fighting corruption, and galamsey is a product of corruption,” he said. The traditional ruler said the fight required collective commitment, particularly from traditional authorities, whose support he considered essential to achieving the government’s objectives. “You are doing a great job and deserve our support. In fact, what you are doing is quite laudable. If we don’t nip problems in the bud, they become difficult to manage,” he said. Togbe Afede warned that allowing illegal mining to continue unchecked could have serious consequences for the country’s water security and economic future. “I am afraid if we don’t stop galamsey, Ghana may soon be importing water into the country. If we don’t kill galamsey, it will sink Ghana,” he cautioned. The former President of the National House of Chiefs recalled efforts during his tenure to persuade government to allow traditional authorities to take a leading role in the fight against illegal mining. He said those efforts did not yield the desired outcome. Togbe Afede also expressed disappointment over what he described as the involvement of some traditional rulers in activities that promote illegal mining, arguing that such conduct had contributed to the worsening of the problem. He urged traditional leaders to support efforts to stop the destruction of the country’s natural resources rather than undermine the campaign. Mr Armah-Kofi Buah, who led the delegation, thanked Togbe Afede for his counsel and guidance during their engagements. He recalled their working relationship in the energy sector, when Togbe Afede served as Minister for Energy and he was Director of Sunon Asogli Power Ghana Limited. The minister commended the traditional ruler for the advice he had offered whenever opportunities arose for them to engage.

items.title: Your brain is exhausted from too many unfinished tasks. Five simple steps can help
items.description: Finding it hard to switch off at the end of the working day? You may be suffering from the ‘Zeigarnik effect’. These tips can help you let go. At any given moment I have dozens of browser tabs open on my computer, usually featuring research I use for this very column. Today I counted 61 on one window alone. As I finish a project it feels cathartic to close the related pages. That’s because each tab represents an unfinished task, which research shows can tax our brains and undermine our focus. But often with work, as soon as one project ends, the next begins. Or, in my case, projects overlap. I spoke to experts about how we can reduce mental exhaustion when tasks are not yet complete. I learnt that there’s a huge mental benefit from being able to switch off, we just need to take conscious steps to do so. ‘We want to finish things’ The idea that unfinished tasks take on a special status in our memory is almost 100 years old. In 1927, Russian psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik published a paper showing people were more likely to remember tasks they’d been interrupted while doing, than those they’d been allowed to complete . The story goes that the inspiration for Zeigarnik’s experiments occurred when her supervisor, Kurt Lewin, observed waiters in a busy restaurant. He noticed that they remembered large orders until they were paid for, at which point the order was promptly forgotten. It reminds me of watching TV, where an unresolved plot encourages me to watch-on and keeps the characters’ journey fresh in our minds. Psychologists still refer to this today as the “Zeigarnik effect”. And while the memory boost relating to unfinished tasks has been difficult to replicate consistently, the effect has inspired numerous studies showing that unfinished tasks continue to occupy our minds . “We have this cognitive need for closure and we want to finish things,” says Christine Syrek, a psychology professor at the University of Applied Sciences Bonn-Rhein-Sieg in Germany. When tasks aren’t finished, keeping the information vivid is useful. “It’s functional because it helps us when we get started again: we have everything cognitively present,” says Syrek. But this mental continuity can come at a cost. Syrek and colleagues have found that incomplete tasks at the end of the week were linked to stress and disrupted sleep , as well as “ work-related rumination .” With that in mind, here are three ways to help your mind switch off. 1. Set time-based goals Ongoing work can leave people feeling less competent. In one study , employees found it harder to switch off when tasks were left unfinished, leading to negative rumination. Alternatively, if they felt they had made progress, their sense of competence and control improved and their stress reduced. This does not mean we have to finish all tasks, says Syrek. Instead, it could involve creating a clear plan for how to finish your to-do list. When individuals proactively plan , set goals and anticipate obstacles, they find it easier to let go. “We need to relax our mind by saying ‘I won’t forget it. I know I’ve written it down’,” says Syrek. Planning at the start of the workday can help too. When individuals prioritised tasks in the morning, one study found it helped them with the transition into their working day. In my case, I find it useful look at my diary each morning to carve out uninterrupted research and writing time – leaving me feeling reassured this column will get finished. 2. Switch off notifications Apps on our phones can make it tempting to be available at all hours. Even in our free time, our brains can be focused on problem solving , says Joan Ongchoco, assistant professor in cognitive science at the University of British Columbia. “[For] my lecture last week, I was teaching in my dreams,” she says. Checking emails can also lead to higher levels of work-family conflict, as this habit allows work to spill into the home, according to a review . A simple way to reduce stress therefore invovles checking your email less. You could wait until you start work, or set specific times to check. The same goes for any instant messaging apps used for work. Detaching ourselves from work on holiday can also extend how much we enjoy our time off. 3. Where possible, avoid project overlap The numerous open browser tabs I see when I start work each day could be contributing to an “ information overload “. This is because we experience a significant cognitive load when transitioning between tasks . Where possible, it can be helpful to finish one task before moving onto the next, to ease the load on working memory, says Ongchoco. “Each time you close a file [in the mind], that frees up resources, which is why you feel energised,” says Ongchoco. 4. Plan deadlines around holidays Festive periods, in particular, can be stressful for many. But one study conducted before and after a Christmas break found those with fewer unfinished tasks had better wellbeing when they returned to work. Managers can help by encouraging employees to plan-ahead. “Before a [holiday] you don’t need to finish everything,” Syrek advises. Instead, leave work in a state that you know you can easily come back to, without having to mentally engage in it all the time or worry you might forget something important. 5. ‘ T he doorway effect’ : Create transition rituals “Transition rituals” can help us to let go of thoughts about work, says Oliver Weigelt, assistant professor of organisational psychology at the University of Groningen. One example is changing your physical environment, which helps signal to your brain that a task has ended. If working from home, that could involve a walk to a nearby park or a shop, or even just walking through a doorway into a new room. “When we’ve walked through a doorway , our system [brain] flushes its memory so that it can free up space for other things that are about to happen,” says Ongchoco. Another simple option is moving your laptop to a different room. This additionally helps us create a psychological distance from any tasks which we may otherwise find stressful, says Weigelt. Taken together, these strategies could help you put workplace stresses into perspective too. “If you are able to step back and think more about the forest instead of the trees, you could gain distance or get rid of unfinished task rumination,” says Weigelt. Bearing all this in mind, I aim to avoid checking my emails out of hours and I’ve started planning my days more carefully. Plus, alongside the Zeigarnik effect, I’m also trying to channel the Ovsiankina effect . This research, released a year later, showed that people are susceptible to going back to unfinished tasks to satisfy their need for closure. So instead of feeling overwhelmed by my open tabs, I use them to inspire me to get stuck back into a project – and finally complete it. Because, as Ongchoco tells me, unfinished tasks can be irresistible. We simply need to better recognise when it can cause undue stress.

items.title: CAN 2025 : pourquoi le Maroc ne pourra pas récupérer le titre devant le Tribunal fédéral suisse
items.description: Le Maroc peut encore prolonger son bras de fer judiciaire avec le Sénégal devant le Tribunal fédéral suisse, mais ses chances d'obtenir gain de cause sont désormais très faibles, voire nulles. Après la décision du Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS) de rétablir le sacre des Lions, la Fédération royale marocaine de football (FRMF) envisage de saisir le Tribunal fédéral suisse. Une démarche qui ne lui permettra toutefois pas de réclamer directement le titre. Cette juridiction n'a ni la compétence ni la vocation de rejuger l'affaire sur le fond. Un recours aux possibilités très limitées La décision rendue ce mardi par le TAS constitue une sentence arbitrale dont la contestation devant les juridictions suisses obéit à des règles particulièrement strictes. Contrairement à une cour d'appel classique, le Tribunal fédéral ne revient pas sur l'appréciation des faits ni sur l'interprétation sportive du dossier. Il exerce uniquement un contrôle juridique limité aux motifs prévus par la loi suisse sur le droit international privé (LDIP). Le Sénégal conservera sa couronne définitivement Parmi ces motifs figurent notamment l'irrégularité de la composition du tribunal arbitral, une décision erronée sur sa compétence, la violation du droit d'être entendu ou encore la contrariété de la sentence à l'ordre public. Le Maroc devra donc démontrer l'existence d'un vice juridique précis. Un simple désaccord avec le raisonnement du TAS ou avec sa décision de rétablir le Sénégal dans ses droits ne suffira pas. Le délai de recours est en principe de 30 jours à compter de la notification de la sentence. Les statistiques de 2025 illustrent la difficulté de cette procédure. Selon le rapport annuel du Conseil international de l'arbitrage en matière de sport (CIAS), 30 recours contre des sentences du TAS ont été enregistrés devant le Tribunal fédéral suisse. Cinq ont été accueillis, 22 rejetés, deux retirés et un était encore pendant. Soit cinq recours accueillis sur 30, environ 16,7 %. Un indicateur qui témoigne du caractère restrictif de cette procédure très encadrée. Une hypothétique annulation du Tribunal fédéral suisse ne donnerait pas le titre au Maroc Deux scénarios sont envisageables. Le premier est le rejet du recours marocain. Dans ce cas, la sentence du TAS restera intacte et le Sénégal conservera définitivement son sacre sur le plan judiciaire. Le second serait une annulation de la sentence pour un motif juridique reconnu par le Tribunal fédéral. Mais même dans cette hypothèse, le Maroc ne deviendrait pas champion d'Afrique. Les juges fédéraux ne peuvent pas se substituer au TAS pour désigner un vainqueur. L'affaire sera de nouveau renvoyée devant le TAS afin qu'il rende une nouvelle décision en tenant compte des observations du Tribunal fédéral. Et ce scénario ne garantirait nullement une victoire marocaine. Si une éventuelle annulation repose sur un vice de procédure sans remettre en cause l'analyse de fond, le TAS devrait simplement rendre une nouvelle sentence confirmant sa décision initiale en faveur du Sénégal. Il ne serait pas tenu de modifier son appréciation sportive et juridique des faits pour la seule raison qu'une irrégularité aurait été relevée sur un autre aspect du dossier. En définitive, le recours devant le Tribunal fédéral du Maroc représente une possibilité de contester la régularité juridique de la sentence, pas une nouvelle occasion de disputer le titre. Le Maroc peut encore tenter de faire annuler la décision du TAS, mais il ne pourra pas obtenir le trophée devant les juges suisses. Autrement dit, le dernier recours du Maroc devant la justice suisse risque encore d'échouer. Game over. Par Cheikh Gora DIOP

items.title: The Agents Howard Lutnick Pulled off Their Jobs
items.description: E arly in his tenure , Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick so alienated members of his regular security detail that some of them quit. He didn’t have to look far for replacements. The Department of Commerce’s own Bureau of Industry and Security employs law-enforcement agents who carry weapons and have the power to arrest people. The department reassigned some of them to serve as Lutnick’s personal bodyguards, pulling away from their duties agents who might otherwise have prevented the smuggling of AI chips to China. Instead, they would now travel on his private jet and guard his various homes, according to five people with knowledge of the matter. Some commerce officials were baffled that Lutnick had diverted personnel for his own protection as the United States is racing to stay ahead of China on advanced artificial intelligence. BIS is the nation’s leading bureau for the enforcement of export controls, and its agents are trained to keep prized U.S. technology out of the wrong hands. In theory, they should be on the front lines of the effort to prevent illicit AI-chip trading—the issue at the center of the controversy over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. (Huang has admitted to the affair but said that he hadn’t known that the woman might have been a Chinese spy.) BIS agents are trained in many aspects of law enforcement, including crime-scene investigation and counterterrorism. They are not, however, trained in protecting VIPs and dignitaries. The Commerce Department has its own Office of Security, and secretaries have been provided with protection since at least 1986. But that protection has traditionally been lighter than what’s provided to senior officials who are more closely involved in national security, who are considered more likely targets. The assignment of BIS agents as bodyguards, former officials told us, seemed driven by Lutnick’s desire to have a detail comparable to that of other Cabinet members, such as the secretary of defense and the attorney general. Democrats and some Republicans have questioned why Lutnick hasn’t done more to prevent illegal sales of advanced chips from Nvidia and other firms, or expanded the list of companies that are barred on national-security grounds from making such purchases. In particular, lawmakers want to know more about Lutnick’s approach to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that’s under investigation by Commerce and the Justice Department for potential chip smuggling. Even after U.S. intelligence, about a year ago, identified the Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as a Chinese-intelligence asset who was in a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the Commerce Department didn’t put Megaspeed on its trade blacklist. The company was added only yesterday, the same day that Nvidia’s board restored Jensen Huang to his roles as the company’s president and chief executive, under pressure from President Trump. The belated addition to the blacklist appears to have been more symbolic than substantive, however: One trade expert suggested that because of the way the regulation adding Megaspeed to the list was written, the company would still have access to many types of AI chips. T he Bureau of Industry and Security has fewer than 200 special agents; most of them work in 10 field offices across the United States, and about a dozen or so work overseas. It wasn’t clear how many agents were affected by the rotations onto and off Lutnick’s protection staff. Two former officials told us that the assignment usually involved three to four agents at a time. A Commerce Department official said in a statement that “at a time when the Secretary was facing the highest level of credible threats in the Department’s history some agents were temporarily detailed to augment executive protection.” The official added that the number of agents at BIS has increased, though she didn’t provide numbers. As artificial intelligence has boomed, the bureau has struggled to keep pace with the global trade in U.S. chips, suggesting that it could ill-afford the secondment of agents elsewhere. The Commerce Department’s Office of the Inspector General, in a June report, found that BIS has not taken adequate action to enforce export controls on goods destined for China and Hong Kong. In a report a month earlier, it found similar enforcement failures regarding Russia and Belarus. [ Read: The limits of positive thinking ] Overall, the number of public penalties and enforcement actions for violating U.S.-export rules has fallen since Lutnick took office in February 2025. Across 2023 and 2024, the annual case rate was close to 100; in the 17 months from March 2025 to the start of August, the annualized rate dropped to about half that, according to The Export Practitioner , a trade publication. Amid the furor over Nvidia, the inspector general last week began an evaluation of the bureau’s oversight of advanced-computing chips. Current and former commerce officials we spoke with put the blame for the bureau’s lackluster performance on Lutnick and his team. They contend that Lutnick and senior officials have repeatedly stressed Trump’s interest in a détente with China and have placed commercial interests above national security. Trump has made clear his desire for a new China trade deal and last week sought to further improve relations with President Xi Jinping at a summit in Shenzhen . Trump’s approach runs counter to the administration’s aggressive posturing about the need to restrict Chinese trade. The diversion of agents to serve in Lutnick’s protective detail has sapped expert resources and prevented agents from doing the high-stakes work they are hired and trained to perform, current and former officials told us. “They’re not trained for protective detail,” one current official told us. “These are professional investigators.” A former official called it “completely inappropriate” to pull agents to protect Lutnick. The Commerce Department, meanwhile, is seeking an increase in staffing. In April, Lutnick told the House Appropriations Subcommittee that BIS needed additional resources and enforcement personnel, including 290 new enforcement officers, to prevent the diversion of semiconductors to China and to protect American innovation. He didn’t mention the redeployment of some of the officers whom BIS already employed. L utnick , a friend of Trump’s and a former Wall Street executive, is one of the Cabinet’s wealthiest members. His most recent financial-disclosure form lists his holdings, which include a $25 million mansion that he purchased in 2024 in the Berkley neighborhood of Washington, D.C. The house, modeled after France’s Château du Grand-Lucé, was until recently the most expensive home ever sold in the capital. Lutnick also owns properties in New York City, the Hamptons, and South Florida. He made much of his money as the CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, a New York financial firm, where his two sons, Brandon and Kyle, hold senior leadership positions. Cantor also held approximately 1.8 million Nvidia shares as of the end of June, which were valued at the time at $362 million, according to the company’s financial disclosures. (The firm has said that it has no material proprietary position in Nvidia, and its holdings mainly arise from its services for clients.) [ Read: The president’s most annoying buddy ] Lutnick no longer has a financial interest in Cantor Fitzgerald, but some in Congress have argued that his close family ties to the firm represent a conflict of interest. Some White House officials have privately expressed similar worries, according to several current and former administration officials. Despite these concerns, and Lutnick’s well-documented feuds with others at the top of the administration, Trump has consistently rebuffed pushes to drop his friend from the Cabinet. Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed to this report.

items.title: Economic Fighters League questions Parliament’s 2027 budget demands amid public hardship
items.description: The Leader of the Economic Fighters League, Ernesto Yeboah, says the financial difficulties facing ordinary Ghanaians must be considered in assessing Parliament’s proposed budget allocation for the 2027 financial year. He argues that while Parliament has raised concerns about the reduction in its budget request, the needs of the wider population should also inform discussions about the resources allocated to the institution. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story on Tuesday, Mr Yeboah said Parliament must provide details of its proposed expenditure to enable a proper assessment of whether the government’s allocation is adequate. He questioned the emphasis on challenges such as malfunctioning air conditioners and elevators in Parliament, arguing that many Ghanaians are struggling to meet basic needs. “Somebody doesn’t have lunch, somebody is hungry, and that somebody cannot eat. I mean, three square meals a day. These are the material conditions plaguing the vast majority of our people,” he said. Mr Yeboah also cautioned against the argument that Parliament should automatically receive whatever amount it requests from the government. He cited the previous proposal for a new parliamentary chamber, which he said should not automatically be considered a national priority. He called for a breakdown of Parliament’s budget request, insisting that the figures should be examined item by item before the government’s decision can be fairly assessed. “I would beg for more information about what the budget entails… What were they asking? And then we can do a fair assessment of whether government has been charitable or otherwise,” he said. His comments follow concerns by the Speaker of Parliament, Alban Bagbin, that the reduction in the House’s proposed 2027 budget could affect capital expenditure, goods and services, as well as the engagement of additional technical personnel and consultants.
