items.title: Colombia: Reporte Plan de Respuesta a Necesidades Humanitarias HNRP 2026 en el Sistema 5W entre enero y septiembre de 2026
items.description: Country: Colombia Sources: El Equipo Humanitario País Colombia, Grupo Interagencial sobre Flujos Migratorios Mixtos, R4V, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached Infographic. Socios humanitarios continúan realizando intervenciones en diferentes regiones del país a pesar de los desafíos del contexto, en respuesta a las necesidades humanitarias que siguen agudizándose en miles de personas que habitan en territorios apartados de difícil acceso, principalmente comunidades rurales incluyendo grupos étnicos. La respuesta tiene un énfasis en asistencia humanitaria vital multisectorial, complementando las capacidades de las autoridades locales y nacionales. Entre enero y septiembre de 2026 al menos 1.6 millones de personas recibieron asistencia humanitaria en 312 municipios de 31 departamentos , gracias al esfuerzo de 89 organizaciones humanitarias. De este total, el 40% de las personas atendidas son niños, niñas y adolescentes, y 26.7% pertenecen a pueblos étnicos (15,4% afrodescendientes y 11,3% indígenas). El 80%de las personas asistidas (1.272.200 personas) se encuentra en zonas con necesidades humanitarias en severidad alta (4), priorizando intervenciones en asistencia alimentaria, WASH, protección, educación en emergencia. Los beneficiarios se concentran en 128 municipios de 16 departamentos de las regiones Pacífico, noroccidente, la frontera con Venezuela y Amazonía. La respuesta también alcanzó a cerca de 330.000 personas en contextos de severidad moderada (2 y 3), enfocada en recuperación temprana y resiliencia comunitaria fortaleciendo la alimentación como medio de vida, acceso a servicios como salud, saneamiento básico, alojamientos y capacidades locales en otros 184 municipios de 29 departamentos, con aras de reducir vulnerabilidades. Estas acciones se han concentrado principalmente en el noroccidente, Amazonía y algunos departamentos del centro del país donde hubo concentración de necesidades por el terremoto. Según los reportes, el 42% de actividades fueron implementadas por ONG nacionales y locales (incluye acciones como socios implementadores de ONGs internacionales o de agencias de Naciones Unidas); el 34% por ONGs internacionales (contempla intervenciones directas o como socio implementador de agencias UN); un 10% corresponde a intervenciones directas de agencias de Naciones Unidas, y un 14% por otros socios quienes también ejecutan acciones locales en el marco de la respuesta del Plan de respuesta del Equipo Humanitario País (HNRP 2026). Gracias al apoyo de diferentes donantes , se han movilizado a la fecha USD 302,2 millones (48,8% del requerimiento total de USD 619,8 que incluye el Adenda al HNRP 2026) incluyendo USD 5 millones del CERF RR asignados en respuesta al terremoto. https://fts.unocha.org/countries/49/summary/2026 A la fecha, también se destaca la respuesta humanitaria complementaria para 514.000 personas (182.000 familias) con graves afectaciones por el terremoto de agosto. Las intervenciones se han llevado a cabo por parte de 42 organizaciones en 99 municipios de los 6 departamentos más afectados (Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas y Quindío), principalmente con atención inmediata con kits de alimentos, agua, saneamiento e higiene, alojamientos con la habilitación y dotación de espacios seguros, protección, salud, entre otras actividades en el marco de la emergencia. Para más detalles acceder al dashboard: https://3is.org/emergenciaslatam/terremoto_choco/ Es importante garantizar la continuidad de acciones multisectoriales y el acceso humanitario de manera oportuna para mitigar las necesidades más urgentes de las poblaciones vulnerables y con doble afectación, dada la convergencia entre conflicto armado, los impactos del terremoto y otros eventos climáticos.

World: Equitable Risk Sharing in Humanitarian Action - An aspiration or an essential power-sharing arrangement? October 2026
items.description: Countries: World, Afghanistan, Myanmar, Pakistan, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine Source: Humanitarian Advisory Group Please refer to the attached file. Executive summary Risk sharing is ultimately a test of power and partnership. It is not demonstrated by a risk register or a signed agreement, but by what happens when conditions change: whether local and national organisations can raise concerns safely, influence decisions, access the resources to adapt, and remain supported when risks materialise. This report shows how humanitarian actors can move from transferring risk down the response chain to sharing responsibility for safer, more effective and locally led humanitarian action. Risk-sharing landscape The sector has developed a growing body of frameworks, pilots and communities of practice, including the Risk Sharing Framework, Dutch Relief Alliance pilots, the Risk Sharing Community of Practice and guidance linking risk sharing with localisation. However, the research found few examples of fully realised, equitable risk sharing in practice. Existing approaches remain more developed in prevention than response, and many practices described as risk sharing are better characterised as risk management or supported risk transfer. Donors and intermediaries often prioritise fiduciary, legal, compliance and reputational risks, while local and national partners are more directly exposed to operational, safety, security, access, political and communitylevel risks. What this paper does This paper examines how risk is currently understood, allocated and managed across humanitarian programs and partnerships. It centres the perspectives and lived experience of local and national organisations, while also considering the institutional perspectives of donors and intermediaries. The research covered Myanmar, Syria, Afghanistan, Pakistan and Ukraine, with additional learning from global and multi-country initiatives. The paper identifies emerging practices that could be strengthened and scaled, rather than presenting a set of fully established models. It is accompanied by an Equitable Risk Sharing Playbook, which translates the findings into practical actions across key risk categories and three phases: before, during and after a crisis. Who this paper is for The paper is intended for donors, intermediaries, local and national organisations, DEC members and broader humanitarian sector. It is also relevant to program, finance, compliance, safeguarding, security and partnership teams responsible for translating institutional commitments into operational practice.

items.title: Burkina Faso : Baisse de 52 % des cas de paludisme sur fond d’adhésion à la communication sanitaire en langues nationales dans le Nando
items.description: Après une escale à Kokologo, la caravane de presse initiée par le ministère de la Santé dans le cadre du Mois de la communication sanitaire en langues nationales a poursuivi son périple à Koudougou, ce 23 novembre 2026, toujours dans la région du Nando. À cette occasion, le directeur régional de la Santé a présenté aux journalistes le bilan de cette campagne. Depuis son lancement le 2 novembre 2026, le Mois de la communication sanitaire en langues nationales connaît un franc succès dans la région du Nando. C’est une initiative du ministère de la Santé qui vise à rapprocher l’information sanitaire des populations en mettant l’accent sur les langues locales. Selon le directeur régional de la Santé du Nando, le Dr Anicet Kpoda, ce sont 12 radios, dont trois radios communautaires, qui ont été mises à contribution. Elles ont déjà réalisé 17 émissions dans le cadre du Mois de la communication sanitaire en langues nationales. Ces émissions ont été diffusées spécifiquement en mooré, en lyélé et en nouni. Il a précisé qu’elles ont été animées par 27 spécialistes des questions de nutrition, de santé de la reproduction, de paludisme et de dengue. « Selon les statistiques, 1 681 000 auditeurs ont écouté ces émissions. Et nous avons reçu 252 appels au cours de ces émissions. Les appels ont permis de répondre à certaines questions parce que c'était là l'intérêt de ces émissions. Les gens voulaient s'enquérir surtout de certains problèmes, certaines difficultés et on a donné des réponses, ce qui fait vraiment la beauté de la chose » , s’est-il réjoui. Il a fait savoir que le succès de cette initiative repose sur le fait qu’elle est menée entièrement en langues locales. Cela a permis aux populations de briser les barrières et de porter leurs préoccupations à l’antenne. Face à l’engouement des citoyens, le DRS du Nando a souhaité d’autres éditions pour rapprocher véritablement l’information des populations. Au niveau des infrastructures, depuis 2022, il a été réalisé dans la région 15 centres de santé et de promotion sociale (CSPS), sept maternités et deux dispensaires. À cela s’ajoute l’octroi de 300 réfrigérateurs, de 10 ambulances et de cinq véhicules de supervision. Le directeur régional de la Santé a ajouté que de 2024 à 2026, 20 postes de santé communautaires ont été construits. Il faut également noter la baisse du coût du scanner qui a permis à 3 284 patients de réaliser des examens. En matière de gratuité des soins, de 2022 au 31 octobre 2026, ce sont 6 629 886 prestations gratuites qui ont été réalisées au profit des femmes et des enfants. Ces prestations sont évaluées à plus de 11 milliards de F CFA. Selon les statistiques depuis 2024, la clinique mobile a effectué 116 sorties dans la région avec la réalisation de 4 356 mammographies. « Nous avons aussi une initiative que nous voulions souligner : la dispensation individuelle nominative au niveau de la pharmacie hospitalière, qui permet de disposer de médicaments dans les services d’urgence. Parce que quand vous arrivez à l’hôpital avec une urgence, au lieu de vous tendre une facture ou une ordonnance pour que vous sortiez chercher les médicaments, dans le CHR et dans les CMA, les centres médicaux avec antenne chirurgicale, on assure d’abord la prise en charge et c’est une fois celle-ci terminée qu’on vous indique le coût » , a-t-il ajouté. De plus, les actions concertées des acteurs ont permis de réduire le taux de paludisme dans la région. Le nombre de cas est passé de 1 118 223 en 2022 à 537 137 en fin octobre 2026, soit une baisse de 52 %. Par ailleurs, les décès sont passés de 241 en 2022 à 52 en fin octobre 2026. Cheick Habib Désiré BAYILI Faso7 L’article Burkina Faso : Baisse de 52 % des cas de paludisme sur fond d’adhésion à la communication sanitaire en langues nationales dans le Nando est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Was a Drug Lord’s Killing in Ecuador Not What It Seemed?
items.description: T he pictures show men splayed on a highway, their faces concealed in pools of blood. A pickup truck riddled with bullet holes. An assault rifle lying by one man’s outstretched hands. Ecuadorean Defense Minister Gian Carlo Loffredo posted the grisly images as proof of his country’s deepening partnership with the Trump administration in its campaign against drug cartels in Latin America. The photos, he said on social media two months ago, stemmed from an operation conducted in cooperation with U.S. Southern Command. “We promised: ‘Jail or hell’ and this one didn’t make it to jail,” Loffredo wrote on X on September 23, saying that the target was a cartel leader known as “Charlie.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth reposted Loffredo’s message the same day, adding that the U.S. military was “proud to stand w/ the Armed Forces of Ecuador.” But the Trump administration is now investigating whether Ecuadorean forces committed crimes or human-rights abuses during that operation—including whether the suspects were killed while in Ecuadorean custody—and whether U.S. forces played any role, one senior administration official and one former official told us. While administration officials look into the raid, the U.S. military has suspended joint operations with Ecuadorean troops, one of the people familiar with the matter said. But the U.S. military has not stopped its push to embed itself in Ecuador’s fight against cartels. (Hegseth visited the country last week.) Ecuador is Exhibit A of the Trump administration’s expanding militarized campaign to strike powerful drug and other criminal groups in Latin America in partnership with Donald Trump–aligned right-wing governments. Stephen Miller , Trump’s longtime immigration adviser, has driven that effort. Miller met with Ecuadorean President Daniel Noboa the day before the “Charlie” raid, while Noboa was in New York to address the United Nations General Assembly. With Miller’s recent appointment as White House chief of staff, those in Trump’s orbit are preparing for an escalation of U.S.-military operations in Latin America in the coming weeks and months. “This is all Stephen’s thing,” the senior official said, referring to the expanding partnerships. “This would not have happened without Stephen.” The U.S. military has forces in Ecuador to train and advise local troops and conduct what it calls “partnered operations”—joint raids or other counter-drug missions. A Pentagon official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the department, told us in an emailed statement that U.S.-military personnel did not take part in the September 23 operation, but declined to provide further details or comment about any review. But officials are still working to establish whether U.S. forces provided intelligence assistance or any other kind of support to the operation, sources told us. The Defense Department “takes allegations of misconduct by our partners seriously,” the Pentagon official said. “The Department remains committed to working alongside sovereign partners, including Ecuador, to confront narco-terrorist networks, strengthen collective security, and defend our shared neighborhood.” Officials from Ecuador’s embassy in Washington did not provide comment before publication. A White House official told us in an email that the drug gangs that the United States is battling alongside Latin American allies represent “a clear and present danger” to U.S. security, and said that the actions taken under those partnerships “have saved countless lives.” The official added that, at the time, Miller served as the homeland-security adviser and was responsible for interagency coordination. “The Trump Administration is the first administration in history to adopt a comprehensive strategy to dismantle and defeat narco-terrorists that are responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Americans,” the official wrote. When we asked the White House which agency or agencies were leading the examination of the raid, it didn’t respond. T rump in his second term has taken a special interest in Latin America, a region that has been largely overlooked by U.S. policy makers in recent decades. The administration wants to choke off the flow of migrants and drugs. That has brought a Trumpian corollary to the Monroe Doctrine—which the president proudly calls the “Donroe Doctrine,” a modern version of the 19th-century principle that the Western Hemisphere must remain under American influence. Miller’s vision for combatting cartels has expanded accordingly. He is a principal architect of the administration’s campaign of missile strikes against suspected drug traffickers at sea, which legal experts and critics have said is likely illegal. (The White House has cited a classified opinion from the Office of Legal Counsel that it insists authorizes the strikes.) The campaign has killed at least 240 people in more than 70 air strikes since last fall, according to a tally of Pentagon announcements. Some of those attacks have occurred in the Caribbean, the military has said, but the majority are in the eastern Pacific, where there have also been a number of interdictions off the coast of Ecuador. [ Read: A chief of staff who ‘will crack skulls’ ] The administration has at times been willing to overlook its Latin American partners’ records on human rights and democracy, depicting the battle against criminal groups as an existential struggle for all in the region. “You have to make a choice here. We’re going to choose on the side of leaders that are going to be serious about taking these groups on and eliminating them once and for all,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Ecuador earlier this year. “Otherwise, those groups—those terrorist groups—will eat these countries up.” The U.S. military touted its relationship with Ecuador in March when it announced the launch of joint operations against cartels. Noboa has put addressing rampant criminality and violence at the center of his presidency. He is among the most public of Trump’s Latin American allies in courting U.S.-military involvement. In his own social-media post within hours of the September raid, Noboa echoed the White House’s view of the fight against cartels as a hemisphere-wide campaign against criminality. “This battle doesn’t end at our borders,” he wrote. The slain cartel leader known as “Charlie” was Carlos Germán Muñoz Jara, according to Ecuadorean media. He was believed to have links to the Ecuadorean gang Los Choneros and the Mexican cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación. The Trump administration has designated both groups foreign terrorist organizations. The administration’s campaign is not limited to Ecuador. It is also seeking to accelerate counter-drug operations with Colombia, historically the most important U.S.-military partner in the region, and Venezuela following the January ouster of the dictator Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth visited Bogotá and Caracas last week to tout expanded military cooperation. The administration’s desire to intensify counter-cartel operations in Mexico, potentially on a unilateral basis, has caused friction between Trump and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum. Mexico captured a top drug boss, El Chapo Isidro, last week, in a sign of Sheinbaum’s determination to show Washington that her country is taking action. [ Read: Claudia Sheinbaum’s impossible dilemma ] Ecuador has approved a dramatic expansion of the U.S. military’s role in the country, including joint operations and the positioning of U.S. troops on the ground to train and advise their Ecuadorean counterparts. At least two MQ-9 Reaper drones are now based in Ecuador, along with other equipment provided by the United States. Noboa has faced accusations of authoritarian tactics employed against political opponents. Human Rights Watch alleged in a report that a March Ecuadorean military raid had resulted in the torture of farm workers. Ecuadoreans have put some limits on Noboa’s efforts, rejecting a 2025 referendum that would have permitted U.S. military bases in the country. Ecuador’s counter-drug partnership with the United States goes beyond the military. In recent months, the Drug Enforcement Administration, FBI, and Department of Homeland Security have also supported the country’s efforts. With the Pentagon and White House pushing for more military action against narco-terrorists, U.S. troops are likely to be busy in Latin America. That cooperation could be a boon for the administration’s vision, but it comes with its own peril—U.S. troops are operating alongside local forces answering to their own commanders, and playing by their own rules. Shane Harris and Kevin Sieff contributed to this report.

items.title: He Thought About Rome Every Day
items.description: The year was 1764, and Edward Gibbon was 27, headed for Rome on his Grand Tour. He had traversed the Alps from France not on a mule but in a chair carried between poles by porters. (He was “no great jockey,” a companion noted.) Gibbon then made his way through Turin and Milan, paused in Florence, and, as autumn set in, continued south. Crossing the Tiber, his destination now in sight, he was overcome. “I can neither express nor forget the strong emotions which agitated my mind as I first approached and entered the eternal city,” Gibbon recalled years later in a memoir. “After a sleepless night I trod, with a lofty step, the ruins of the Forum; each memorable spot where Romulus stood or Tully spoke or Caesar fell was at once present to my eye; and several days of intoxication were lost or enjoyed before I could descend to a cool and minute investigation.” Gibbon loved his rhetorical couplings—those harnessed pairs of verbs or adjectives that are sometimes at odds (“lost or enjoyed,” “express nor forget”), pulling the reader in different directions, as the critic Clive James once observed . The oddest pairing of all is that of Gibbon himself and his monumental work, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire , which he began writing seven years after that first (and only) visit to Rome. Gibbon was, by his own description, “puny”—4 feet 7 inches tall. His masterpiece is towering, a million and a half words published over the course of little more than a decade. The first of the six volumes—an immediate best seller in Britain—appeared the same year as the Declaration of Independence and The Wealth of Nations . There was no real precedent for what Gibbon had achieved. The Decline and Fall was an attempt to write history in a way we now take for granted : that is, by seeking to explain what actually happened. Gibbon was neither an annalist nor a zealot. He had arguments to make—about the unrivaled stability and happiness enjoyed for a spell by the Roman empire’s subjects, about the defeat of liberty by despotism and decadence, about the corrosive effects of corruption and Christianity—but his account is not subservient to them. He is often imprecise, as well as confident in his imagination. But he also weighs evidence. He compares cultures. He shifts perspective. Gibbon’s appetite for written sources was gargantuan and his knowledge of them profound, though he did not bring a modern critical faculty to their interpretation. He was an impresario, not a pedant—judicious, skeptical, and ironic, with a taste for drama. And the writing! At times so over-egged as to make Henry James seem like Hemingway, but seductive in its rhythms and illuminated by epigrammatic flashes: “A good soldier should dread his own officers far more than the enemy.” “Revenge is profitable, gratitude is expensive.” The narrative is at once sweeping and detailed—equal parts Balzac and Trollope, George Lucas and TMZ. The Decline and Fall ’s influence has been immense. The work created the basic storyline of Roman history , from “good emperors” to barbarians, and for generations has shaped an understanding of imperial ruin as “the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness.” It captivated newly independent America, whose Founders cherished republican government but feared that the Roman past held danger signs. People continue to explore its claims and insights, as well as the experiences that shaped its author: Was Gibbon a fatalist or, living at the core of a young empire himself , an optimist? Whatever the answer, his eyes seem to follow us around the room. Gibbon the man is a figure, as Martha Saxton writes in her posthumously published The Conversions of Edward Gibbon: A Modern Biography , who appears almost laughably devoid of the majesty his prose leads you to expect. As a boy, his ungainly body and unhappy experiences with peers left him deeply insecure and drove him to books. In later life, he grew obese and suffered from a hydrocele—a scrotal swelling—that further hampered his movement. He was vain and foppish, with a habit of waving his snuffbox didactically when he wanted to make a point. People acknowledged his brilliance but also made him an object of ridicule and even contempt. James Boswell, who knew Gibbon as a member of the Club, a literary group that included Samuel Johnson, described him as an “ugly, affected, disgusting fellow.” Saxton, a feminist historian and for many years a professor at Amherst College, is the author of acclaimed biographies of Jayne Mansfield, Louisa May Alcott, and Mary Ball Washington (the mother of George). She came to Gibbon from an unusual angle, her attention drawn initially by the notable misogyny of the Decline and Fall . Powerful women are painted as gorgons or succubi. The few whom Gibbon approves of are described as possessing “manly” virtues. In Gibbon’s lexicon, decadence is often a synonym for effeminacy . But Saxton’s response to Gibbon is complicated. She describes herself as both repelled by his venom and dazzled by the Decline and Fall —by its writing, scope, and command, and by the mark it left. She also finds Gibbon’s misogyny baffling. Male writers of the Enlightenment were eager to engage a female audience. Gibbon himself enjoyed close friendships with several women, in particular an aunt, Catherine Porten, who first cultivated “a taste for books, which is still the pleasure and glory of my life.” Aunt Kitty would be Gibbon’s friend and counselor for nearly four decades. Saxton doesn’t have a ready explanation for Gibbon’s attitudes, and doesn’t try to force one. Instead, she broadens her inquiry to explore the inner life of a man who repeatedly broke with convention—the “conversions” of her title—only to scramble back to safer ground. A lonely misfit emerges from her book, confident in his abilities but wounded in his soul, who escapes into a world of words as the only place where he can exercise complete control. Saxton is hardly protective of her subject, but she also has no patience for the cruelty of men like Boswell, whose remarks about Gibbon give her “much sympathy for the tiny, affected, brilliant, scarred man.” [ From the January 1878 issue: William Dean Howells on Edward Gibbon ] Gibbon was born in South London in 1737 to a family of wealth and property. Though sickly himself, he was the only one of seven children to survive infancy. His unloving mother died when he was 10. His difficult father was a stern traditionalist who kept a tight hold on money and behavior. Young Edward was sent away for schooling. The most significant event from Gibbon’s brief time at Oxford was his rebellious embrace of Catholicism—not a route to advancement in 18th-century Britain. He was sent to stay with a Calvinist pastor and his family in Lausanne, Switzerland. The prospect of disinheritance proved to be a potent theology. As Gibbon later wrote, “The various articles of the Romish creed disappeared like a dream.” But the five years spent in Lausanne also made him a French-speaking child of the Enlightenment, with continental manners and republican values. He took inspiration from the Swiss fight for democracy—a movement, he once wrote, from which “the dullest stranger would catch fire.” He acquired habits of reading and study that he never relinquished. Lausanne was also where he met an intellectually intrepid young woman named Suzanne Curchod and embarked on the one romantic adventure of his life. But his father refused to bless their engagement—Suzanne had no wealth and no desire to live in England—and Gibbon broke it off. “I sighed as a lover,” he recalled years later. “I obeyed as a son.” In fact, he did more than obey. Returning home, he made a kind of peace with his father, slipped into a caricature of Englishness, and adopted the macho swagger of his class. By way of reward, he was eventually permitted to embark on his Grand Tour. In Saxton’s telling, every time Gibbon ventures into the realm of possibility, he finds his way back to a more comfortable and conventional path. After taking a seat in Parliament—a chamber then being roused by the voices of Edmund Burke and Charles James Fox—he sat silently for years, forgoing even the formality of a maiden speech. In his votes, the youthful idealist who had applauded the republican virtues of Switzerland opposed American independence and supported the pro-war policies of Lord North and King George III, though with more detachment than passion. The main interest he showed in Britain’s corrupt society—the rotten boroughs, the pervasive grift—was how to secure a comfortable place in it. He set himself up handsomely in London, hiring servants, dining at Boodle’s, consorting with blue bloods. The single conviction to which Gibbon held true all his life was that he should write. The world he conjured with his pen was a world where he felt assured and free, and he seems to have recognized this early. In his memoir, Gibbon recalled a teenage ambition to embark on a historical study, subject matter unclear: “Unprovided with original learning, unformed in the habits of thinking, unskilled in the arts of composition, I resolved to write a book.” He pursued this ambition in fits and starts until, one night during that visit to Rome in 1764, he found the inspiration for his life’s work. [ Read: The brain of a man who is always thinking about ancient Rome ] Gibbon’s description of the moment is famous. In his embellished recollection, the idea for the Decline and Fall sprang to mind “as I sat musing amidst the ruins of the Capitol, while the barefooted friars were singing vespers in the temple of Jupiter.” He did not start writing seriously until 1771, a year after his father died and he at last came into his inheritance. He was 34 years old, and more than half his life was gone. With remarkable speed, he produced six volumes. The first three covered the period from the peak of the Pax Romana, in the first and second centuries C.E.—“the period in the history of the world, during which the condition of the human race was most happy and prosperous”—through the collapse of the Western empire, in the fifth century. The last three volumes, at a gallop, covered the next millennium, up to the fall of Constantinople. The original full set weighed 30 pounds. Within the walls of his study on Bentinck Street, in London, Gibbon was an omnipotent ruler, dispatching emperors, summoning invaders, hurling judgments. He looks beneath and beyond the golden age to depict a Roman world of violence, injustice, excess, and caprice. Gibbon’s wit, stentorian but sly, is allowed to unfold slowly. Of one emperor, he wrote, “Twenty-two acknowledged concubines, and a library of sixty-two thousand volumes, attested the variety of his inclinations, and from the productions he left behind him, it appears that the former as well as the latter were designed for use rather than ostentation.” Gibbon pioneered the use of footnotes, which he deployed by the thousands to raise a hackle, settle a score, or supply a punch line. Volume I of the Decline and Fall , published in 1776, sold out quickly. As more volumes appeared, Gibbon’s celebrity grew. He was corpulent now, the target of jokes about his own immoderate greatness. But Gibbon labored on, coming to “the last lines of the last page” with, he recalled, a sense of satisfaction: When he finally laid down his pen and strolled the grounds of his home, “all Nature was silent.” Martha Saxton died in 2023, her book not yet finished. Her daughter, Josephine Saxton Ferorelli, describes in a foreword her mother’s career and her deepening interest in Gibbon’s tortured character—a man who could neither open his heart nor look into it. In an afterword, Saxton’s friend, the critic Judith Thurman, who edited the book, outlines some of the themes that Saxton never fully addressed. Saxton is a superb writer, and the 200 or so pages that she completed have an essayistic flavor. She tells stories and thinks aloud. But the biography stops abruptly with an account of Gibbon’s death. It’s missing some of the critical reflections on the Decline and Fall —including its relevance to the world today—that Saxton had been saving for the end. [ Listen: The David Frum Show with Mary Beard on why America isn’t Rome ] The fact that Saxton’s book is unfinished gives it a haunting dimension. What would have come next? We have some clues. Many passages in The Conversions of Edward Gibbon point to big questions on her mind, if not always to what her answers would be. As Thurman explains, Saxton also left behind working notes for the final part of the book. In so many ways, Saxton’s biography is built around tensions: between finished and unfinished; between Gibbon the man and Gibbon the historian; between past and present. A question that Saxton raises more than once has to do with values. “Gibbon apparently didn’t see a contradiction, or at least feel a moral scruple, in revering and serving the British Empire while loathing the Roman one,” Saxton writes. “He decried Roman corruption, but he wasn’t interested in reforming his own corrupt government.” He was not blind to the parallels. “When we want to paint the most distant centuries,” he wrote to Suzanne Curchod after Volume I was published, “we end up drawing them, without realizing it, based on the models we have in front of our eyes.” Was he nothing more than a hypocrite? Saxton resists a simple verdict. In his writing, he is unsparing about human nature; in his life, he is desperate for acceptance. It’s a discordant but not uncommon coupling—like one of Gibbon’s harnessed pairs. A larger question involves Gibbon’s legacy. In the closing lines of the last volume, Gibbon underscored the grim majesty of his subject matter. The destruction of the Roman empire, he wrote, had been “the greatest, perhaps, and most awful scene in the history of mankind.” The Decline and Fall has been holding up a mirror ever since, inviting readers to see their own world in an ancient one. Historians and critics, along with the architects of America’s imperium, have wrestled with Gibbon for a quarter of a millennium. Does Rome’s fate offer useful guidance? Can it prompt reforms and prevent mistakes? Are all empires doomed? Gibbon himself was both wistful about the Roman empire’s impermanence and clear-eyed about its often monstrous nature. Wistfulness, filtered through the gauzy lens of the Romantics, continues to color popular attitudes; the sight of a broken column beneath the umbrella pines may still elicit a sigh. But it can be a good thing when empires die, and it was definitely a good thing that this one did. None of us would want to live in the imperial-Roman world—a world based on slavery and steeped in terror, with no concept of human equality or true democracy. Gibbon died in 1794, perhaps the result of an infection after surgery to relieve his hydrocele. He hadn’t had much to say about what the future might hold, but he’d been fatalistic about the ills that bring down empires—they were “natural and inevitable.” He had seen Britain lose its American colonies, though he harbored no animus toward the Americans themselves and even thought they might one day come in handy. [ From the April 2021 issue: No, really, are we Rome? ] At one point in the Decline and Fall , Gibbon steps back—poking his head out from the page as he sometimes would—and reflects on the cultured and wealthy Europe that had emerged after centuries of darkness. He admires what he sees: “our general state of happiness, the system of arts, and laws, and manners.” Would barbarism ever return? Yes, some “savage conqueror” might one day ride forth from “the deserts of Tartary.” The foe would of course be met by “the numerous armies of Germany, the gallant nobles of France, and the intrepid freemen of Britain.” These groups might even “confederate for their common defence.” But despite best efforts, he concedes, the challenge could prove too great. Gibbon does not worry. Driven back to the beaches, the plucky remnant of defenders would have one more chance: They could board “ten thousand vessels” for the beckoning New World across the ocean, where Europeans had already begun to live. Freedom, justice, progress—they would surely be safe in America. This article appears in the January 2027 print edition with the headline “He Thought About Rome Every Day.”

items.title: Burkina : Le ministre Dingara se fait enrôler pour l’Identifiant unique électronique et invite ses services à suivre l’exemple
items.description: Le ministre de l'Enseignement de base, de l'Alphabétisation et de la Promotion des langues nationales (MEBA-PLN), Jacques Sosthène Dingara, a donné l'exemple le lundi 23 novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou, en se soumettant à l'enrôlement pour l'obtention de l'Identifiant unique électronique. Par ce geste, il a traduit son engagement en faveur de la mise en œuvre de ce dispositif de modernisation de l'administration publique et invité les travailleurs de son département à s'approprier le processus lorsque les agents chargés de sa mise en œuvre seront déployés sur le terrain. Le ministre de l'Enseignement de base, de l'Alphabétisation et de la Promotion des langues nationales (MEBA-PLN), Jacques Sosthène Dingara, à son Identifiant unique électronique. L'opération d'enrôlement du MEBA-PLN, Jacques Sosthène Dingara, s'est déroulée en plusieurs étapes. Le ministre Jacques Sosthène Dingara a reçu son récépissé qui devra servir au retrait du de son identifiant unique électronique Après la collecte des empreintes digitales des quatre doigts de chaque main et des deux pouces, les agents ont procédé à la capture de l'iris et à la prise de photographie. Une copie de la pièce d'identité fournie par le ministre Dingara a également été archivée dans le système. À la fin du processus, Jacques Sosthène Dingara a été invité à vérifier les informations collectées avant la délivrance de son accusé de réception, servant de justificatif pour le retrait ultérieur de sa carte. Au-delà de l'identification des citoyens, cette initiative présente un intérêt particulier pour le secteur éducatif, selon Jacques Sosthène Dingara. De ses dires, le département en charge de l'enseignement de base entend notamment s'appuyer sur cet identifiant pour renforcer le suivi du parcours scolaire des apprenants et améliorer la gestion des données éducatives. « Nous avons le fichier national des élèves qui était un fichier alphanumérique. Aujourd'hui, le département en charge de l'enseignement de base et le département en charge de la transition digitale travaillent à mettre en cohérence ces deux projets », a expliqué le ministre Dingara. Selon lui, l'ambition est de mettre en place un identifiant unique qui accompagnera chaque élève tout au long de son parcours scolaire, du cours préparatoire première année (CP1) jusqu'à l'Université. Ce dispositif devrait notamment faciliter le suivi des apprenants lors de leurs déplacements d'une localité à une autre, particulièrement pendant les périodes d'examens. Le ministre de l'enseignement de base a estimé que cette base de données constituera un outil essentiel pour une meilleure planification des politiques publiques, notamment dans le domaine de l'éducation. Il a ainsi invité les acteurs du système éducatif à se mobiliser pour participer à cette opération d'enrôlement sur l'ensemble du territoire national. « C'est une base qui va beaucoup nous être utile puisque nous allons partir de cet identifiant pour renseigner le fichier national des élèves », a souligné le patron de l'éducation de base, appelant ses collaborateurs et les acteurs de terrain à se faire enrôler afin de contribuer à la constitution de cette base nationale. Le Président du Faso, Chef de l'État, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, avait lui-même été le premier à se faire enrôler. À travers cette initiative, les autorités entendent renforcer la fiabilité des données administratives et éducatives, tout en facilitant la planification et le pilotage des politiques publiques au Burkina Faso. Jean-François SOMÉ Minute.bf

items.title: SAFER Sudan Gender-Responsive Integrated Market, Livelihoods,and Labour Assessment - June 2026
items.description: Country: Sudan Source: CARE Please refer to the attached files. Executive Summary Introduction and Background CARE International (CI) operates through its Members, Candidates, and Affiliates in more than 100 countries, delivering lifesaving humanitarian assistance and long-term development support. With over 75 years of experience, CARE works to address the structural causes of poverty and inequality through a commitment to social justice, gender equality, diversity, and inclusion. The SAFER Sudan action ('Strengthening Access to Protection, Foster Care, Economic Resilience, and Reintegration') is a 48-month intervention implemented under the leadership of CARE Nederland as the Lead Applicant, in partnership with Plan International (UK), Danish Red Cross, Sudanese Red Crescent, Talawiet Organization for Development, and Child Development Foundation. The programme is implemented across six target states: Khartoum, South Darfur, South Kordofan, Red Sea, Gedaref, and Kassala, under the European Union's NDICI–Global Europe framework. The programme adopts an integrated, multi-sectoral approach that connects protection services, family-based alternative care, child protection systems, livelihoods and economic resilience interventions, and structured pathways for social reintegration. This integrated design strengthens both immediate protection outcomes and longer-term recovery and resilience capacities within affected communities. The action is aligned with European Union priorities under the NDICI–Global Europe framework, particularly in relation to human development, social inclusion, and resilience strengthening in fragile and conflict-affected settings. Programme Outcomes and Objectives : The SAFER Sudan programme has two main outcomes: • Outcome 1: Increased access to safe, gender-sensitive, and age-appropriate protection services for vulnerable populations, including women, children, youth, persons with disabilities, IDPs, and survivors of gender-based violence. • Outcome 2: Improved livelihood opportunities, with a particular focus on the equal and meaningful inclusion of the most vulnerable groups, enabling them to restore income, reduce reliance on negative coping strategies and strengthen resilience and social reintegration. The overall objective of SAFER Sudan is to provide protection and socio-economic reintegration to at-risk groups in displacement-affected communities, through a deliberate and integrated approach that links protection outcomes with sustainable economic recovery pathways.

items.title: 21ᵉ édition de la Semaine du Numérique : Le Premier ministre appelle à une transformation digitale souveraine et inclusive
items.description: Le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean-Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a procédé, ce 24 novembre 2026 au lancement officiel de la 21ᵉ édition de la Semaine du Numérique. Prévue jusqu'au 27 novembre 2026 au Salon international de l'artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO), cette rencontre se tient autour du thème : « Souveraineté technologique : accélérer la transformation digitale sécurisée et inclusive ». Cette édition traduit la volonté du Burkina Faso de faire du numérique un levier stratégique d'indépendance, de modernisation administrative et de développement économique. Elle offre un cadre privilégié d'échanges d'expériences et de présentation d'innovations, axé sur la maîtrise des infrastructures, des données, des compétences et des choix technologiques nationaux. Selon Rimtalba Jean-Emmanuel Ouédraogo, la simple dématérialisation ne suffit pas. Les procédures doivent être repensées en amont afin de supprimer les étapes superflues, de réduire les délais et de limiter les déplacements des usagers. Le bilan de l'année 2025 fait état de 146 plateformes opérationnelles sur les 272 initiées depuis les Assises nationales sur le numérique de 2023, ainsi que de 3 114 infrastructures publiques interconnectées et de 69 nouvelles solutions développées ou en chantier. Pour le chef du gouvernement, l'objectif est d'harmoniser ces outils, notamment par la mise en place d'un identifiant unique afin d'éviter aux citoyens de fournir plusieurs fois les mêmes pièces justificatives. Cette dynamique vise également à créer de nouvelles opportunités pour les entreprises et des emplois pour la jeunesse. Le Burkina Faso veut maîtriser ses infrastructures, ses données et ses compétences -©Faso7 « Les réseaux et les plateformes soutiennent désormais nos services publics et notre économie. Une panne, une attaque ou la perte de données peut perturber le pays. Nous devons être capables de prévenir ces risques, de rétablir nos services et de décider par nous-mêmes. Cette exigence concerne les systèmes de l'administration tout comme les outils dont dépendent nos entreprises et les citoyens » , a-t-il déclaré. Prenant la parole au nom des ministres en charge du numérique de la Confédération de l'Alliance des États du Sahel, le ministre chargé du numérique du Mali, Alhamdou Ag Ilyène, a salué cette initiative. Pour lui, la souveraineté des États se joue désormais aussi dans les centres de données, les réseaux et les compétences de la jeunesse, loin d'être un simple slogan. « Le chemin reste long, certes, mais un pas important de notre progression, notamment en zone de l'AES, a été franchi en matière de numérique. C'est pourquoi l'inclusion doit être une exigence de chaque jour, pour chaque citoyen » , s'est-il exprimé. L'objectif est d'harmoniser ces outils, notamment par la mise en place d'un identifiant unique afin d'éviter aux citoyens de fournir plusieurs fois les mêmes pièces justificatives -©Faso7 L'événement est placé sous le co-parrainage du ministre d'État chargé de l'Administration territoriale et de la ministre chargée de la Solidarité. S'exprimant au nom des parrains, la ministre chargée de la Famille et de la Solidarité, le Lieutenant-colonel Passowendé Pélagie Kaboré, a rappelé que cette initiative vise à renforcer l'autonomie décisionnelle de l'État et à améliorer la qualité du service public. Selon elle, la digitalisation rapproche l'administration des usagers, mais impose en retour le devoir impérieux de garantir la sécurité et la confidentialité des données personnelles. « Pour la solidarité nationale, le numérique permet d'envisager une meilleure digitalisation des mécanismes d'aide, un ciblage plus précis des interventions et un suivi rigoureux des appuis destinés aux bénéficiaires » , a-t-elle souligné. Au programme de cette 21ᵉ édition figurent plusieurs espaces de réflexion et d'innovation, notamment les Conf'Days, le Village des start-up, des démonstrations de robots humanoïdes et quadrupèdes, ainsi que la compétition de robotique « RoboKids » . Lazard KOLA Faso7 L’article 21ᵉ édition de la Semaine du Numérique : Le Premier ministre appelle à une transformation digitale souveraine et inclusive est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Hours-long road closures around Karachi’s PIDC junction cause traffic congestion
items.description: KARACHI: Commuters in Karachi’s Saddar area faced traffic congestion on Tuesday after authorities closed some roads around the PIDC junction for a few hours in response to a sit-in call by the Sindh Indus Lawyers Forum (SILF). In an alert issued at 1:16pm, Karachi Traffic Police said both roads from PIDC Chowk towards the State Life Building, as well as Dr Ziauddin Ahmed Road, were closed to traffic. In an update at around 6pm, the traffic police said the cut from PIDC Chowk towards State Life Building and both sides of Dr Ziauddin Ahmed Road have been reopened to commuters. As an alternative route, traffic was previously being diverted from PIDC Chowk towards Club Road and from the State Life Building towards Beaumont Road. This screengrab from Google Maps shows traffic near the PIDC junction at around 4:30pm on Nov 24, 2026. According to a statement issued by SILF, lawyers staged a sit-in outside the Sindh High Court. They also staged a rally from Shahrah-i-Liaquat towards CM House through Court Road, Sindh Secretariat Chowk, Sindh Assembly and Aiwan-i-Sadr Road. The forum has put forward 16 demands under the banner of ‘Sindh Demands’, including opposition to the division of Sindh and the construction of Jalalpur Canal. The protest call comes as a debate over a “system reset” in the country has intensified over the past few months. In July, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi stirred a political storm by calling for the creation of new administrative units , arguing that the current system of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”. The PML-N-led federal government has insisted on holding a referendum across the country on the establishment of new provinces or administrative units. However, the suggestion has faced severe backlash from its ally PPP, with party chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari saying that any “forced” attempt to divide provinces, particularly Sindh, could lead to bloodshed. SILF said its demands also include “opposition to constitutional amendments and the proposed amendment”, apparently referring to the 26th and 27th Amendments, though no new amendment has been officially proposed. Moreover, SILF’s demands, according to its statement, include stopping alleged irregularities in the Sindh Public Service Commission and alleged government intervention in lawyers’ bars . “Corporate farming and mining in Karoonjhar mountain should be stopped and political prisoners should be released,” SILF further said. On Sunday, a large number of people from across Sindh took to the streets of Karachi in a rally organised by the Jeay Sindh Rahbar Committee, an alliance of four nationalist parties, to protest against any plan for the creation of new provinces or administrative units in Sindh.

items.title: World Vision Launches ADH-funded Programme to Address Learning Gaps and Strengthen Child Well-being Across Eight Schools in Ukraine
items.description: Country: Ukraine Source: World Vision KYIV, 23 November – Among the children surveyed in a World Vision assessment , 90% attend school regularly and 97% have progressed to the next grade. Yet only 28% say they understand their lessons well, while 57% say some lessons are hard and 6% say most lessons are very hard. World Vision and its local partner SpivDiia are responding with a 14-month programme funded by Aktion Deutschland Hilft e.V. The programme combines catch-up classes, psychosocial support and measures to strengthen school resilience. It will reach 5,465 children across eight schools in Dnipropetrovsk and Mykolaiv oblasts, while also contributing to stronger national systems for child protection. “We surveyed 558 children and assessed 19 schools. What we found is that attendance does not necessarily translate into learning. Air raid alerts repeatedly force children to switch between classroom-based, blended and remote learning, disrupting their education and widening learning gaps. They need structured catch-up classes to recover what they have missed,” said Arman Grigoryan, World Vision Ukraine Crisis Response Director. “But catching up academically is only part of the challenge. Almost half of the children we surveyed live with fear caused by bombing or shelling near their homes. It is very difficult to learn when you do not feel safe. Teachers remain children’s most trusted source of safety, yet they are under sustained strain, experiencing high levels of burnout and exhaustion. That is why this programme supports teachers and caregivers as well as children,” Grigoryan added. Children aged 6-17 will participate in small-group catch-up classes in Ukrainian, mathematics and English, alongside history and primary-level subjects where needed, with integrated Social-Emotional Learning activities. Adolescents aged 12-18 will benefit from First Aid Arts, an eight-session programme that uses art, movement, music and breathing techniques to strengthen resilience and emotional regulation. Individual counselling will be provided to 300 children and 140 caregivers, while teachers and facilitators will be trained to identify children who need additional help and refer them to specialised services. Support will extend beyond the classroom, with 600 caregivers and 200 teachers receiving training to better address children's learning and emotional needs. Teachers and psychologists will also share approaches to catch-up education and exchange experience to improve the support they provide. To ensure that learning can continue despite power cuts and other emergencies, the programme will strengthen the resilience of eight schools through energy assessments and the provision of backup equipment, including portable charging stations, laptops and printers. The programme will also seek to extend access to education and strengthen child protection beyond the eight participating schools. In partnership with the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine , the initiative will fund the development of online Ukrainian Language and Reading courses for primary school pupils, hosted on the national All-Ukrainian School Online platform. At the national level, World Vision will work with the National Social Service of Ukraine (NSSU) to conduct policy-oriented research identifying gaps, barriers and opportunities in interagency coordination, children's rights protection, family-based care and cross-border child protection. The findings will inform practical recommendations and tools, while training for the NSSU's central and regional staff will support their implementation and help strengthen coordination across child protection services. “The research will provide an evidence base on challenges in interagency coordination among child protection services, education authorities, and other stakeholders, particularly in relation to identifying children living in difficult life circumstances, detecting cases of non-enrolment or interruption of education, information sharing, and ensuring timely responses to violations of children's rights,” said Viktor Zelenyy, Director of the Department of State Control of Children's Rights Compliance at the NSSU. “This will support us in improving the legal and regulatory framework and related procedures, developing methodological guidance and training materials for practitioners, and strengthening international cooperation on cross-border child protection,” he added. The project runs from 1 September 2026 to 31 October 2027. ENDS Notes to Editor: About World Vision Ukraine Crisis Response : World Vision Ukraine Crisis Response has supported children and families affected by the war since March 2022, reaching more than 2.4 million people, including over 1 million children, through programmes focused on education, child protection, mental health and psychosocial support, livelihoods, cash assistance, winterisation and basic needs. For further information, please contact: Laurentia Jora | World Vision Ukraine Crisis Response Advocacy & Communications Manager | Email: laurentia_jora@wvi.org

items.title: le Premier ministre mise sur la transparence et l’intégrité pour renforcer la compétitivité du Sénégal
items.description: À l’ouverture du premier Forum du Maritime Anti-Corruption Network (MACN), consacré à l’efficacité et à l’intégrité dans les ports sénégalais, le Premier ministre Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed LO a appelé à une transformation profonde de la gouvernance portuaire. Digitalisation, harmonisation des procédures et renforcement des mécanismes de contrôle figurent parmi les principaux leviers identifiés pour faire du Sénégal un hub logistique de référence en Afrique de l’Ouest. La modernisation du secteur portuaire sénégalais ne saurait se limiter aux investissements dans les infrastructures. Elle doit également s’accompagner d’une gouvernance fondée sur la transparence, l’intégrité et l’efficacité opérationnelle. C’est le message porté par le Premier ministre à l’ouverture du premier Forum du Maritime Anti-Corruption Network (MACN), consacré à l’efficacité et à l’intégrité dans les ports au Sénégal. Présidant cette rencontre, le chef du Gouvernement a réaffirmé l’ambition du Sénégal de consolider sa position de plateforme logistique et commerciale en Afrique de l’Ouest. Une orientation qui s’inscrit, selon lui, dans la vision de l’Agenda national de Transformation portée par le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye. À cet effet, Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed LO a rappelé que le Programme d’Optimisation logistique et de Modernisation portuaire vise à renforcer l’efficacité de la chaîne logistique, à travers la modernisation des infrastructures, l’automatisation des processus et le développement de zones logistiques intégrées. L’extension du réseau portuaire, avec la mise en service prochaine des ports de Sendou et de Ndayane, participe de cette ambition. Toutefois, le Premier ministre estime que les infrastructures, à elles seules, ne suffisent pas à garantir la compétitivité. « La compétitivité d'un port ne se mesure pas uniquement à la profondeur de ses quais, à la capacité de ses terminaux ou au volume des marchandises qu'il peut accueillir », a-t-il souligné. Elle s’apprécie davantage, selon lui, « à travers la qualité de ses services, la célérité de ses opérations, la prévisibilité de ses procédures et la confiance inspirée aux opérateurs économiques ». Trois chantiers pour transformer la gouvernance portuaire Pour concrétiser cette ambition, le chef du Gouvernement a identifié trois axes prioritaires. Le premier porte sur la standardisation et l’harmonisation des procédures portuaires. Celles-ci doivent être « documentées et accessibles à l'ensemble des usagers » afin de réduire les marges d’interprétation, de limiter les pratiques abusives et de garantir un traitement équitable des opérateurs économiques. Le deuxième chantier concerne la digitalisation et la transparence des opérations. Le Premier ministre préconise notamment la dématérialisation et l’automatisation des formalités portuaires et douanières, ainsi que l’interconnexion des systèmes d’information. Une démarche qui doit permettre d’améliorer la traçabilité des interventions, de faciliter le signalement des incidents et de renforcer le traitement des réclamations. Enfin, le troisième axe concerne le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination, de contrôle et de redevabilité. Pour le chef du Gouvernement, la performance portuaire est « une responsabilité partagée » qui nécessite l’implication de l’ensemble des acteurs, des administrations publiques aux opérateurs privés, en passant par les autorités portuaires et les services de sécurité. Dans cette dynamique, l’expérience nigériane, présentée au cours des travaux, devrait nourrir les réflexions. Le Premier ministre a toutefois tenu à préciser qu’il ne s’agissait pas de reproduire un modèle étranger, mais plutôt de « s’inspirer des meilleures expériences internationales afin de construire un dispositif national adapté à notre contexte et aligné sur nos orientations stratégiques ». Ndayane, futur modèle de gouvernance portuaire Au-delà des réformes générales, le chef du Gouvernement a particulièrement attiré l’attention sur le futur port de Ndayane. Il souhaite que cette infrastructure devienne une référence en matière de gouvernance portuaire. « Il ne s’agit pas seulement d’une infrastructure de dimension internationale, mais surtout d’un nouveau modèle de gouvernance portuaire, fondé sur la digitalisation, la fluidité des opérations, la transparence des procédures et la responsabilité des différents intervenants », a-t-il déclaré. Pour atteindre ces objectifs, le Premier ministre a insisté sur la nécessité d’une mobilisation collective. Il a ainsi encouragé les participants à faire du forum « un véritable espace de dialogue franc, constructif et orienté vers des solutions concrètes ». Il les a également invités à s’accorder sur des engagements précis, assortis de responsabilités clairement définies et d’un calendrier de mise en œuvre. L’adoption d’une déclaration d’engagement, l’élaboration d’une feuille de route et la mise en place d’un comité national de suivi constituent les premiers jalons proposés. En conclusion, le chef du Gouvernement a rappelé que l’intégrité ne devait pas être considérée comme une simple contrainte pour les acteurs du secteur. « Elle est une condition de confiance mutuelle, un facteur d’équité, un élément de mesure de la compétitivité et un instrument de protection des intérêts économiques de la Nation », a-t-il affirmé. A. N

items.title: Cameroun : Anne Féconde Noah, le charme du PCRN dans le Mfoundi
items.description: © DR Candidate déclarée du Parti camerounais pour la réconciliation nationale (Pcrn) dans le Mfoundi, Anne Féconde Noah va à la conquête d’un espace politique longtemps resté la chasse gardée du parti au pouvoir, le RDPC. Le Parti camerounais pour la réconciliation nationale va à la conquête des électeurs dans le Mfoundi avec comme atout charme, Anne Féconde Noah, candidate à la députation dans le département du Mfoundi couvrant la ville de Yaoundé. La vice-présidente du PCRN est au cœur de la compétition électorale dans une zone presque déjà acquise au Rassemblement démocratique du peuple camerounais. Le parti au pouvoir a raflé les sept députés du Mfoundi à l’issue des élections législatives du 09 février 2020. Ils ont exercé la mandature qui s’achève avec l’ambition pour le parti de rééditer l’exploit en 2027. Le PCRN s’engage à faire barrage à une nouvelle élection des candidats du Rdpc aux prochaines législatives. Le parti a choisi l’une des femmes les plus influentes parmi ses militants pour faire d’elle la tête de liste de ses candidats à la députation. Porte-parole du président Cabral Libii, Anne Féconde Noah se fait entendre depuis des années pour défendre la cause des populations qui n’ont point de voix. A travers son initiative « Je veux ma CNI » lancée en 2021, elle a pu gagner la sympathie de nombreux Camerounais indignés par la non-délivrance et le retard de plusieurs années dans délivrance de leurs CNI. En plaidant pour cette cause commune, la juriste d’affaires âgée de 42 ans, s’est montrée disponible à œuvrer pour résoudre les problèmes de la société. Directrice de campagne du candidat Cabral Libii lors de la présidentielle 2025, Anne Féconde Noah Biloa a tenu d’autres postes de responsabilités hors du cercle politique du PCRN, en dirigeant le cabinet Compétences SAS et en étant directrice de publication du journal Capitale Info. Son expérience et son engagement la poussent aujourd’hui à vouloir embrasser la responsabilité de député de la nation. Elle fait réagir de nombreuses personnalités politiques en particulier des femmes qui lui témoignent leur soutien. Sa camarade et militante du même parti, la députée Rolande Adèle Ngo Issi Mbock reconnait en elle « une femme de poigne » qui « n’a jamais transigé avec ses valeurs et les combats qu’elle mène ». Elle reconnait aussi en la candidate, celle qui œuvre pour l’intérêt général et non pour sa satisfaction personnelle. Certains citoyens lui reconnaissent des qualités de dynamisme, de patriotisme, de foi, ainsi que de constance sans oublier sa jeunesse. Cathy Meba, cadre du RDPC s’appuie sur le talent pour promouvoir Anne Féconde Noah. Pour elle, la candidate se caractérise par « la sincérité, la conviction, l’engagement ». Aussi, « même si nous ne sommes pas du même bord politique, je soutiens la femme que tu es, parce que je reconnais ton talent et ta valeur. » a-t-elle adressé à la candidate à la candidature du PCRN en attendant la validation de son dossier par le Conseil électoral. Cet article Cameroun : Anne Féconde Noah, le charme du PCRN dans le Mfoundi est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: UN Special Envoy for Yemen concludes visit to Kuwait | United Nations Peace Operations
items.description: Country: Yemen Source: UN Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen Amman, 24 November 2026 - The United Nations Special Envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, concluded a visit to Kuwait, where he met with Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah. Discussions focused on recent political and military developments in Yemen, the implications of renewed hostilities for Yemen and the wider region, and ongoing diplomatic efforts. Grundberg underscored the importance of sustained regional and international coordination in responding to the evolving situation and its political, security and economic ramifications, particularly in light of the growing pressures on the Yemeni population. The Special Envoy expressed his appreciation for Kuwait’s sustained commitment to peace in Yemen and its support for the Yemeni people, building on a longstanding engagement in UN-led peace efforts. During his visit, Grundberg also delivered an address at the Saud N. Al-Sabah Kuwait Diplomatic Institute to an audience of Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry officials, members of the international diplomatic community and international relations students. The address was followed by an exchange on developments in Yemen, the complexities of mediation in the current regional context and the role of diplomacy in conflict resolution.

items.title: Nominations au ministère de la Culture : trois hommes, la dynamique se poursuit et l’équipe se renforce
items.description: Par décrets du Président Mamadi Doumbouya, 41 cadres dont trois figures bien connues du paysage culturel et médiatique guinéen bénéficient de la confiance du chef de l’Etat au Ministère de la Culture, du Tourisme et de l’Artisanat (MCTA). Macka Traoré, Ahmadou Oury Bah « Hamza » et Ali Bongo Leno. Trois profils complémentaires, une même mission: donner corps à la politique culturelle impulsée sous le créneau du programme Simandou 2040. Macka Traoré, un nouveau challenge dans la confiance renouvelée Pour Macka Traoré, nommé Directeur National de la Culture, il ne s'agit pas d'une découverte, mais d'un nouveau challenge dans la confiance renouvelée. Homme du sérail, il connaît les arcanes du département pour avoir occupé jusque-là le poste de DGA des industries culturelles et créatives. Connu pour ses œuvres et son déploiement au service l’épanouissement du secteur culturel, sa nomination à la tête de la Direction Nationale de la Culture sonne comme une reconnaissance de son travail, de sa constance et de sa loyauté. Autour du Ministre Moussa Moïse Sylla, il aura la lourde tâche de piloter, coordonner et impulser la politique culturelle nationale. Un poste stratégique où il devra transformer les ambitions en actions concrètes, sur tout le territoire. Ahmadou Oury Bah « Hamza », l'homme de terrain et d'expérience C'est la nomination qui a surpris, puis séduit. Ahmadou Oury Bah « Hamza », nouveau Directeur Général Adjoint des Infrastructures et Équipements Culturels et Artisanaux, quitte la presse privée pour intégrer nouvellement la sphère de l'administration publique. Un journaliste aguerri, un reporter pétri d'expérience qui a tutoyé les événements marquants de son pays. Un homme de terrain, engagé pour la promotion des valeurs culturelles de son pays. Il arrive pour apporter son expérience professionnelle, sa connaissance du terrain et son riche carnet d'adresses à l'équipe du Ministre Moussa Moïse Sylla. À ce service qui n'en demande que ça pour mieux répondre aux nombreuses attentes du secteur. Infrastructures à construire, équipements à moderniser, artisanat à valoriser, il connaît les besoins parce qu'il les a racontés pendant des années avec sa son micro et sa plume. Ali Bongo Leno, l'expertise du management culturel à portée Comme Hamza, Ali Bongo Leno est lui aussi un transfuge de la presse privée qui intègre nouvellement l'administration publique de la culture en Guinée. Nommé Directeur Général Adjoint des Industries Culturelles et Créatives, il arrive avec l’expertise du management culturel à portée de main. Connaisseur fin du milieu artistique, des acteurs culturels et des mécanismes de production et de diffusion, il incarne cette passerelle tant attendue entre la création et l'économie. Dans un secteur où le talent guinéen est immense mais encore sous-exploité, son rôle sera décisif: aider à structurer, professionnaliser et rendre viables les industries culturelles et créatives. Avec lui, la culture guinéenne ne sera plus seulement à célébrer, mais aussi à rentabiliser, au profit des artistes et du pays. Avec ces trois nominations parmi tant d’autres, c’est trois profils pour une même dynamique. Désormais, le Ministère dirigé par Moussa Moïse Sylla se renforce davantage et se dote sans aucun doute d'une équipe à la fois expérimentée, créative et enracinée dans le réel. La fougue, le professionnalisme et la connaissance du terrain sont désormais au service de la vision du Président Mamadi Doumbouya. Le chantier est immense, mais l'équipe est bien en place pour faire le job. Bernard Leno L’article Nominations au ministère de la Culture : trois hommes, la dynamique se poursuit et l’équipe se renforce est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Pakistani Prisoners Face Poor Access to Health Care
items.description: Click to expand Image People exit the main entrance of the Karachi Central Prison in Karachi, Pakistan, January 28, 2021. © 2021 AP Photo/Fareed Khan When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system. Human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care. Many inmates who fall ill in custody fail to receive prompt or decent care at all. After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers. Colonial-era laws have long-enabled Pakistani officials and powerful people to interfere in prison operations, sometimes making use of poor conditions to harass jailed political opponents. In a November 16 letter released by his lawyer, former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed for urgent medical care for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, citing his high blood pressure and her need for eye surgery. Khan’s appeal echoes complaints about medical care in custody from former President Asif Ali Zardari and former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. All have alleged that prison services denied access to medical care as a form of punishment. Federal and provincial governments in Pakistan should bring health care in jails and prisons in line with international standards, notably the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Mandela Rules), which require that prisoners receive necessary free medical care to the same standard available in the community, with prompt attention in emergencies. In October, Justice Project Pakistan called for common standards across provinces so prisoners can see medical specialists when needed and continue treatment after release. Pakistan’s federal and provincial governments should provide prescribed medicines free of charge and require prisons to record how long patients wait for care. When care requires an urgent hospital transfer, prison authorities should promptly facilitate transport. Authorities should ensure all prisoners, regardless of political affiliation or status, receive timely and adequate medical care, with continuity of treatment.
